MOB HANGS FOR KILLING Negro Seizes the Jailor Intending to Escape. TWO WHITE YOUTHS AID Sheriff Is Made Prisoner and His Hands Tied. CROWD DECIDES TO LYNCH Fire Company Refuses to Help Disperse the Mob.
Hattiesburg, Miss., Aug. —A negro, Amos Jones, was hanged by a mob here tonight for shooting and mortally wounding Jailer M. M. Sexton. Jones and another negro, named McElroy, who were prisoners, seized Sexton, intending to break from the jail. McElroy threw Sexton down, and two white youths, also prisoners, held him. The negroes disarmed Sexton and Jones shot him, inflicting three wounds that are said to be fatal. A crowd gathered outside the jail, while a deputy and several others entered and overpowered three of the prisoners. In the confusion McElroy escaped from the jail. The crowd outside decided to lynch Jones. Prominent men urged them to desist and the wounded jailer sent word to leave the man unharmed. The mob later seized Sheriff Batson and tied him. The fire brigade was requested to trun out and help disperse the mob, but refused. The mob then broke into a window of the jail and cut the negro out of his cell with chisels. He was brought out to the crowd of about 500 men and boys, a rope was tied around his neck and he was dragged through the town to Gordon creek bridge, where he was hanged to a telegraph pole and bullets were fired into his body. It is thought he was dead before he was hanged. The sheriff had telegraphed to the governor when the mob first assembled and an order came to the local militia to turn out, but it was too late. While the mob was forming and threatening to lynch the white prisoners also, the sheriff spirited them out of town.

THEY UTTER THREATS.

Valparaiso, Ind., Aug. 8. —John Wilson, a powerful negro, this afternoon attempted to assault Mrs. Hugh F. Bitt, at her home, four miles in the country. She was in the house with her two little children when the negro appeared at the door and asked for matches. When he attacked her the children screamed and the negro ran. Over a hundred neighboring farmers and farmers' hands started in pursuit. The negro jumped a passing freight train and escaped to Warsaw. The telephone had been used and Deputy Sheriff Matthews and William Wilson, a school teacher, were at the depot. The negro drew a knife and attacked Matthews, but was knocked unconscious by a stone thrown by Wilson. He confessed.

Tonight the streets of the town have been filled with angry farmers of Washington township, muttering threats of vengeance, but no attack on the jail is feared.

Col. H. F. Holloway, a leading Texas planter, has furnished to the public what he claims a method of successfully exterminating the Mexican boll weevil. His device consists of a flat pan, with a lamp in the center, elevated just above the surface, and fed by kerosene. He covers the pan's bottom with water, then covers the water with a thin film of kerosene and sets it out in the cotton patch. He has a number of these scattered over the patch and he lights them every night. He catches decidedly more than a bushel of bugs each night. He says there are not enough birds in Texas to do all season the work one lamp does in a single night.

"Calamity Jane," a notorious western character, and wife of the equally notorious "Wild Bill" Hickox, died a few days ago at Terry, S. D. The woman's maiden name was Martha Canary. She was born at Princeton, Mo., and went with her parents to Nevada in 1862. Shortly after their emigration from Princeton, Mo., an Indian war separated child from parents. She fell into the hands of an unworthy old woman, who allowed her to select what she would from the law-free life of the camp. It was horse-back riding and crack pistol shooting that first came to the girl, and not many years after she was to be found astride saloon bars, regaling rough men with songs and stories. It was about that time that real Indian fighting in the West began, and the girl was eager to display the horsemanship and marksmanship which she counted her virtues. She applied at a number of posts, attired as a man, before she found one where she was not known. Gen. Crook accepted her as a scout and she was happy. For a time she served under Col. William F. Cody (Buffalo Bill), and that soldier, her life-long friend, recently said of her record as a scout: "Though she did not do a man's share of the heavy work, she has gone in places where old frontiersmen were unwilling to trust themselves, and her courage and good fellowship made her popular with every man in the command. In her neat scout's uniform, Martha Canary made a handsome picture, especially when astride a good horse and riding like mad over the plains on some wild expedition." Rufe Cantrell, whose confession of the operation of a gang of grave robbers at Indianapolis, Ind, about a year ago, caused a great sensation, has now confessed that his gang even went so far in the traffic of bodies as to commit murder. Several physicians of local prominence were arrested on Cantrell's evidence, and it was proven by examination of graves that hundreds of bodies had been stolen and used in medical colleges in the vicinity of Indianapolis.

Postmaster General Payne has decided to make the experiment of employing baggagemen on trains which are not provided with mail clerks to take charge of and deliver and open newspaper mail. This decision has been reached after much consideration and in response to a petition filed by many of the leading newspaper publishers of the country, who asked the postoffice department to provide facilities for distribution of open bundles of papers along the lines from trains which carry only closed pouches.

A mob at Whitesboro, Tex., got charge of a negro suspected of criminal assault, and, taking him to the woods, placed a rope about his neck and swung him clear of the ground. Just at this stage a posse of officers dashed through the crowd and let the negro down in time to save his life. The mob then visited the section of town inhabited by negroes and cruelly whipped a number of men and warned them to leave the community. The governor and local authorities declare they will exert every effort to punish members of the mob.

The terrible storm which swept over the West Indies last week seems to have wrought the greatest havoc on the Islands of Jamaica and Martinique. At Port Antonio on the north coast of Jamaica, only six houses were left standing. Vessels were blown from their moorings and dashed to pieces at sea, while wharves and store houses were completely demolished. On the island of Jamaica hundreds of lives were lost, and it is said the property loss will exceed ten millions. The storm was equally severe in the eastern and western ends of the island.

Dr. Frankenfield, an attache of the weather bureau at Washington, in a special report on the floods of the Missouri valley which created such havoc recently, places the property loss in excess of $7,000,000. The report, when completed in every detail, will be transmitted to congress. It will include estimates of the cost of the erection of flood gauges at different point along the Missouri and its tributaries and the expense of sending the special information gathered from them to the headquarters of the bureau in Washington. It will be the design to show that if the government had been able to maintain a few river observers along the tributaries and the channel of the Missouri ample warning could have been given to the people so that they could not only have reached places of safety themselves but removed their stock

count of scarcity of cotton.

ExGov. Hubbard of Texas, who is in his ninetieth year, was married a few days ago for the third time. His bride is said to be a young woman.

A fast mail on the M., K. and T. jumped the track twenty miles north of Nevada, Mo., and twenty-one persons were injured in the wreck, but fortunately none fatally.

"The land can not be cleansed of the blood shed upon it save by the blood of him who shed it," quoted Thomas Marcum in closing a most dramatic address to the jury at Cynthiana, Ky., trying Curtis Jett and Thomas White for the assassination of his brother in the court house at Jackson, Ky.

Taft, now governor of the Philippines. The above information is contained in a dispatch from Oyster Bay. Secretary Root will return to his law practice in New York.

American Riflemen Lost by 2 Points. BISLEY, England, July 13.—In the Waldegrave competition, which was won to-day by Major Oxley, with an aggregate of 99 points, the American, G. E. Cook, was third with 97 points. Cook used the Krag-Jorgensen service rifle, while his opponents were armed with the finest match rifles. Anderson and James Will Play.
CHICAGO, July 13.—Entries closed this evening at 6 o'clock for the open golf championship tournament of the Western Golf Association to be held at Milwaukee on Thursday and Friday of this week. The open champion, Willie Anderson, and National amateur champion, Louis James, have both decided to play. There are thirty-eight professional and twenty-two amateur players entered for the tournament.

Cooper in Serious Condition.

DETROIT, July 13.—Tom Cooper, a bicycle rider, was operated on to-day at Grace Hospital for appendicitis. Cooper's trouble is said to have been developed from a strain he sustained on July 4 at Lexington, Ky. The physicians say Cooper is in no immediate danger of dying.

Joe Nelson Won.

PROVIDENCE, R. I., July 13.—The match race between De Guichard and Nelson, twenty miles motor paced for $1,000 a side, was won to-night by Joe Nelson, who defeated De Guichard by four and a quarter laps, covering the distance in 28:20 1-5.

Canadian Minister Resigns.

OTTAWA, Ont., July 13.—Hon. A. G. Blair, minister of railways, has resigned his position in the Cabinet. The difficulty between himself and his colleagues appears to have arisen over the eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific proposal. Mr. Blair has been opposed to the extension to Moucton, as he said that would be parallelling the government line.

Filipinos Will Have a Good Exhibit.

ST. LOUIS, July 13.—Dr. W. H. Wilson, world's fair commissioner to the Philippines, returned to-day, after an absence of three months. Commissioner Wilson reports that the Governors of forty provinces have interested themselves in the collection of ex-

hibits, and that the Philippine exhibit will be a great attraction at the fair. The first shipment, consisting of 500 tons, is now on its way to St. Louis. The exhibit will include 800 Filipinos.

FIGHT WITH NEGROES.

Twenty Shots Fired and One Black Seriously Wounded.

BARBOURVILLE, Ky., July 13.—A desperate fight occurred near here last night between a band of eight Clay county negroes and deputy sheriffs of Barbourville. The negroes attempted to rob county stores and when the posse pursued them they gave resistance. Twenty shots were fired, one negro being dangerously wounded. The negroes escaped to Clay county.

The balance of the band escaped to Clay county. WOUNDS WERE FATAL. With His Brother Smith Attacked An Officer and Was Shot. Hartford, Ky., July 11.—Lincoln Smith, who was shot by Town Marshal Sam Keowe, of Fordsville, died Friday evening. The Smith brothers, Lincoln and Cutton, were offended because the marshal had levied on a cow belonging to their mother. It is charged they attacked him with fists and knives, and he fired, the bullet going through Lincoln Smith's body. Honor Their Dead Chief. Sergent, Ky., July 11.—In the presence of many mountaineers Wilson Bryant, aged 28, was hanged at Clintwood, in Dickenson county, Virginia, just over the Kentucky line, at 1:45 Friday, for the murder of William Vanover, aged 60 years, his cousin, on George's Fork, in October, 1902. Tom White Indisposed.

Lexington, Ky., July 14. — Tom White, the Breathitt county prisoner who is in confinement here, is under the care of a physician, he being indisposed. When the news of his attack reached the ears of Curtis Jett the latter became greatly alarmed and dreaded that it might be typhoid fever.

KENTUCKY WHITE MAN LYNCHED.
Murderer Had Been Given Life Sentence, But Was Waiting for Third Trial.

A mob enraged at the tardiness of the courts broke into the Flemingsburg (Ky.) jail Wednesday morning, and hanged William Thacker, a white man, who had been given a life sentence once for the murder of John Gordon, two years ago. Gordon was an unoffending man and a good citizen. Thacker in a quarrel with Gordon at Foxport shot and killed him, and then sat on the body, Winchester in hand, while he smoked his pipe, and dared any one to attempt to arrest him. At the time Thacker escaped, but was later arrested and lodged in jail at Flemingsburg. He was given two trials, and finally got a life sentence. He appealed to the court of appeals and was waiting for another trial. He had some money and was able to command the support of some influential men, and it was feared by Gordon's friends that he might escape punishment altogether.

Civil Officers Must Keep Peace.

Gov Durbin, in a letter Saturday to Judge Rasch of Evansville, Ind., explaining his position in declining to sanction holding the troops at Evansville until after the trial of the negro, Lee Brown, charged with the murder of Policeman Massey, which murder led to the recent race riot, said: "It is for you to determine when the prisoner shall be returned for trial, and it is for the sheriff of Vanderburg county to make such provisions for the preservation of peace and order in the community as, in his judgment as a responsible officer, circumstances may require. Nothing could be more salutary should further disturbance arise, than that the civil authorities should demonstrate their supremacy by stern use of the force they are empowered to employ in resisting lawless efforts at interference with the exercise of their just functions. Nothing could be more unfortunate, as suggested in my dispatch of the 9th, that there should be a resort to the military arm of the government without the civil authorities first exhausting their resources in an effort to subdue lawlessness."

Brown may never be taken from the Indiana reformatory in Jeffersonville to Evansville to stand trial for the murder of Policeman Massey. Pneumonia developed in his wounded lung, and he has only a slight chance of recovery.

Raiding Negroes in Texas.

Nearly all of the negroes have been driven from the Sour Lake oil fields, as the result of the shooting of Brakeman Thompson of Houston, Tex., by a negro Thursday last week. Two camps of negroes, one in the shoe-string district of the oil field, and the other composed of construction forces of the Southern Pacific railroad, were raided Thursday night by a mob of 500 men. The blacks fled precipitately, and about 100 shots were fired at them. It is not known whether any of them were killed or wounded, as the shooting was in the darkness. One of the Mexicans in the construction gang had his head beaten into a pulp and will die. Proprietors of hotels and restaurants were warned Thursday night to discharge all negroes in their employ at once, as they would no longer be tolerated in that field. About 25 negroes remain in Sour Lake, most of these being guarded in one of the restaurants.

Race Rioting in New York.

Several negroes have been hurt in a resumption of the race rioting which broke out in the vicinity of West Sixty-second street and Amsterdam avenue, New York, Sunday. Several young colored men attacked and severely beat a son of Alderman Harrington. Police hurried to the scene and made one arrest. On the way to the station they were assailed by volleys of bricks thrown from the housetops. When the police disappeared crowds of white men attacked every negro in sight and chased them from the streets. Several were severely beaten.

A desperate fight occurred near Barbourville, Ky., Sunday night between a band of eight negroes and deputy sheriffs. The negroes attempted to rob county stores and when the posse pursued them they gave resistance. Twenty shots were fired, one negro being dangerously wounded. The negroes escaped.

Farmers who have returned to their homes near Savannah, Ga., say they caught "Ed" Claus, the negro who committed an assault on Miss Johnson at Darion Junction Monday, and lynched him near Eastman.

STATUE OF WASHINGTON IN LONDON.

A committee was appointed at a meeting of the executive committee of the Pilgrims' club in London Wednesday night to give effect to the recent suggestion to erect a

statue to George Washington in London. Archdeacon Sinclair in submitting the plan to the society said:"Englishmen have at last fully recognized the great qualities of Washington." He announced that he was authorized to offer a place for the statue in St Paul's cathedral.

THREE DEAD IN LUMBER CAR.

Unknown Men Found Crushed to Death in Philadelphia.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa., Sunday.—Three unknown men were found dead yesterday in a Pennsylvania Railroad gondola car loaded with lumber. The car left Williamsport, Pa., on July 25 and arrived here yesterday. The lumber was loaded on the car in two piles, one at each end. The men were lying in the open space between the lumber, and the theory of the railroad men is that the lumber came together while the train was on a steep grade.

The bodies were so badly crushed that they are practically unrecognizable and there was nothing found on them to identify the men.

ALBANY MOB WOULD LYNCH A NEGRO

Policemen Draw Revolvers to Save Bert Hazelock from Angry Crowd.

[SPECIAL DESPATCH TO THE HERALD.] ALBANY N.Y. Sunday. An attempt

ALBANY, N. Y., Sunday.—An attempt was made to lynch a negro named Bert Hazelock in Albany this afternoon, but the intended victim was protected by a policeman with a drawn revolver.

Two negroes were fighting in the street when John Scharff, white, tried to separate them. Hazelock drew a razor and slashed Scharff in the back. A crowd of fifty white men, attracted by the brawl, made a rush for the negro, who ran down Third street.

Cries of "Lynch the nigger!" and "Hang him!" were uttered, and stones, bricks and other missiles were thrown at the fugitive. A paving stone broke his arm and knocked him down, but he regained his feet and continued his flight, followed by the crowd, which had grown to two hundred.

Hazelock ran into a house in Second street, near Swan street, frightening the women occupants, and bolting the door to save himself. The crowd had surrounded the house when John Begley, a policeman, arrived. He went into the house to arrest Hazelock.

As the policeman took the negro out several men rushed forward to seize the prisoner, but Begley drew his revolver and kept them at bay until the arrival of other policemen, who escorted the negro to the station house.

Saloon Demolished in Effort to Secure One of Them-Mob Finally Dispersed by the Mayor.
LORAIN, O., July 28.—A fierce riot, in which a mob of 300 whites chased two colored men, threatening to lynch them, took place here to-night. Early in the evening two colored men, Charles Hall and Robert Pleasant, became involved in an altercation with a white man named Daniel Cronan. A mob immediately gathered, and the negroes were chased over the entire south end of the city, one of them taking refuge in a saloon, the entire front of which was battered in with stones. Wheeling, W. Va., July 29.—But for the timely arrival of policemen, John Posteoh, a Hungarian steel worker, would have been strung up by an enraged mob on Wheeling island last night. Posteoh, who was drunk, caught in his arms and embraced a well-known and respected woman who was walking on the street. A mob chased him, but the foreigner drew a dirk fully 12 inches in length and held the enraged men at bay for a time. A cobble stone hurled the knife out of the man's hand. THE MOB DISPERSED.
A Cutting Affray Arouses the Blood of West Virginia Residents of Lorain.

Lorain, O.—Great excitement prevailed here for three hours Tuesday night. A crowd of 300 lawbreakers threatened to lynch two Afro-Americans named Charles Hill and Robert Pleasant. All the day and night the police force was called out and special policemen were put on duty. Shortly after 7 o'clock Daniel Cronan (white) and the two men mentioned got into an argument in a saloon and a fight ensued. One of the latter drew a razor and cut Cronan on the face and neck. When the news spread a mob formed and he was chased all over the south end of the city, but finally escaped. He entered a saloon owned by Robert Fountain, and the crowd threw stones and clubs at the building, breaking almost every pane of glass in the house. At 9 o'clock Pleasant was arrested and hustled off to a side street to the mayor's office. He was placed under a bond of $100 and landed in the city jail. Meanwhile the mob continued its threats and a number of shots were fired. At 10 o'clock Mayor King went to Ninth avenue and addressed the mob, warning them to disperse and let the law take its place. He stated that Cronan's injuries were not serious and advised them all to go home. His words had the proper effect and within a few minutes the crowd dispersed.

Nigger-Chasing In Massachusetts.
Mexican Herald:
Mexican Herald:

The noble game of nigger-chasing has begun in the fine old State of Massachusetts where the early abolitionists used to be fanned with brickbats and enthusiastically egged off public platforms. On the 26th ultimo, 400 whites in Lawrence gave hot pursuit to two negroes, Charles Hall and Charles Pleasant, one of the black gentlemen having, after an altercation with a scion of Irish royalty, named Cronan, cut that paleface with a razor. The negroes took refuge in a barroom, the front of which was at once battered in with stones thrown by the angry mob. The alcalde of Lawrence ordered out his gendarmes and restored order, although the mob was furious and fired some shots at random.

Thus early, earlier than we had looked for, were the predictions of Professor William James, the Harvard professor of psychology, confirmed by events, and it is quite on the cards that, within the year, negroes will be burned at the stake in the elm-shaded plazas of Massachusetts cities, yea, even on Boston Common where Quakers and Baptists in Puritan times were flogged and otherwise dealt with for the good of their souls.

Shades of Wendell Phillips and William Lloyd Garrison! To this complexion has come the land where once were numerous the stations on the Underground railroad. We see little hope for Massachusetts unless Governor Bates, commander-in-chief of the land forces and admiral of the sea flotilla of the Commonwealth, declares martial law and orders out the Ancient and Honorable Artillery.

ANGLETON, TEXAS. — (Special.)
Thursday night several men entered a cell of the county jail in which Ransom O'Neill and Charles Tunstall were confined with a number of other negroes and shot the two men to death.
The other prisoners were warned to cover their heads with blankets, which they did. The bedclothing of the cots occupied by the negroes caught fire, and O'Neill had a leg and an arm burned off. The negroes were charged with the murder of County Attorney Ed C. Smith, at Columbia.

PUT TO DEATH.
Two Negroes Killed in Jail at Angelton, Tex., by a Posse of Men.
Angleton, Texas, Jan. 15.—Late Tuesday night several men entered a cell of the county jail in which Ransom O'Neal and Charles Tunstall were confined, with a number of negroes, and shot the two men to death. The other prisoners were warned to cover their heads with blankets, which they did. The bed clothing of the cots occupied by the negroes caught fire and O'Neal had an arm and a leg burned off. The negroes were charged with the murder of County Attorney Ed C. Smith, at Columbia, several weeks ago.

REUNION OF CAMP OWEN VETERANS.

On Friday next, the 21st, there will be a reunion of Camp Owen veterans at Lebanon. The "old vets" are to be served with a barbecue dinner as well as to share in the "plenic" dinner. The public are cordially invited and will be expected to bring well filled baskets so that all may have enough and some left for the cooks. This annual reunion has always been largely attended and an occasion of great pleasure to all present, and we hope this time will be no exception to the general rule.

JEFFRIES AND CORBETT.

At San Francisco, California, last Saturday night the 15th, these two world famed puglists met in the presence of a great multitude of people to witness the fight for the heavy weight championship of the world.

Both men had been in training for months and each was at his best, in fine trim and excellent spirits. Tickets were sold from five to twenty dollars. Gate receipts $54,000.

Jeffries knocked Corbett out on the tenth round and is now the heavy weight champion of the world.

At the close of the fight Corbett and Jeffries shook hands and Corbett said, "you have won the fight fairly, and I have fought my last fight. I did my best; you were too much for me."

BETHEL AND LEBANON NEWS.

Mr. and Mrs. A. K. Drennan will be at home to their friends at Bethel in a few days.

Mrs. Sallie Drennan returned from Due West last Saturday, where she had been called to the bedside of one of her grandchildren—a child of Mr. and Mrs. Arch Kennedy. The little one is now better.

Mrs. Mattie Wilson and children are visiting relatives near Cedar Springs.

Miss Isabelle Evans is expected home tomorrow (Thursday) from a very pleasant stay with friends near Hodges and at Antreville.

Miss Isabelle Evans is expected home tomorrow (Thursday) from a very pleasant stay with friends near Hodges and at Antreville.

ECHOES FROM SHARON.

Miss Maggie Pennal of the city is the guest of her cousins, the Misses McCanty.

Miss Nannie Gilliam and her brother, Mr. Henry Gilliam, after a pleasant stay with friends and relatives at Sanford, N. C., are expected home this week.

Miss Belle Knox after a pleasant stay with her cousin, Miss Rosa Knox, was called to her home at Mt. Carmel last week on account of sickness.

Mr. Nicholas Schram was in the city last Monday.

Mr. J. G. Walker was a visitor, in the city on Monday.

Mr. William McNelll, of Turkey Hill, returned home last Monday from a business trip to Abbeville.

Mr. John Penney and daughter, Miss Ada, were guests of friends in the city last Saturday.

IN AND ABOUT THE CITY.

Invitations are out from the German club of this city to a grand ball to be given at the Eureka Hotel on Friday evening next, the 21st instant, in honor of the opening of the hotel.

Mr. W. T. McFall, of Anderson, is the proprietor and is in every sense of the word a "hotel man," and is a general favorite with the traveling salesmen North, South, East and West. The hotel is finished in modern style, water works, electric lights, efficient polite and attentive servants, newly and nicely furnished large airy rooms, spacious verandas and everything looking to the pleasure and comfort of its guests. With such a beginning, and under the management of so genial a host, we predict much business for the Eureka.

'THERE'S MUSIC IN THE AIR."

The Baldwin Military Band will give open air concerts every Thursday afternoon at 6 o'clock at the "grand stand," just erected in front of the city park. This is a new feature for Abbeville and will add greatly to the pleasure and enjoyment of our citizens. Let our city fathers fix up the park and arrange comfortable seats so the ladies and children of the city will have comfort in the enjoyment of this musical treat.

Mrs. J. H. Wells, of Greenwood, spent last week in the city, the guest of Mrs. W. C. DuPre.

Mrs. S. A. Morgan and her charming daughter, Miss Bertha, spent several days of the past week with Mrs. Andrew Penney, returning to their home at Dearling, Georgia, last Monday.

Miss Bessie Murray, after a delightful stay with friends and relatives in and around Greenwood is expected home this week.

Mrs. F. B. Gary and son, Frank, returned home last week after several weeks delightfully spent at Tryon. We are glad to note that Master Frank is much benefitted by the trip.

Miss Josie Lyon is back at her place at the post office.

charlie-stark-1903-08-16.A2:
A little more than a week ago a negro by the name of Charlie Stark appeared at the home of a gentleman in the Sharon neighborhood, and seeing the house in darkness, proceeded to a window of the room in which his daughter slept and at once proceeded to raise the sash which awakened the young lady, who seeing him at the window gave the alarm, but by the time the household were up the negro had disappeared.

On last Saturday night he again made his appearance and as the window was fastened down he did not succeed in raising the sash, so went to one of the doors when the young lady heard the noise, and again called her father, but before he could get out the negro had left under cover of the darkness, but this visit was just after a rain and his tracks were plainly to be seen, so in the morning (Sunday) a party set out to track him up and were soon up with him. Finding where he had stopped at a negro's house and changed his shoes for a larger number, they followed and came up with him at Turkey Hill about three or four miles distant. The news of his capture soon spread far and near and in a short time more than fifty well armed and determined men were gathered around the prisoner, when calls "lynch him," were heard from many throats; others wanted to burn him, and a fire was soon kindled, while some of the crowd wanted him drowned in the river. A jury was empanelled to dispose of his case, and after the wise counsels of older heads being given under mature deliberation the jury stood three in favor of lynching him and seven not to take his life, so he was taken out into the public road and given a severe whipping, and turned loose with instructions never to be seen in that section again.

It seems from all we could learn he was a Georgia negro, and was loafing about through the country. He worked part of last year for a farmer in that neighborhood and finally ran away, slipping his contract.

The negro confessed that he was the one they were looking for, and said he was trying to arouse some one to give him some peaches. If he had been in his Georgia home his fate would most likely been very different.

The young lady is one of the most popular and well beloved in all that section, being largely and well connected, and having hosts of friends who sincerely regret the circumstance.

charlie-stark-1903-08-16.A3:
A "Peeping Tom" Flogged.
Twice within two weeks Charlie Stark, a young negro man from Georgia, nad been at the window of a beautiful young woman in the Sharon section of Abbeville county, evidently for an evil purpose. He called the young woman's name in a low voice, and when she heard him she called her brother, who slept in an adjoint room, and the negro fled.

The second time he came the men of the neighborhood gave chase. He was overtaken at the Turkey Hill place, near the Island ford, over Little river, on the Savannah side of the county. The determination was to kill him at once, but some of the older men of the pursuing party prevailed upon the crowd to let him off with a whipping. Procuring a buggy trace, they laid upon his back 210 lashes.

cornelius-lee-plaquemine-1903-01-25.A1:
Nearly a Race Riot.
What came pretty near proving a race riot occurred at Plaquemine, in the parish of Iberville, on the 25th inst. Reports of the matter say that Mr. Andre Gourrier, Assistant Cashier of the Bank of Plaquemine, who is well-known to the writer, and his wife and child, were returning from a walk on the river bank, and were passing the store of Joseph Newchurch, at the lower end of the town, when he was set upon and badly beaten by a crowd of vicious negroes. Messrs. Mr. M. E. Davidson and G. A. Martinez, passers-by, seeing the difficulty, went to the assistance of Mr. Gourrier, and were also badly beaten. News of the affray spread rapidly and in a few minutes several more white men appeared on the scene and the negroes were dispersed. During the stampede a shot was fired which struck one of the negroes, named Cornelius Lee, from the effects of which he died the next morning. Messrs. Gourrier and Martinez were so badly injured that they were compelled to take to bed. There was nothing in the reports to indicate what was the cause of the trouble or how it originated. The negro killed was a surly, impudent, trifling and worthless fellow and we heard an old and repeated citizen of the town tell him one day if he had his just deserts he would be in the penitentiary. Young Gourier is an upright, well-behaved and highly-esteemed young gentleman, and we are pleased to learn that he was not seriously injured.

The favors were picture hats with flowers for the girls and hearts with pictures for the men. Lynched a Dying Negro.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Feb. 19.—Cornelius Lee, colored, has been lynched near Plaquemine, La. On Jan. 25 Lee attacked Andrew Gardner, cashier of the Bank of Plaquemine and his wife. Gardner was badly beaten, but was saved by a passerby, who shot and wounded Lee. He was confined to his bed and was dying, gangrene having set in from his wound, when the mob broke in and took him from his bed and hanged him to a tree.

Marshall, Texas, February 20.—On February 18 at Plaquemine, La., Cornelius Lee, a negro, who had been in bed suffering from a pistol wound since Sunday afternoon, January 25, when he attacked Andrew Gourrier and wife, was taken from his bed last Tuesday night by a crowd of unknown men and hanged. The inquest over the remains, conducted by Coroner W. E. Baker, developed only the fact that Lee would have died in a short while, as gangrene had set in from the wound he had received in the trouble Sunday afternoon.

esau-lovely-franklin-1903-07-12.A1:
MOB PERSUADED TO LEAVE.
Senator Foster of Louisiana Helps to Save a Negro From Being Lynched.
NEW ORLEANS, July 13. After much persuasion from United States Senator Foster, Circuit Judge Allen, District Judge Smith and Sheriff Sanders the mob which went last night to the St. Mary's parish jail to lynch Esau Lovely, alias Possum, a negro confined there, dispersed and agreed to let the law take its course if the negro was tried promptly. Lovely is an ex-convict and is regarded as dangerous. On Sunday he attacked Mrs. René Hebert while she was driving to church and robbed her, leaving her in a serious condition from the shock of the attack.

Several hundred neighbors of the Heberts went to the jail to lynch Lovely, but were dispersed by the speeches of Senator Foster and the others. It was announced that a special jury would be impanelled to-day, and, as Lovely had already confessed to the crime and the evidence against him was conclusive, no doubt could be entertained of the administration of justice.

According to agreement, Lovely was brought to trial before the District Court in Franklin to-day. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to the penitentiary for thirty-four years. Immediately after the sentence he was removed to the parish prison for safety. There was no demonstration to-day against the prisoner.

Standing Up for the Law.
The following appears in today's Washington Post under a New Orleans date line:

"United States Senator Foster last night saved a negro from the hands of a determined mob bent on a lynching. The crime for which the negro was wanted was an attempted assault upon Mrs. Kene Roberts, wife of a prominent planter of St. Mary's parish. Senator Foster is a citizen of St. Mary's parish, and when he learned of what had happened and was told that the negro had been jailed, he went to the building and awaited the inevitable demand for the prisoner.

"With the senator were Judge Allen. Judge Smith and Sheriff Sanders. It was just midnight when the mob reached the jail. Senator Foster addressed its members. He told them that the negro would be tried at once, and pleaded with them not to soil the history of the state by a lynching which was not to be excused. Sheriff Sanders assured the mob that he would protect the prisoner, and other addresses were made. It was Senator Foster, however, who won the fight for law and order."

The excuse offered for lynching in cases involving this crime is that white men worthy of their race are moved naturally and immediately to vengeance. They cannot contain themselves in the presence or in the neighborhood of a wretch who has thus violated the holiest law of life. Their uncontrollable impulse is to seize him and make way with him by the swiftest and most terrible means possible. The severest punishment is too mild. The suggestion, and sometimes the open charge, is that white men who are not so moved are lacking in spirit, in chivalry, in the proper appreciation of their duty to their womankind. Respect for the law at such a time is the sign of a pigeon-liver. The real man takes the law into his own hands.

Now, here were four men, all officials, who remembered the law at such a time, and successfully championed it. Two are judges, one is the sheriff of the parish and the other is a United States senator. Are they not worthy citizens of their section? Otherwise how could they have attained to their positions? Are they lacking in courage, or in solicitude for the safety and honor of women? Were they ill-employed in asking that the law take its course? Is their action likely to encourage creatures of brutish instincts in that locality to a gratification of their passions? Are women there less safe because of the saving of that wretch from the hands of a mob?

These questions answer themselves. All honor to Senator Foster, to Judges Allen and Smith, and to Sheriff Sanders, for exerting themselves in the interests of law and order! They have shown themselves to be worthy of their commissions; and it is to such men that the country must turn in this the hour of its grave peril for a support which will bring us back to a saner and better order of things.

Justice Brewer speaks soberly and truly when he says that lynchers are murderers. No other view of the matter is consistent with our institutions, with our aspirations, with the explanation of our civilization. He is right, too, in predicting an early reaction against conditions which have grown to be a curse to, and a reflection on, the whole country.

SAVED NEGRO FROM LYNCHING.

United States Senator Foster Add-
resses Louisiana Mob.

REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

New Orleans, July 13.—United States Senator James Murphy Foster saved a negro from being lynched last night. That moral and physical courage which gave him the triumph in the tremendous fight against the lottery ring in Louisiana and the eloquence which made him master of many men, in great political struggles overcame the deadly purpose of 400 lynchers, who gathered at St. Mary's Parish jail and attempted to lynch a negro who attempted to assault Mrs. Rene Habert, wife of a prominent planter.

The mob appeared at midnight and demanded the keys to the jail. Senator Foster, warned of the attempt, reached the jail before the mob and commanded the men to listen. Senator Foster promised that a speedy trial would be given the negro and justice meted out. With all the power of his eloquence he begged the men not to soil the history of the State with another lynching. The mob listened, then quietly dispersed.
esau-lovely-franklin-1903-07-12.A9:
THEY WILL GET HIM.
Franklin, La., Wildly Excited Over an Attempetd Assault. Franklin, La. July 12. This town
Franklin, La., July 12.—This town is in a state of wild excitement tonight over the attack this morning upon Mrs. Rene Herbert by a negro named Boas. The negro was captured today, and is now in jail here. The identification is complete, and threats of lynching are freely expressed.

The negro was armed with a stout rope and a piece of heavy iron pipe in making his attempted assault.

Mrs. Herbert is a daughter of A. A. Delahoussaye, of Franklin, and a niece of Capt. Delahoussaye, of New Orleans. She is now in a serious condition from the shock of the attack.

Sheriff Sanders executed a fine piece of detective work in capturing Boas. He was making for the swamps and was intercepted by a narrow margin.

Excitement grows hourly here, and it is feared that officers will not be able to retain their prisoners.

A mob of two hundred men gathered at the jail bent on lynching the negro. United States Senator Foster and Judge Smith addressed the crowd and pleaded to allow the law to take its course. At 10 o'clock the mob is dispersing.
esau-lovely-franklin-1903-07-12.A10:
DAYLIGHT AHEAD.
An occasional ray of comfort is apparent in the appaling lynching habit. Governor Durbin of Indiana takes high ground in the Evansville horror, Senator Foster of Louisiana has just successfully opposed his strong personality and the weight of his office against an attempt in his State, and a sheriff in New York State by his quick and ready resource has prevented a similar blot upon the fair name of his community. The pendulum is swinging in the other direction. The conscience of the country is awake and we shall soon see the end of the iniquity.

Now let the reproach of the law's delay be removed, and above all let our ministers and teachers, those who come into closest touch with our depraved and illiterate from whom the ranks of the criminal clasess are always recruited, continue to preach bravely and persistently the gospel of decency and morality, as not only the just concomitants of religion but also as excellent investments in the economy of life in this world and in the respect of their neighbors, both black and white. To the upright and worthy among us we counsel patience and if possible stricter adherence to the precepts instilled into us in our early education and we shall ere long see the gray lawn of a brighter day.
esau-lovely-franklin-1903-07-12.A13:
SWIFT JUSTICE.
On last Sunday morning while Mrs. Rene Habert, accompanied by her little son, in a buggy, was on her way to Franklin to attend church, she was attacked by a negro by the name of Esau Lovely, in the cut-off about three miles above town and robbed. On her arrival in town she immediately reported the attack to her relatives, who together with the sheriff and his deputies and a crowd of citizens immediately went in different directions on a hunt for the culprit. Fortunately for the negro Sheriff Sanders captured him and had him in jail before the crowd knew of his arrest. Late in the evening there gathered near the jail a crowd of about 250 citizens from the town and vicinity, no doubt, with the view of capturing the prisoner and lynching him, but at no time was any demonstration made towards the capture of the prisoner. Judge A. C. Allen, District Attorney W. K. Wilson, Senator M. J. Foster Judge H. D. Smith, and Sheriff Sanders assured the relatives and friends of the estimable lady who was robbed, that if they would let the law take its course, the prisoner would be given a speedy trial, and with this assurance, the crowd quietly dispersed, and left the matter in the hands of the officers of the law.

On Monday morning about 10:30 o'clock the prisoner was arraigned, pleaded guilty to the charge filed against him and was sentenced to the full limit of the law, thirty four years in the State
charg's filed against him and was sentenced to the full limit of the law—thirty-four years in the State penitentiary at hard labor. The prisoner was immediately taken to Baton Rouge on the first train. In forty-eight hours after the negro had committed the robbery, he was tried, convicted and placed behind the bars of the State penitentiary. This is what we call just and swift justice, and the only method to be followed in all such cases. The prompt action in this matter by our court officials speak volumes for the good name and standing of St. Mary Parish. If all the Judges throughout the country would take the stand that Judge Allen did in this case there would be no need of mob violence.

The quick disposal of the prisoner Monday by the court is indeed much better than mob violence, and shows to the world that in St. Mary such criminals will be dealt with speedily and given the full extent of the law. Let us hope we will not have any more such cases in fair St. Mary.
esau-lovely-franklin-1903-07-12.A14:
SATURDAY, JULY 18, 1903. CAUSE OF LYNCHING.
The cry of stop lynching of negroes in the south which always came from the northern states, is not as loud now as it used to be, because the disease is spreading in those states, and the disease is from the same cause, assaulting of white women by negroes.

The lynching of negroes all over the country is always for the assault of our white women, and as long as a negro will assault a woman, he will and should be lynched. The lynching of a negro is a lesser violation than the outraging of a white woman by a negro brute. And, as a wise preacher recently said, lynching can be stopped by the negroes themselves, by simply stopping their assault upon our women, and the preaching of the humanitarians in favor of the negro brutes, should be addressed to the negroes instead of the lynchers.

The lynching of the negro brutes, violent as the punishment, has not stopped their criminal assault, and this week we learn that a mob of two hundred from Franklin and the surrounding country had gathered Sunday night in that town to make an assault upon the jail for the purpose of lynching the negro ex-convict Lovely, who attacked Mrs. Rene Hebert the same evening.

Had it not been for the influence of Sheriff Sanders, Senator Foster and Judges Smith and Allen, who pleaded with the infuriated crowd, to allow the law to take its course, the negro brute would have been lynched. And who would have been responsible for this lynching, the negro himself.

Lynching can easily be stopped, not by the lynchers, but by the negro brutes who assault white women.

SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1903.
GRAND JURY REPORT.
To The Honorable A. C. Allen, Judge of the 23rd Judicial District Court, holding session in and for the Parish of St. Mary, State of Louisiana:

We, the Grand Jury, organized for duty, during the term prescribed by law, respectfully submit this report of our actions. Pursuant to your instructions, we have investigated all criminal charges presented or known to us, and file herewith our findings thereon.

We find but few prisoners in the Parish jail, charged with crime and awaiting trial; these cases have received our attention and action.

We notice with regret that there are five or six insane persons, retained in our parish prison, and that some of them have been confined therein for several months.

Our Parish officers, we are happy to say, are not responsible for this, for our investigation plainly shows that our Parish officials have made every effort to have these prisoners and helpless people taken to the State Asylum for the Insane. They have failed because the managers of that institution refuse to receive them, for the reason that they have not the room to accommodate more patients. This is deplorable. Our government is pledged to care for and treat humanely our indigent insane. No jail, no matter how well kept or how considerate its keeper can give that tender treatment which the condition of these helpless people requires.

We listened with approbation to that part of your Honor's charge, in which you commended the law-abiding spirit which pervaded the best people of our Parish, and the ways and means you propose, a fair and prompt execution of the laws; we repeat your words as the most certain way, "That the officers of the law should so act as to always retain the full confidence of the people." While thinking of this question, we as representative people of this Parish now express our praise for the prompt and firm action of your Honor, of our Sheriff, and of our District Attorney of disposing of the case of the highway robber, Esau Lovely. The patience of our people also in this matter is to be commended. The inducement for illegal violence was strong, because the provocation was great, a weak people would have yielded to violence, but they were not unreasonable. They only demanded a speedy trial and showed confidence in our officers by allowing the law to take its course.

We have examined the public buildings of the Parish, the Court House is in bad condition. In our opinion it would be unwise to attempt to put any permanent repairs on it. The police jury should, when the Parish funds can meet the expenses, provide a new Court House.

We find the Parish jail in a good condition, well kept. We recommend that the Police Jury should provide mosquito bars for the inmates of the jail during the summer months.

The public roads throughout the Parish are in a fair condition, no doubt caused in part by the dry weather as prevailed for some time.

The public schools are in excellent condition. The session, which ended a few weeks ago, was successful. The attendance was large and the teachers and officers in charge of them have been zealous in the discharge of their duties.

We are pleased to report that we find the Clerk's office in splendid condition. The arrangement of the record books and papers are much more convenient than ever before.

We regret to report that we find the Treasurer's books not regularly balanced and that it is a difficult matter to check them up, and would recommend that the Police Jury see that they are balanced monthly.

We regret to report that we find no funds in the Treasury.

We express our appreciation for the kindness and courtesy shown us by the District Attorney and other Parish officials in the discharge of our duties.

Respectfully submitted,

E. Wm. DREIBHOLZ,
Foreman Grand Jury.

Franklin, La., July 22nd, 1903.

WHITECAPPERS
WILL MEET
On Saturday the 3rd Day
of January.
HOUR AND PLACE NOT NAMED
Negro Question the Prominent Issue in Lincoln County
OPPOSED TO NEGRO LAND OWNERS
Special Term of Court Will Be Called if Whitecappers are Arrested.
Special to the Daily Progress.
Jackson, Dec. 29. — Word has reached here from Amite county that a call has been issued for a meeting of the whitecappers of the county, otherwise known as the "Farmer's Club" on Saturday, January 3rd. The hour and place of the meeting is not named in the call, but is supposed to be understood by the members of the organization. It is further learned that the officers of the county will attempt to secure an entrance at the meeting.

The troubles with the whitecappers in Franklin, Amite, Pike and Lincoln have reached a most acute stage, and a sharp clash is expected when the citizens who have resolved to bring order out of chaos in their movement and endeavor to secure the arrest and conviction of the lawless element.

The four counties present varying phases of the trouble, but the negro question is the predominant issue. In Lincoln county the whitecappers object to the employment of negroes in saw mills and are attempting to relegate them to the farms, while in Amite the motive of the movement is to prevent negroes from owning farms or tenanting the lands of non-resident owners. Franklin county's trouble is somewhat akin to that of Amite, and Pike more nearly resembles that of Lincoln, each county having its local conditions which the whitecappers are seeking to remedy by radical methods.

Special court terms will be called in the four counties to try the whitecappers in case the crusade should result in the arrest of the supposed members of the organizations, and the officials have been warned to see that no person suspected of having been associated with the outlawry is allowed on a jury panel. The chief obstacle to the crusade at present is the lack of determined leaders who will publicly declare themselves and take initiative in the campaign. Many of those who frown on the disorder fear that the first hostile step taken would inestimably result in ambush and assassination, and before the campaign can be successful it will be necessary to stimulate courage among the people.

MRS. WILSON WAS POISONED. State Chemist Finds Arsenic in His Analysis Mrs. Manson's Hearing To-day.
WILLIMANTIC, Conn., Jan. 1.—The preliminary report of Dr. A. J. Wolff, State chemist, who has had for analysis the parts of the body of Julia A. Wilson, who died at her home in Ashford on Dec. 13, was presented to State's Attorney John L. Hunter to-night. The report says that the woman's death was caused by arsenic poisoning. With the report Dr. Wolff presented four tubes and in each there is a quantity of arsenic.

Mrs. Manson, accused of poisoning Mrs. Wilson, is said by the jail authorities to show signs of breaking down. For the past two days she has been uneasy. Wilson, the accused son, continues indifferent to all proceedings thus far. The hearing in the case will be held to-morrow.

M. RICHT THROWN FROM HORSE

Lakewood-Injury Not Serious.

LAKEWOOD, N. J., Jan. 1.—Marcus Richt of New York was thrown from his horse on the Lake Drive near George J. Gould's estate this afternoon. He struck on his head and was knocked unconscious. This evening his physician, Dr. Charles F. Iindley, says that he is not seriously injured. The accident was caused by the breaking of a stirrup.

Toy Pistols Cause the Deaths of Four Boys NORFOLK, Va., Jan. 1.—The five-year-old son of John A. Brumsey, a bookkeeper in a large store here, was the fourth victim of the toy pistol used here on Christmas Day. He died of lockjaw this afternoon. The other victims were Charles Morris, the thirteen-year-old son of Capt. A. T. Morris of West Norfolk; Harold Horney, 6 years old, and Willie White, a negro boy, 6 years old.

Terrorized Negroes Still Leaving Louisiana. NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 1.—In spite of the recent compromise agreement the negroes continue to be terror-stricken by lawless bands in Amité county and are leaving in droves. They leave mostly at night and take the train chiefly at way stations. The farmers and business men are sleeping on their plantations with shotguna vowing to kill any night raider who molesta their tenants.

TERROR FOR NEGROES.
Lawless Whites in Mississippi Make Nightly Raids.
Mobile, Ala., Jan. 3.—Information reached this city that negro laborers continue to be terror-stricken by lawless bands of white men in Amite county, Miss., and are leaving almost in droves. It is stated that they leave mostly at night and take the train at way stations.

Farmers and business men are becoming desperate and are sleeping on their plantations with shotguns and rifles, avowing the purpose to kill any night riders who appear to molest their tenants regardless of who they may be.

The center of this disturbance is said to be at a point between Gloster and Liberty, Miss. It is thought the plantation owners will in a short time appeal to the state for aid.
event-1903-01-03.A5: cappers in Pike, Franklin, Amite and Lincoln counties. The latest notable threat made by the night riders was left at the home of B. F. Binn, in Amite county, who has been ordered to leave the country, with all his laborers, or his houses will be destroyed by fire. Mr. Dixon has publicly posted a defiant notice to the whitecappers, and declares that he will shoot out the liver and lights of the first person who attempts to interfere with his affairs. Thus far he has not been molested. One troublesome feature of the work of suppressing the whitecappers is that many of the officers in the four counties affected are candidates for re-election this year, and they are afraid to institute a vigorous campaign, knowing that it will cost them the votes of the lawless element. In nearly every instance they know, or have good reason to believe, who belongs to the night riders bands, and political reasons prevent them from taking the proper steps toward suppressing the organizations. The audacity of the labor agents, who are taking advantage of every phase of the situation, is causing fresh complications to be added to the situation every day, and the nergoes are leaving the counties in droves. The trouble now threatens to spread over the southern border of Copiah county, which adjoins Lincoln county on the north.
