event-1903-01-03.A10:
WHITECAPS PERSECUTING AND DRIVING OUT.
In many parts of the south, it is well known, that there are communities of colored people who are noted as being the most orderly and well-behaved of all classes. Indeed, they are thrifty and prosperous, toiling on their farms, the year in and year out. They have learned the art of saving and of making the most of their opportunity. Many have accumulated wealth and are moving right on in the industrial pursuit of life. It is not a matter of surprise to see them for miles around ardouly engaged in the work of the farm. Though hampered and handicapped in their honest endeavor to do an honorable part as humble citizens, yet they are confronting almost insurmountable barriers against which they are struggling for dear existence. They constitute the labor element of the south. They have carried burdens but for which the people of the southern section could not have enjoyed riches and prosperity. Regardless of these stubborn facts, there is a disposition on the part of a certain class of the whites to smite the Negro in his helplessness. The white caps feigning themselves regulators visit these poor people in the dead hour of the night and inflict the most merciless and heartless cruelties upon them. It is a startling fact that the blacks are fleeling from their homes seeking refuge for succor and for safety. For years this persecution has been going on, and God only knows why the poor and harmless laborer must continue to be the victim of spite and resentment. The judgment of the vengeful white man is upon them. Why? is the question not answered. But the Negro has been faithful in attending to business and he has prospered. Toil and endurance is a part of his nature and he remains unyielding in his task and to duty. Down in the bottom of the central Mississippi valley he has plied his energies in the hard toil and heat of the day, adding to his earnings, and it is here verily that a reign of terror and persecution has played its deadly hand. From Amite and the lower counties of the state of Mississippi they are moving to the Delta and hundreds have been passing through Vicksburg. It is the better class of Afro-Americans who are now fleeing from the white caps sworn to drive them from the country. Being ordered to leave
From Amite and the lower counties of the state of Mississippi they are moving to the Delta and hundreds have been passing through Vicksburg. It is the better class of Afro-Americans who are now fleeing from the white caps sworn to drive them from the country. Being ordered to leave they must do so or suffer the awful consequences of a merciless and riotous mob. Even the white planters who find it to their interest to have the blacks in their own employ dare not interpose against these clandestine clans. The south, "the best(?) friend of the Negro," tolerates these outrages, while bad men prowl around at midnight to destroy and kill. Driven from their humble homes and peaceful possessions, we can only wonder what next.

george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A1:
MOB AFTER HUMAN BLOOD
Negroes Who Injured Two Small Boys Are Surrounded. Hartford City, Ind., Aug 3.--Two negroes who maimed a boy here today are surrendered three miles from town this afternoon. A mob is bent on lynching them.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A2:
Did Not Find Them and Dispersed Without Doing Violence or Damaging the Prison.
CRIME COMMITTED ON A BOY
HORRIBLY MUTILATED BY TWO NE GROES WHILE HUNTING.
Woods Searched by Farmers, Who Later Visited the City Bent on Lynching the Men If Found.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal. HARTFORD City. Ind. Aug.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

HARTFORD City, Ind., Aug. 3.—For a time to-night this city was in control of a mob, but it dispersed without harming any person. The mob wanted two negroes, but they were not found in the jail as expected.

Monday morning while hunting squirrels in the woods on his father's farm three and one-half miles southwest of here, George Hershey, aged nineteen, was attacked by two negroes who are said to have attempted to mutilate him. Fearing that the boy's cries would attract the attention of some passerby, they are said to have first filled his mouth with plaintain leaves, then searching his pockets and finding a penknife they committed a horrible crime, according to the boy.

One of the negroes is reported to have kept saying: "Kill him; kill him," but the other said: "No, unman him, and that will be worse than death." After having committed the deed, the boy says, they threw his gun away and left him to die alone in the woods. The boy dragged himself home and his cries were heard by his father, whose first presumption was that the boy had shot himself. When he learned what had been done he drove to town for a physician. The news of the crime spread rapidly and the father was followed home by the sheriff with a posse of nearly 300 men at his back.

As yet nothing has been learned of their whereabouts, but it is safe to say that if they are caught Judge Lynch will preside at their funeral. This evening it was currently reported that they had been caught and were being kept hidden to avoid danger of lynching. The knife used by the fiends was dull and the pain suffered by young Hershey, he says, was excruciating.

A mob of fully 500 persons gathered around the jail here about 9 o'clock to-night and a committee, which had been appointed for the purpose, demanded that Sheriff Morrical deliver the keys of the jail. The men had been told that the negroes who had tortured Hershey had been secretly taken to the jail, and they demanded admission. The sheriff opened the jail and allowed them to make an investigation. The mob seemed satisfied and immediately dispersed, after being assured the negroes were not there. Had the sheriff refused their request it is thought the mob would have stormed the jail.

It is now rumored that the boy may have committed the outrage himself, although he strenuously denies it. So far no one can be found who has seen the negroes, either before or after the crime, except the boy.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A3:
MUTILATED TWO PROWLING NEGROES MEET A BOY AND ABUSE HIM. Finding No Money on His Person, They Stab Him.
Hartford City, Ind., Aug. 3.—George Hearshey, an invalid, aged 19, while hunting squirrels on his father's farm near here at noon today, was approached by two prowling negroes. They grabbed the boy, searched his clothing for money and, finding none, tore his clothing from him. While one negro held him, another mutilated him with a knife. The boy succeeded in reaching home. He told his story and his father gave the alarm, mounted a horse and called for volunteers to wreak vengeance on the fleeing negroes. Two hundred men and boys joined in the chase. Neighboring farms and towns were warned by telephone and the country was scoured. No trace of the negroes was found. The hunt proceeded until nightfall. The sheriff, with a detachment of deputies and police, followed the mob to prevent a lynching if possible.

BAD HARVESTS.

They Are at Fault for the General Unrest.

Madrid, Aug. 3.—The threatened general strike commenced today in several centers, including Barcelona, Murcia, Cadiz, Ronda and Alcoy. The general unrest is largely attributed to bad harvests, but the immediate motive for the strike is to reinforce the demand for the release of numerous workmen who have been thrown into prison for offences in connection with recent strikes. The leaders of the movement are exhorting the members of the trades unions not to return to work until all the imprisoned men have been released.

The government has taken stringent measures to cope with disturbances. The military forces and the civil guards have been reinforced wherever necessary and the troops have been confined to the barracks. The instigators of the strike are threatened with severe penalties.

The residence of the mayor and a number of private houses at Alcala, province of Cadiz, have been attacked by strikers, who exchanged shots with the gendarmes.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A7:
NEGROES' HORRIBLE WORK ON BOY.
Two Hundred Indiana Men and Boys Hunt for Them.
Hartford City, Ind., Aug. 3.—George Hearshy, an invalid, nineteen years old, while hunting squirrels on his father's farm near here to-day, was approached by two negroes. They grabbed the boy, searched his clothing for money, and, finding none, tore his clothing from him and mutilated him with a knife. The boy succeeded in reaching home. He told his story and his father called for volunteers to wreak vengeance on the fleeing negroes.

Two hundred men and boys joined in the chase. Neighboring farms and towns were warned by telephone and the country was scoured. No trace of the negroes was found. The hunt proceeded till nightfall. Sheriff Morigel, with a detachment of deputies and police, followed the mob to prevent a lynching if possible.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A14:
REWARD FOR NEGROES
FARMERS OFFER $300 FOR CAPTURE OF A YOUTH'S ASSAILANTS.
Victim of the Blackford County Outrage Probably Permanently Disabled—No Trace of the Blacks.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.
HARTFORD CITY, Ind., Aug. 4.—Notwithstanding armed men stood guard all last night surrounding the Willman woods in which the negroes, who mutilated George Hershey, a 19-year-old farmer boy, not the slightest trace of them could be found. While a few entertained the possibility of the young man injuring himself, the straightforward story he tells cannot be disputed. There is no motive in either case.

The search was practically ended this morning and no further effort will be made by posse to apprehend them. To-day the farmers in that vicinity and the citizens here raised a $300 fund to be given as a reward for the capture of the negroes. The attending physician has stated that from the nature of the wounds it would have been impossible for the young man to inflict them on himself. His condition today is much worse than yesterday and it is now said by the physician that he will be permanently injured.

It is probable the leaders of the mob that gathered at the jail last night and demanded that a committee be sent through it to see if the prisoners were really there, will be prosecuted. The excitement has entirely subsided and the officers are almost a unit in saying that if the negroes were captured they would not be brought to this city.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A16:
Lynchers Still Active.
Two negroes who assaulted and mutilated a white cripple in Indiana are being hunted by lynchers. There have been a large number of arrests in connection with the recent lynching at Danville, Ill.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A17:
HIS STORY IS DOUBTED
Boy Who Charges Two Negroes with Cruelly Mutilating Him Without Cause.
CURIOUS FACTS ARE MADE KNOWN
That Make the Story Still More Curious—Hoosier Hearers Give Tillman the Hiss.
Hartford City, Ind., Aug. 5.—After nearly a twenty-hour search by a posse of 100 farmers, the impression prevails that there were no negroes who assaulted young George Hershey, the 19-year-old farmer, who asserts that he was mutilated by two colored men. The woods in which the fugitives were believed to be hidden was guarded all night by men armed with every conceivable weapon, and no negro was seen nor any sign of one.

They Wonder at His Story.

More than that, notwithstanding the thorough search by the posse, numbering 100 men, and the close watch on the roads by guards, not a person saw the negroes, either before or after the mutilation of young Hershey. For this reason many, including some of the officers, have begun to wonder at the boy's story. That the young man allowed his captors to escape, with a shotgun loaded in both barrels at his feet, or that the negroes did not take the loaded weapon for defense, or even unload it, has caused many to doubt his story.

Gagged Him with Plantain Leaves.

The binder-twine with which the boy says the men first tied his wound, to keep him from bleeding to death, then afterward came back and cut off, was taken from his own pocket, and his own knife was used. The only other article in his pocket was a handkerchief, and the boy says that they stuffed plantain leaves in his mouth to prevent an outcry.

Tells a Straight Story.

The boy tells a remarkably straight story, and when informed that it had been reported that he might have done the work himself he became greatly agitated and positively denied it. The attending physician expresses a similar belief. Notwithstanding all the reports, the negroes were not seen by any one, either before or after the outrage, except by the boy. The boy's condition is serious.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A25:
Justice to George Hrshey.
Hartford City, Ind., Aug. 8.—The story of George Hershey that he was mutilated by two negroes is now generally credited, not only because of his energetic disclaimer that he mutilated himself, but because a number of responsible persons have been found who saw two negroes in that vicinity at the time indicated by the youth.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A26:
DURBIN WANTS TO KNOW
GOVERNOR IS SPURRING COUNTY OF FICIALS TO DO THEIR DUTY.
Inquiries Made as to Progress of Cases Against Vanderburg, Monroe and Blackford Lawbreakers.
Judge Louis O. Rasch, of Evansville, informed Governor Durbin by letter yesterday that the men under indictment for participation in the riots that occurred in Evansville the first week in July will be placed on trial Sept. 8 and that the prosecution will be pushed as actively as possible. It is understood that this letter came in response to an inquiry from the Governor as to the status of the cases against the rioters. A similar inquiry from the Governor in regard to the cases against the Bloomington whitecappers brought from Judge J. B. Wilson, of the Monroe Circuit Court, a statement to the effect that the men will be placed on trial the first week in October. Some weeks ago six or seven men while on a spree brutally whipped a white woman, using a strand of wire for a lash. The men have been thrice indicted, the first two sets of indictments having been found defective on technical grounds. The Governor has been displeased with the delays in the cases. The Governor has also written the judge and prosecutor of Blackford county asking what steps have been taken for the prosecution of the men who comprised the mob that was formed there last week to revenge the alleged brutal assault by two negroes on a white boy. The mob scoured the county for the negroes, and then came into Hartford City and searched the jail. Later it developed that the alleged assault was altogether mythical and that the boy had himself inflicted the injuries on his body, but this discovery was made too late to have prevented a probable lynching of any negroes who might have been so unfortunate as to have been in the mob's way. The Governor has received no reply to his letter.
george-hearshy-hartford-city-1903-08-03.A27:
Mob Investigation Ordered.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

HARTFORD CITY, Ind., Oct. 26.—Judge Edwin C. Vaughn, who made such a sweeping charge to the grand jury in regard to gambling and liquor violations at the last session and at which some 150 indictments were returned, gave the grand jury similar instructions to-day. He also laid particular stress on the investigation of the members of the mob who demanded the life of the negro assaulters of George Hershey.

isaac-ford-1903-07-23.A1:
ARRESTED FOR RAPE. EXCITEMENT IN NORTH TEXAS OVER A NEGRO'S CRIME. Criminal Assault Upon Seven-Year-Old Girl—Considerable Excitement at Dahlson and Sherman, and Negro Taken to Fort Worth.
Special to the Light.

Sherman, Tex., July 21.—A negro was arrested last night, near here, charged with criminal assault upon seven-year-old Lillian Moran in Sherman.

He confessed his crime, but was taken to Fort Worth before the Sherman people knew of his arrest.

Considerable excitement prevails here.

ALLEGED RAPIST ARRESTED.

Negro Captured in North Texas Said to Have Confessed His Crime. Special to The Light.

Denison, Tex., July 21.—Deputy Sheriff Wise, of Bonham, and Sheriff Russell, of Grayson county, arrested a negro charged with criminally assaulting Lillian Moreland in Sherman on Sunday, July 12. He was brought here and jailed last night and taken to Fort Worth for safe keeping by Deputy Sheriff Duer this morning. He made a full confession of the crime. The arrest was kept a secret till the negro was taken away.
isaac-ford-1903-07-23.A2:
Secretary Hollis Dead. New York. July 23.—Frederick W. Hollis, secretary of the American delegation to The Hague peace conference and more recently a member of the international court, died suddenly early this morning at his home at Yonkers. NEGRO HANGED HIMSELF ISAAC FORD FOUND DEAD IN JAIL IN FORT WORTH. H. Was the Alleged Assailant of Seven-Year-Old Lillian Moreland at Sherman and Was in Fort Worth Jail for Safekeeping.
Special to the Daily Light.

Fort Worth, Tex., July 23.—Isaac Ford, the negro in jail here for safekeeping, charged with criminal assault upon Lillian Moreland, at Sherman, this morning hanged himself in jail here.

Ford was a young negro who was brought to Fort Worth from Sherman for safekeeping. His victim is the seven-year-old daughter of a prominent citizen of Sherman.

Upon his arrest Ford made a confession, and in a subsequent interview he denied his guilt, alleging that he could prove an alibi.

The crime was committed in Sherman Sunday.

In his denial the negro said: "I was on my way to work at a thresher on Monday morning when I met four men, two white and two black. They accused me of the crime and I denied it and told them I could prove that I did not do it. Then they told me that I was guilty and said that if I did not admit that I was they would kill me. I refused to say I did it and then one of the white men struck me on the head with something, cutting a gash over my right eye. (The negro here called attention to the wound, which evidently was inflicted about the time he indicates.) They continued to threaten me until, I was so badly frightened that I told them I did it."
isaac-ford-1903-07-23.A3:
SUICIDES IN JAIL.
Isaac Ford, Charged With Criminal Assault, Ends His Existence. Fort Worth, July 23—Isaac Ford, a
Assault. Ends His Existence.

Fort Worth, July 23—Isaac Ford, a negro held in jail here for safe keeping, charged with criminally assaulting seven-year-old Lilian Moreland at Sherman, made a rope of pieces torn from a blanket, placed it around his neck and tied one end to the bars of his cell. When discovered he was dead.

Ford worked all Wednesday night making the rope, in plain view of fellow prisoners. During Thursday morning he prayed in a vehement manner. At 11 o'clock Ford stood on a bucket, tied the end of the rope to the grating overhead, knotted it under his chin and kicked the bucket. Death ensued from strangulation. Wednesday he heard a prisoner read from a paper the charges against him.
isaac-ford-1903-07-23.A5:
NEGRO KILLED HIMSELF TO AVOID LYNCHING
(By Associated Press.)

(By Associated Press.) FORT WORTH, TEX., July 23.—Isaac Ford, a negro, accused of criminal assault on a little girl in Grayson county, committed suicide in jail to-day by hanging himself. Mob violence was threatened.
isaac-ford-1903-07-23.A7:
Negro Hangs Himself.
Dallas, Texas, July 23.—A special to the News from Fort Worth says:

Isaac Ford, a negro accused of criminal asault on a little girl in Grayson county, committed suicide in the jail today by hanging himself with a rope made of a blanket.

isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A1:
MISSISSIPPI WHITE CAPPERS.
Again Terrorizing the Negroes in Three Counties.
Jackson, Miss., Nov. 20.—Word has reached the city that whitecappers in the counties of Amite, Franklin and Lincoln, again are terrorizing the negroes. Several nights ago a band of whitecappers visited the house of a negro named Dillon in Franklin County and riddled it with bullets, some of them falling on the cover of the bed in which the negro was sleeping.

The whitecappers have given notice to the negroes in many neighborhoods in these counties to leave and they are doing so and negro labor is very scarce there. This section of the State has been affected with whitecappism for some years, but the authorities prosecute them so vigorously that they have been guilet for the past nine months.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A3:
Gates in Galveston. Special to the Sunday Light. Galveston, Tex., Nov. 21.—John W. Gates is here for a hunt at Lake Surprise, Chambers county. NEGROES ARE LEAVING. WHITECAPS ARE TERRORIZING BLACKS IN MISSISSPPI. One house riddled With Bullets, Several or the Missiles Passing Through the Cover of a Bed in Which a Negro Was Sleeping—Labor Scarce.
Special to the Sunday Light.

Jackson, Miss.—Nov., 21.—State Senator McGhee, of Franklin County has arrived here and reports that whitecaps have broken out again in Franklin, Amite and Lincon Counties. The whitecaps are engaged in these counties in riding over the country at night, shooting into negroes cabins generally. They have given the negroes orders to move, and many of them are acting on these orders and are going. On Monday night these whitecaps visited the home of an old negro living in Franklin County, and riddled the house with bullets. Several of the bullets passed through the cover of the bed in which a negro was sleeping. Senator McGhee reports that negro labor is getting scarce in his section of the state in consequence.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A6:
NIGHT RIDERS BREAK LOOSE. Negroes Terrorized by Fresh Outbreak of Whitecapism. BLACKS BEING RUN OUT Change of Venue Granted Slayer of Sheriff Williamson at Hernando--- Construction of Mobile, Jackson and Kansas City Railroad Completed.
The white cappers have broken out again in what was known as the McCall's Creek neighborhood in Lincoln, Franklin and Amite counties, and it is reported that negroes are being terrorized and driven away. Senator McGee, of Franklin county, who was a recent Jackaon visitor brought the story of the reappearance of this band, who have been operating in these counties for a number of years. He says that the other night they visited the house of Isaiah Dillon, a peacable, quiet old negro, who attended strictly to his own affairs; that the white cappers shot into the house of the negro with their revolvers, riddling its sides with bullets, and several balls passed through the cover of the bed upon which the old man was sleeping. This is a favorite way the white cappers have of ridding the country of negroes and similar treatment has been meted out to other members of the race. The white cappers have given many of the negroes verbal orders to leave for other parts of the country, and to waste no time in making up their minds to get away. The result is that all the negroes are frightened. many have left the neighborhood, and it is almost impossible to secure a negro laborer.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A7:
WHITECAPPERS AT WORK.
Negroes in Several Mississippi Coun- ties are Ordered to Leave.

News was received in Jackson, Miss., Friday night that whitecappers in the counties of Amite, Franklin and Lincoln are again terrorizing the negroes.

The whitecappers have given notice to the negroes in many neighborhoods in the counties mentioned to leave, and thy are doing so.

The section mentioned has been affected with whitecapism for some years, but the authorities prosecuted them so vigorously that they have been quiet for the past nine months.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A12:
ANTI-WHITE CAP MEETING. Citizens of Franklin County Meet and Resolve.
McCall Creek, Miss., Dec. 2, 1903.—At a meeting of the citizens in Franklin county, District Number 4, U. G. Barlow was elected chairman, E. C. Ford, secretary. The chairman stated the object of the meeting and appointed a committee on resolutions composed of Dr. A. M. Newman, J. H. Cotten, and J. M. Ford.

The committee reported the following resolutions, which on motion were adopted:

Whereas, There has been committed in our midst, District No. 4, several lawless acts, undoubtedly committed by irresponsible parties, by shooting into houses and giving orders to the negroes of our District; and,

Whereas, These acts have been committed at the dead hour of mid-night and are calculated to do our county irreparable injury; Therefore be it

Resolved, That we, the citizens of Franklin county, District No. 4, desire to place our condemnation on all such acts.

Resolved, That we hereby pledge ourselves to use all lawful means to discover and bring to justice the perpetrators of such crimes, and we do now ask and call upon the perpetrators of such crimes to desist from any further lawless acts and thus avoid the fearful consequences.

Be it further resolved, That we do call a mass meeting of all the citizens of Franklin county
at Meadville on Monday, December 7th, to take some steps to stamp out such lawlessness.
On motion the Franklin Advocate, Brookhaven Leader and the Hamburg Gusher be requested to publish the proceedings of the meeting.
U. G. BARLOW, Chairman.
E. C. FORD, Sec'y.

Our Great Annual Clothing Sale will take place on Friday and Saturday, December 18 and 19.
L. COHN & BROS.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A14:
VS. WRITE CAPPING.
Proceedings of the Citizens' Mass Meeting at Meadville Last Monday.
At a mass meeting of the citizens of Franklin county, held at the court house in Meadville on Monday, the 4th day of December, 1903, R. E. Bennett was elected Chairman, and D. Q. Griffing, Secretary.

The meeting was addressed by J. M. McGehee, Dr. A. M. Newman and others.

On motion the following committee on resolutions was appointed by the Chairman: R. J. Allen, C. A. Lehmann, A. M. Newman, J. H. McGehee, W. S. Calcote and J. W. McDonald.

The following resolutions were presented by the committee, which were unanimously adopted:

Resolved, That the Chairman appoint a committee of one hundred on secret work, twenty from each supervisors district, whose duty it shall be to look up any local detectives who will be suitable to employ to secure testimony against any law breakers.

Resolved, further, That a committee of five on finance shall be selected and appointed by the Chairman, who shall select and appoint also, a chairman, secretary and treasurer for said committee. It shall be the duty of said committee to take subscriptions from all persons willing to subscribe money to a fund to be known as the law and order fund; such moneys to be paid to the secretary and treasurer for said committee, who shall deposit it in some bank to be designated by said committee, and shall be subject to the order of said committee and drawn out on endorsement of the District Attorney in payment of any lawful expenses.
Resolved, further, That the Chairman be empowered to fill any vacancies that may occur on said committee.
J. H. McGEHEE,
Chairman Finance Committee.
Pursuant to the resolutions adopted, the chairman appointed the following committee: District 1 W. S. Calcote: 2. O. G.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A15:
SUPPRESSING WHITECAPPING.
Dr. A. M. Newman, sheriff elect of Franklin, was in Jackson one day last week and expressed himself as follows to a correspondent of the New Orleans Picayune, concerning the white capping in that county:

"We are going to stop the whitecapping. If we can't stop it, we are going to move ourselves. The whitecappers and the law abiding citizens of that section can't live in the same community or county. One or the other must go, and I think it will be the whitecappers. The people have had enough of their lawless doings, and have organized to put an end to it. A committee composed of the leading citizens from each of the supervisor's districts in Franklin county has been appointed for this purpose, and $1,000 has been raised to secure detectives to catch the lawless band and their leaders.

"Some years ago whitecappers appeared in Franklin county, near Amite county line, and terrorized the negroes, but the movement was suppressed. There have been occasional outbreaks, and about three weeks ago this organization started their work again, and the negroes have been afraid for their lives. Many have left the community for safer and more welcome parts, and labor has been greatly disturbed."
It is certainly high. time some such steps as the above were being taken by the law abiding farmers and good citizens of Lincoln county. Two negro farmers have been assassinated in or near their homes in this county, hundreds of negroes are in a state of terror and leaving their homes, and, thus far, not a step has been taken or word of protest or disapproval of such outrages has been uttered by any citizen of the community where these things are going on, so far as the public is advised. Men of Lincoln, it is a shameful state of affairs and will be proclaimed everywhere to your discredit, if you do not rise up in your indignation and might and stop such crimes and bring the perpetrators to justice.
isaiah-dillon-1903-11-16.A17:
WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND.
The people of Franklin county, who have been engaging in the whitecapper outrages for the past year or so, are now reaping the fruits of their folly. A new farming season is at hand, and it is impossible to induce Negro laborers to go to that section for love or money. Fancy wages are being offered to induce Negro immigration to Franklin county, but without any degree of successful result. The consequence will be thousands of untitled acres in the county during the coming year and a long train of evils are following in the wake of the lawless conduct that has been carried on by white men under the gulse of enforcing law and order.

In Amite county and some sections of Lincoln the situation is equally as bad. The Negroes have steadily drifted out of the three counties, going to the cano fields of Louisiana, the rich plantations of the delta or the saw mills of south Mississippi, until today the three counties lack at least 80 per cent of the labor they need to properly till the soil and raise the usual crops.

jake-hines-walterboro-1903-02.A1:
HOG THIEF WHIPPED NOW HE IS DEAD.
No Legal Investigation Because Magistrate in This South Carolina District is Prisoner on Murder Charge.
on Murder Charge.

Columbia, S. C., Feb. 12.—Jake Hines died this morning from the effects of a whipping, administered a few nights ago by a party of whitecappers. Hines, a negro, lived on Young's Island, near Charleston. He was suspected of stealing hogs:

A party searched his house, found no pork, but did find a bag of fertilizer under his bed. Hines was taken out and beaten until he collapsed. He would not tell whether he had accomplices, and because of that the beating was long continued.

The Lexington Dispatch.
Wednesday, February 18, 1903.
Random Thoughts.
Greenville is plastering herself all over with vanity on account of the prospective establishment of a cigar factory in that city.

Germany it seems is just spoiling for a fight. If she keeps on monkeying with Uncle Sam it is morally certain she will get a real good spanking. Uncle Sam's patience endureth not forever, and it is proverbial that he is long suffering, but when he is aroused something is going to happen and that pretty quick.

Jake Hines, a young negro buck, suspected of stealing meat, was visited by a party of 10 or 12 white caps at his home on Young's Island, in Colleton county, a few nights ago, and severely whipped. His wounds have since proved fatal. No meat was found in the house, but three sacks of guano were hid under his bed. He denied stealing them but implicated another negro in the theft. The world is growing older every day. It has withstood the storms and vicissitudes of the warring elements since the dawn of that glorious day "when the Morning Stars sang together for joy" ages and ages ago. Yet, notwithstanding she has been kicked and cuffed about by Father Time, she is as beautiful and bright today as the time when the first streak of light cast its refulgent beams across the void and shapeless mass of wild raging waters. There is nothing little or mean about this old world of ours. With a lavish hand she has contributed from her vast storehouses everything necessary for the happiness, comfort and enjoyment of man, and if he does not accept the golden clusters of fruits and the rich gifts placed at his disposal, and persists in looking upon the shadowy side of nature, he has only himself to blame for his failure to do so.

There is most assuredly a very fertile field in this as well as other States, for the moral reformer to use his best endeavors.

NEAR A LYNCHING UP-STATE.
NEGRO ASSAULTS FARMER'S 11- YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER.
Crowd of Neighboring Farmers Gathers and While Plans of Hanging Negro Are Being Discussed Sheriff Removes Prisoner--Threats by Girl's Father.
ALBANY, July 14.—A lynching bee probably was averted in Coxsackie to-day through the prompt action of the authorities. James Little, colored, of Somerville, N. J., criminally assaulted Emma Cole, the eleven-year-old daughter of Joseph Cole, this morning, on the outskirts of New Baltimore.

The girl is a daughter of a farmer living a mile below New Baltimore, which is twelve miles below Albany on the Hudson River. She, with her five-year-old sister Hazel and another child named Maud Lobdell, aged 12, was berrying in the Vanslyk woods on the Hudson River road at 9 o'clock this morning. Little, who has been attached to the Society Charitable Circus, which is making a tour of the cities in this section, left the circus at Albany and started to walk to his home in Jersey.

When he saw the berrying party Little requested something to eat of the girls. The Lobdell girl said she would get some food from her mother, but shortly returned, saying her mother was out. Little, who is a nineteen-year-old, slight built fellow of 120 pounds, then grabbed Emma Cole, who weighs 110 pounds, and started to drag her into the shrubbery.

The Lobdell girl grabbed the negro's arm, but he threw her to one side, stunning her. He then dragged Emma into the shrubbery and her companions started to give the alarm. When Emma's father arrived, with several farm laborers and neighbors, the negro had disappeared.

Emma told her father what had occurred and he took her at once to his house and summoned Dr. Parish of New Baltimore, the family physician. To-night her condition is serious.

Word was sent to the police authorities along the river front, and at 2 o'clock Little was caught by Roy Cutler, near the West Coxsackie Hotel, four miles from the place of the assault, as he was walking along the railroad track. He was put in the Coxsackie lockup and finally admitted his guilt.

When it was learned in New Baltimore that Little had been caught the farmers thereabouts, headed by Emma's father, started for Coxsackie, and a lynching was feared. Arriving there they visited the lockup, which is a rude affair with a wire netting serving the purpose of iron bars. Little could have been secured without difficulty, but the crowd of about one hundred men, without molesting the negro, withdrew to a nearby hotel to discuss plans for dealing with him.

While they were deliberating about hanging him to a telegraph pole on the corner near the lockup, Deputy Sheriff Sumner Van Loon removed Little to the Catskill jail, six miles below Coxsackie. The deputy sheriff took Little there on the steamer Ursula, which plies between Albany and Catskill and left Coxsackie shortly after 6 o'clock, before the would-be lynchers were aware of it. There was much excitement when the people found that the negro had been taken to Catskill.

Little will be arraigned before Justice of the Peace Joseph Nelson at New Baltimore at 9 o'clock to-morrow morning, and trouble is feared. The girl's father said to-night:

"If my plans carry, Little will not get out of here alive."

Albany, N. Y., July 15.—James Little, the negro who assaulted a little girl near New Baltimore yesterday and who was removed to Catskill for fear a mob would lynch him, was taken from the Catskill jail at 7.23 o'clock this morning and put aboard a boat bound for New Baltimore. The purpose of the removal was the arraignment of the prisoner before a local justice. The negro was an abject wreck, through fear, although he was guarded by an especially strong sheriff's posse in anticipation of trouble.

At New Baltimore a mob composed of farmers, striking molders from Cosackie and boat hands had gathered. Among them was Joseph Cole, the father of the 11 year old girl assaulted. Cole was in an excited state and as the boat docked, drew a revolver. He was quickly disarmed by Deputy Sheriff Gould, whos ucceeded in quieting him.

The prisoner was taken without molestation to the Town Hall but Justice of the Peace Joel Nason refused to proceed with the arraignment until a lawyer was present for his own guidance. This delayed the case for two hours while a lawyer was coming from Catskill.

In the meanwhile news of the favorable condition of the child victim had been widely spread and the girl's father had yielded to wiser counsel, so that by the time the examination began all danger of an outbreak had subsided.

Little pleaded not guilty to the charges of rape and assault in the first degree, waived examination and was bound over to the Greene County grand jury which will not meet again until November. He was then taken back to Catskill, and in default of bail committed to jail. There is no excitement at Catskill over the matter.

NEW-YORK MOB MENACES NEGRO.
Violence Prevented by Prompt Action of Sheriff's Deputy.
Albany, July 15.—What might have been summary vengeance on James Little, the negro accused of assaulting an eleven-year-old girl near New-Baltimore yesterday, was prevented to-day by the prompt action of Deputy Sheriff Gould. Little was removed to the jail at Catskill yesterday, for fear a mob would capture and lynch him, and this morning was returned to New-Baltimore for arraignment, under a strong guard of Sheriff's officers.

At the steamboat landing at New-Baltimore a mob of farmers, striking moulders from Coxsackie and boat hands gathered, and, as Little was dragged off the boat, an abject wreck, from fear, the situation looked menacing. In the crowd was Joseph Cole, father of the negro's victim. He was wild with excitement, and as he caught sight of Little he drew a revolver, but Deputy Sheriff Gould promptly disarmed him, and finally succeeded in calming him. There was no further threatening after that.

Little pleaded not guilty to the charges against him, and was bound over to the Greene County grand jury, which will not meet again until November. He was then taken back to Catskill. There is no excitement at Catskill over the case.

Tennessee Mob Avenges Death of White Man.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Ripley, Tenn., Dec. 19.—Joe Drake, a young negro, was taken from the Lauderdale County Jail last night and lynched for the murder of Chester Conner, a white man, at Ashport, yesterday.

A mob of about 100 men overpowered Jailer Andrew Crockett at 10:30 o'clock, took his keys and entered Drake's cell. The mob secured the negro and dragged him out of the jail to a spot about 150 yards away, where he was strung up to a limb. After he was thought to be dead—his body was riddled with bullets, something like fifty shots being fired.

The spot where the hanging occurred was the scene of a similar occurrence three years ago, when Louis Rice, a negro, was lynched.

Everything was accomplished in a quiet manner. The leaders of the mob were masked. The jailer was thrown to the floor and held down until the negro had been secured. Not a word was spoken until the street was reached, and then all the talk was in an undertone.

The jailer was taken by surprise, as he was under the impression that the idea of lynching the negro had been abandoned. The funeral of young Conner took place this afternoon.

Cleveland, Ohio.—After writing and mailing a letter to a friend telling him that he intended to murder his family, Roscoe W. Derby, a machinist, killed his wife and three children, and then committed suicide. The crime was one of the most deliberate ever committed in this city. Derby, who was thirty-nine years of age, lived with his family in the Albion Terrace, on Barbara street. To all ap pearances the family was in comforta ble circumstances. Derby had work and earned good wages. The crimes were extraordinary in their thoroughness and there was, evi dently. no mishap in the enactment. The wife was killed first, while sleep ing at her husband’s side in bed; two of the children were killed as they ran hither and thither through the house in the darkness of early morning endeavoring to escape their merciless parent. The third child was killed in its bed after the elder brother and sister had been killed. The dead are: Roscoe Derby; his wife. Della: Harold, aged eight; Alice, aged seven, and Thomas, aged five. Derby had been out late one night. When he got home, his wife and he talked with a neighbor who had been calling, over the approaching festival. Derby seemed pale and nervous. Short ly after his arrival at home the neigh bor left and the Derby family went to bed. The crime is believed to have been committed about 4 o'clock in the morn ing. Mrs. Derby was shot to death in bed, two bullets' having been fired into her forehead, and a third, probably fired after the children had been exter minated, in the back of the neck. Mrs. Derby probably was killed during sleep, the expression on her face show ing no sign of a struggle, and it was calm and peaceful. Two of the children, however, proba bly had a struggle with their infuriated parent, because they had been awak ened by the noise of the revolver being fired and sought to escape him, but without avail. Harold's body was found lying in a pool of blood in the kitchen, and that of Alice in the dining room with her face to the floor and a bullet in her breast. After the extraordinary crimes had been committed, the perpetrator of them went into the bedroom where his wife had been killed, and lying down at her side fired a bullet into his own brain, and died at his wife’s side. The coolness of the murderer was in dicated by the fact that each of his vic tims was shot through the head. In all he fired nine bullets into the four victims. Driven from Town by a Mob.
FREMONT, O., May 20.—John Dixon, colored, was driven from town by a mob today after an exciting encounter last night in which his home was stoned. Dixon had been employed at the Clauss shear plant and did not go out when the strikers did. His wife and children escaped the fury of the mob by going to jail. Dixon hid all night and escaped to Norwalk to-day.

For the Week Ending May 23.

Fire practically wiped out the mining town of Thornwood, W. Va.

The business portion of Dunkirk, O., was practically wiped out by fire.

Great damage was done in Ohio at Delhi, Home City and Fernbank by a cloudburst.

The Masonic temple at Bay City, Mich., was burned. Loss, $100,000; insurance, $40,000.

One section of Montana is eaten up by locusts, while another is under three feet of snow.

At the confederate reunions in New Orleans Gen. Gordon was reelected commander in chief.

Maxim Gorki, the Russian novellist, blames Russian society for the frightful massacre at Kishineff.

The Seaboard Air Line railway shops at Portsmouth, Va., were burned, the loss being $750,000.

LONGINO AND MONEY.
"News comes from all parts of the State that Gov. Longino grows more popular every day. His magnificent administration is being appreciated by the tax payers who think that his merit and his devotion to the best interest of Mississippi, splendidly qualify him for a seat in the United States Senate. Senator Money's best friends have been unable to show any great thing he has done during his nearly a quarter of a century tenure in congress. Gov. Longino is in the prime of life, and judging records by results, he would make a Senator that would do something for Mississippi, and not waste time by discussing frivolous and impractical things. Senator Money's refusal to meet Gov. Longino in joint debate, especially since his sad experience at Hernando, has immeasurably weakened him with the people and dispirited his own following. The Meridian Press, a Money supporter, admits that Money cannot afford to decline Gov. Longino's challenge to joint debate. This is the first time in the history of the State where a Senator's tenure was challenged by an adversary, and he declined or refused to confront his opponent and give an account of his stewardship in his presence, and before Mississippiians."—Greenville Democrat.

Such expressions as the above, from the Greenville Democrat, edited by Hon. L. Pink Smith, Clerk of the House of Representatives, which are quite general in the press of the State, clearly indicates the drift of public opinion. It is not surprising either, since the tax payers of Mississippi fully appreciate the excellent administration which Gov. Longino has given the State.

There is a long list of articles for the cornerstone.

That Recently Occurred in the Northern States.
The following is a list of "Southern outrages" that didn't take place in the South. The list was made up by the Memphis Commercial-Appal. It clear shows that the "cruel and barbarous treatment of an inoffensive race" is not the result of a "deep-rooted and unreasoning prejudice" peculiar to Southern whites. After having whipped, driven away, hanged and burned negroes indiscriminately, it is to be hoped that the North will hereafter withhold any criticism whenever the South finds it necessary to lynch some black brute who has forfeited his right to live by the commission of the most heinous crime known to society: Here is the list:

On April 10, at Indianapolis, a Dr. Alexander, accussed of grave robbery, tried to shoulder the crime on a negro named Cantrill, and to destroy the evidence against himself sought to have Cantrill pronounced insane and railroaded to the lunatic assylum.

On April 26, at Bloomington, Ill., a mob whitecapped Joe Shivley, a negro, and two white girls, on the ground that improper relations existed between them. Shively was whipped with barbed wire and badly lacerated.

On April 26, near the village of Santa Fe, Ill., a mob of wrathful farmers took a young negro away from the officers of the law and hanged him. FINE FOR NEGRO BAITER
EVANSVILLE YOUTH SENT TO JAIL IN DEFAULT OF PAYMENT.
Others Are Under Arrest-They Had Pursued a Negro Through the Streets-Arrests at Danville.
EVANSVILLE, Ind., July 29.—Jacob Keil, eighteen years old, was fined $10 and costs and sent to jail this morning by Judge Mattison for his part in chasing and assaulting John Hawkins, a negro, who came near faring badly at the hands of a mob on the streets of this city last evening. Albert Merkel and George Walters, charged with being members of the mob, are under arrest and others will be taken into custody.

Both the court and prosecutor took the position that had Hawkins turned and fired on the mob pursuing him the act would have been justifiable in the meaning of the law, yet had he done so the probabilities are that a lynching would have followed. Judge Mattison declared that negroes have the same rights as white people under the law and the whites have no right to persecute them. He said that unless these race outbreaks cease he will deal most vigorously with the offenders.

The outbreak in question was the second since the Danville riot and lynching of Sunday morning.

The local police department has information to the effect that the wife of Robert Lee, the negro who murdered Police Officer Massey, of this city, on July 3, last, and which led to the rioting in this city, had lost her life while crossing a railroad bridge at Madisonville, Ky. The woman left here on the night of the rioting and was in a terrible state of terror, and her mind later became temporarily deranged and this fact no doubt led to her death.

CORONER RETURNS VERDICT.
Blame Not Fixed for Ten Deaths in the Evansville Riots.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

EVANSVILLE, Ind., Aug. 1.—Coroner Wailing this evening returned his verdict regarding the deaths of the ten persons, some of whom were killed outright and others who died later, as a result of the clash on the evening of July 6 last between a mob and the local company of state militia. The coroner tells how and in what manner the parties came to their deaths, but does not fix the blame. He says he examined about sixty witnesses—persons who were present—but is unable to determine who did the firing.

John Alvis, Walter Wilson and Robert Burns, whose ages range from eighteen to twenty-one years, pleaded guilty in the City Court yesterday to the charges of stoning houses of negroes on Monday night last. Judge Mattison postponed his decision. Albert Merkel, nineteen years old, was tried for an assault and battery on John Hawkins, a negro, who was assaulted by a gang on the street last Tuesday, and who had a narrow escape. A decision in Merkel's case also was postponed.

AN UNCANNY PLANT.

Takes Away the Senses of Those Who Come With It; Its Powerful Influence.

St. Louis, June 10.—The Instituto Medico of Mexico City, says the Mexican Herald, will send to the World's Fair an exhibit of about 50 medicinal plants of the country and the products

derived therefrom. Accompanying the exhibit will be a complete explanation as to the place where the plants are found, the procedure for converting them into medical products and the aments which they are destined to cure. Included in the exhibit will be a plant of marvelous qualities. It grows wild and abundantly in the state of Michoacan. The Indians claim that whenever they enter a wood or place where this plant grows, its aroma makes them lose their way and they are unable to return to their homes or reach their destination until they cease to smell the plant. The statement is said to have been fully confirmed a number of times by learned people. The Instituto is going to make a scientific study of its physiological effects and an analysis of its properties. A delegate has been sent to Michoacan to obtain a sepcimen of the plant. It has been further added that a person wearing a branch of this peculiar plant in his buttonhole, will often be lost in his native city, but the latter statement has not been confirmed. This plant will be an interesting exhibit at the fair and if it is sent in large quantities and keeps its qualities in a foreign and distant land, the police of St. Louis will have many visitors to guide during the exposition.

Stories of Trainmen.
The murder of the marshal was the indirect result of the halting of trains at Raton last night. Trainmen who came in last night say that five of the colored porters drank enough to become quarrelsome. They went to the saloon and sought to play craps. The rules of the saloon forbid colored men from gambling, and they were refused. The porters became abusive and started a rough house. The night marshal, John Jones, was called to quell the disturbance. He knocked two of the porters down, either with his fist or his gun handle, when they resisted arrest. One of them got up and started for the door. Just as he passed through the swinging door that leads to the passage way, he pulled a gun and fired at the marshal. The ball struck the officer in the head, penetrating the brain. Notwithstanding, the unfortunate man lived until 3 o'clock the following morning.

The colored men fled, but according to the stories of the trainmen, four of them, including the one who did the shooting, were speedily captured by the officers. The fifth was seen by passengers on the train which arrived at 2 o'clock this afternoon making for the foothills. He was still wearing his porter's uniform, and when the train came in sight he tried to hide.

There was a wild scene in Raton after the men were recaptured. Mobs gathered and lynching was freely talked. However, wiser councils appear to be prevailing. The men are in jail and strongly guarded. If tonight passes without an attempt on the jail the danger of such a disgrace may be considered over. One pullman conductor said this afternoon that he believed the jail would be forced tonight and the four negroes lynched. Most of the trainmen thought the law would be allowed to take its course.

There is a clear case against the negro, W. M. Mimms, by name, and he will hang sure if his case comes to trial. The certainty of this tends to allay the strong feeling. Night Marshal Jones was a popular man in the Gate City, and many would like to assist in avenging his death.

Mimms is a porter, known to many here, as he had been on the run for some time. He is said to be quarrelsome when drinking, but has never been in any serious trouble before, as far as known.
john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A6:
MAN WHO MURDERED MARSHALL JOHN JONES OF RATON IS IN JAIL
Accompanied by Four Associates Brought to Las Vegas by Sheriff Littrell to Prevent Lynching.
GATE CITY JAIL FORCED BY MOB--MEN ARE GONE
Sheriff Littrell and Deputy Nail were there with the porters. No one had thought of the ruse adopted by the nimble-witted marshal and there was no further trouble. The train arrived at Las Vegas at 7:30 this morning and the terrified colored men were soon in the jail on the west side.

The man who did the killing is Wm. Mimms. The other porters, all dining-car men, are C. P. Puckett Claude Fosten, F. M. Mitchell and Thos. White. The man who escaped to the hills was recaptured last night.

Sheriff Littrell told The Optic that he was assisted in effecting the escape of the prisoners by a number of law-abiding citizens at Raton and that two brothers of the murdered man had told him they were anxious that no violence should be done. The sheriff believes that if the mob had secured the prisoners they all would have been lynched.
john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A14:
RACE FEELING WAS HIGH. White Men Refused to Work With Colored Men at Raton Round House.
As a result of last week's heavy rains, a portion of the Santa Fe Railway's roadbed on the Blossburg spur was undermined near Blossburg, and a train toppled over on its side in passing over the place Friday. Several persons were on the train and were shaken up considerably, but no passenger was hurt. The engineer and fireman sustained painful cuts and bruises, but were not seriously hurt.

A meeting of the executive committee for the Raton Fourth of July celebration was held Thursday at Raton at which it was decided to offer liberal purses for sports, including horse races. A big display of fireworks will be given at night.

Miss Lida Burkhard, who was assistant teacher of the Raton high school last term, will be married on Wednesday, June 24, at Trinidad, Colo., to James Lawrence of the latter city.

Considerable feeling has been occasioned by the killing of Marshal Jones in Raton by the negro porter of one of the Santa Fe trains. The following day the white men of the Santa Fe round house declared that either they or the negro workmen had to get out. They then put the matter to a test and drove the colored fellows away with picks, shovels, and similar weapons.

Work on the Ratoh oil well had to be suspended last week owing to the heavy rain. The mud was so deep that coal could not be hauled to the site where the hole is being bored. An attempt was made to haul a load to the drill with a four horse wagon but the vehicle stuck in the mud and it was impossible to move it.

Carl Blazer, a Santa Fe conductor, and Miss Bessie M. Lyttle of Raton, were married in the latter town Thursday.

During a terrific electric storm at Raton last Thursday, the residences of M. R. Mendleson and A. R. Quick were struck by lightning. None of the inmates of either house was seriously injured, but all were more or less shocked.

john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A16:
Night Watchman Killed.
On the night of the 10th instant John Jones, night watchman at Raton, was murdered by a Negro dining car porter in a saloon of that city. Two or three trains were delayed at Raton on account of washouts and these porters were off drunk taking in the town, when some difficulty arose, causing the night watchman to strike one of the Negroes. This was quickly followed by a shot from the pistol of Wm Mimms hitting Jones in the head, killing him instantly. The whole number were arrested and jailed and to get them away from a mob were moved to Las Vegas in the night. Two hundred armed men went to the jail and broke in the doors but found the criminals gone.
john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A17:
JUDGE LYNCH.
The recent lynchings of negroes in Illinois, Indiana and Delaware are a disgrace to these states, and to the republic. The case doesn't look any more favorable for these states because their press has been prompt and vigorous in denouncing the attitude of the south toward the negro. The treatment of the negro by the south may be in individual cases unpardonable, but the treatment of this unfortunate by the north is infinitely worse. The north hates the negro, while it pretends to believe in his equality. The south has a sort of disregard for him, but denies him any social or political recognition. The problem is a serious one, but the south has come nearer to a solution than the north. Certainly the time has passed when the "holier than thou" people north of the Mason and Dixon line can point
the holier than thou people north of the Mason and Dixon line can point the finger of scorn at those who live to the south of it. With the negro it has become a question not so much of a right to vote, as it is a right to live. North, and to some extent south, the sin of one individual is visited on a whole village.

New Mexico seems to be about the only state or territory where legal justice can be assured. Had the recent riot at Raton ended in the lynching of the negroes in jail, the whole country would have gotten black in the face exclaiming over the barbarity of this territory and pointing out its unfitness for self-government. But, nevertheless, the prompt action of New Mexico authorities in arresting and punishing leaders of the mob, and the generally expressed sentiment of the people of the territory against mob violence, speak volumes for our citizens and for the prevalence of law and order.
john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A19:
LYNCHING CAN BE STOPPED.
The Washington Post in a recent editorial asks the question: "Can lynching be abolished?" Of course it can. This territory is a case in point. There have been no lynchings within the territory of New Mexico for 21 years. The reason for this very gratifying state of affairs is near at hand and not at all difficult to ascertain. While, at times, and during the regime of Grover Cleveland, the courts of this territory have been guilty of political bias, still, when it came to prosecutions for such crimes as murder, felonious assault, cattle stealing and the like, the courts in most of the districts have been very prompt to punish, grand juries to indict, and petit juries to convict. In all of the counties the people feel that they can safely allow the courts to do the work of punishing criminals for them and that they need take no hand in such proceedings except as jurors and witnesses.

The record of New Mexico in this respect is most gratifying and commendable when compared with that of some of the most powerful, most populous and the richest states in the Union. What is more, the people of New Mexico propose to see that this record shall continue unstained and clean for all time to come.

A recent case in point: But a few weeks ago the city marshal of Raton was shot by a colored porter of a Pullman car and died from the wounds received within a few hours. This colored man and some friends were promptly arrested and there was some talk of organizing a lynching party for their benefit, but Governor Otero, Chief Justice Mills, in whose district the crime was committed, District Attorney Leahy at Raton, and Sheriff Marion Littrell of Colfax county, took prompt and vigorous measures to prevent a breach of the peace and the organization of a lynching court, and the prisoners were immediately hurried under guard to Las Vegas, the county seat of the next county, where they were safe from mob violence. Some of the leaders of the mob were also arrested, placed un-

der bonds, and no doubt will be indicted by the grand jury of Colfax county at its next session. Actions like this by the territorial authorities will inform the Washington Post and other eastern newspapers why no lynchings have taken place in this territory for more than twenty years.

There is no doubt in the minds of well-informed persons that the Washington Post is correct when it says that the recent horrible and brutal outbreaks of violence in Belleville, Ills., Wilmington, Del., Evansville, Ind., and Bluefield, Va., would not have taken place if the people of those towns and sections had had confidence in the courts and had believed that prompt and condign punishment would have been meted out to the miscreants who assaulted women or committed murder in these localities.

Here is another argument in favor of statehood for New Mexico. The people of this territory are law abiding, and the laws of the commonwealth are, as a rule, fairly and efficiently executed in criminal cases such as brought about mob violence in the instances cited above. Still there are United States senators and representatives in congress from the states of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana and Virginia who are opposed to granting New Mexico statehood autonomy and self-government although the record and history show that the people of this territory even under the territorial form of government can govern themselves much better than can the people of the sovereign states named above.
john-jones-raton-1903-06-10.A25: The wise and virtuous people of the far east who think the people of New Mexico and Arizona are not capable of self government should inspect the penitentiary records at Santa Fe and Yuma. The Liberal has noted how the judge of the district court in Graham county recently sent a number of men to Yuma for rioting. During the past year there has been a great deal of rioting on some of the trollly lines of New England, but there has been no report that any of the rioters were sent to the penitentiary. In New Mexico a similar record has been made. Last spring some trains were tied up at Raton, by floods. The colored porters from the Pullmans got out and took in the town. One of them killed the city marshal. The murderer and several of his companions were arrested and put in the county jail. That evening a mob started for the jail to lynch the negroes. The sheriff got his prisoners away, and saved their lives. The leaders of the mob, A. C. Webber and Wm. M. Johnson were arrested for the attack on the jail. They were convicted, and last week were sent to the penitentiary for a year each. This was the first attempt in years to take prisoners out of a New Mexico jail and lynch them, and the records show the treatment of the men who led the mob was prompt and severe. johnson-decatur-1903-07-03.A1:
A COSTLY WAY OF CELEBRATING
The returns of Fourth of July casualties are not all in yet, but it is evident they will greatly exceed those of any former year. Every city and town, and almost evey village and hamlet, contributed its quota of deaths, injuries and mutilations. Twenty in this city, five at Muncie, three at Madison, three at Logansport, two at Terre Haute, and so on. Up to yesterday morning reports from the country at large showed 28 deaths and 1,485 mutilations, many of which will prove fatal. This list will be considerably increased by later returns. On the Fourth of July, 1902, 31 persons were killed and 2,649 seriously injured. The casualties increase every year with the growth of population and the multiplication of dangerous devices for making noise. A large proportion of the injured who do not die will be mutilated for life. In addition to personal accidents there is always a list of fires with losses aggregating several hundred thousand dollars caused by explosion and fireworks. In view of these annual losses of life and property and infliction of injuries and deformities for life, is it not about time to inquire whether our manner of celebrating the Fourth should not be reformed? Is it not a barbarous custom that leads us to identify patriotism with noise and to celebrate the Nation's birthday by killing or maiming two or three thousand persons every year? For some weeks before the last Fourth the boards of health in different cities were promulgating and the press was publishing directions how to treat wounds caused by fireworks, etc. Thus we fully expect and deliberately prepare for the annual sacrifice. How long will it be before we get past the firecracker, the torpedo and the tom-tom stage of civilization that can find no better way of celebrating independence and expressing patriotism than in the making of hiedous

noises and killing of two or three thousand men and boys every year? It is not only a very senseless custom, but a very costly mode of celebrating that involves the annual sacrifice of so many lives. CIVILIZATION IN DECATUR.

The method of celebration of Independence day at Decatur, Ind., by a mob of fifty or more men, calls public attention to the fact that in Decatur, as in at least two other Democratic strongholds in Indiana, exists a state of affairs with regard to the negro surpassing anything that has ever existed in the South or in any other part of the world, so far as the Journal knows. Since the civil war it has been the boast of a goodly portion of the residents of these towns that "no nigger can live here," and there is a disposition to enforce this rule with mob violence. A year ago an inoffensive negro was "run out" of Decatur for no other reason whatever than because he was a negro, and on Saturday the performance was repeated, with this important difference: the police strenuously resisted the efforts of the mob and were assisted in their work by a number of the better citizens of the town. But, just the same, they had to hurry their man away to save him, and the purpose of the mob to banish the negro was thus accomplished.

What a disgrace to our civilization! What a narrow, provincial state of public sentiment is here discovered! Not only must no negro be permitted to live within the borders of Decatur, but none can even visit the town to make purchases, but he must run the risk of being set upon and beaten by a mob. It sounds more like a chapter of an imaginative historical novel, dealing with the dark ages, than a story of real life within the boundaries of a State famed the world over for its educational system and the literature it has produced. Surely this cannot be the sentiment of a majority of the thousands of inhabitants of Decatur. And yet, if they permit the leaders of this mob to go unpunished, all must help to bear the sting of the disgrace, all must share the disgrace of entertaining a species of race prejudice that one might expect to find only among a tribe of savages. And, if the Decatur authorities do not take up the matter promptly, it is to be hoped that the State government will show the same promptness and zeal that it has shown in going after whitecap outrages and lynchings.

The enterprising corner druggist has made the discovery that a mixture of sulphur and potash, subjected to concussion, will explode with a remarkably loud noise, and he has wasted no time in putting the small boy in possession of the information that he can thus obtain a cheap combination which, placed on the street-railroad track, will split the ears of the living and wake the dead. And thus it has come about that since about Thursday last the lot of the average passenger on the cars has been a most unhappy one, while invalids and nervous persons residing along the car lines have been driven frantic. For a short time the company succeeded in stopping the trouble by equipping its closed cars with track brooms, but the open cars have no attachment for this purpose, and, since it requires but about one trip to wear out a broom, the supply ran out in a few hours. Without any more harmful intent than greed on the part of the druggist and a desire to be noisy on the part of the small boy, they have together caused a vast amount of distress. Some cases of deafness have been reported, and the number of nervous prostrations will never be known. Before another celebration comes around the business of placing explosives on the car tracks should be interdicted by city ordinance, which should be rigidly enforced.

Newspapers in the East are very properly taking up a crusade against signboards along the trolley lines and country highways, but it might be just as well to at the same time conduct a crusade against billboards in the towns. If anything more offensively ugly than the average billboard, whether its be in town or country, could be conceived it would be interesting to know what it is.

johnson-decatur-1903-07-03.A3:
Some Good Citizens Have Headaches,
Deptort Ind July 6-A negro
Some Good Citizens Have Headaches, Decatur, Ind., July 6.—A negro named Johnson, of Wren, O., was driven from Decatur by a mob of 100 citizens. Officers had a clash with the mob in attempting to rescue the negro, and used their clubs freely. Several citizens were badly beaten. This is the second race riot here during the last year. Johnson is a respected citizen of Wren and was walking along the street when attacked.
johnson-decatur-1903-07-03.A4:
Decatur, Ind., Has the Disease.
Decatur, Ind., July 6.—Fuel was added to the flames of public indignation here against the negro when it became known that Will Foreman, leader of the mob in the race riot here Friday night was fined but the $1 for assault and battery. No other arrests were made.

johnson-decatur-1903-07-03.A8:
Race Question in Indiana.
Recent occurrences in Indiana indicate that a general movement against the negroes in that state is under way. There may be no organized movement to that end, no agreement among the different sections of the state, but the very widespread attempt to drive out the negroes demonstrates that the feeling is largely shared in all over the state. The lamentable occurrences of the past four days at Evansville are the more conspicuous, but at Terre Haute, and at Decatur, and at Linton, and Mount Vernon, and in other cities the word seems to have gone forth and the terrified colored people are fleeing for their lives, and hiding from the fury of mobs, their only offence being the color of their skins. When it comes to this, it is high time for every power of the state and national government to be invoked for the protection of these helpless and innocent ones. Crime, actual crime is the only outlawry, and the punishment of this is in the hands of the courts and not of the mobs. But, the movement in Indiana is not a movement against criminals, but against a race. A race of American born men and women of color, who as a race are law abiding and obedient, and are certainly loyal American citizens and entitled to all the protection that the law affords to any of its subjects. It is not the offenses and crimes of a solitary negro here and there that is to be considered here. The matter has far outrun that phase of the race question in Indiana and in one or two places in the south, but nowhere to the extent that it has in Indiana. This prejudice against the colored race is insane. At least it is insane for an American, who knows the history of the negro in his relation to this country, and the outrage and injustice of British slave trading by which he was fastened upon the colonies. The masses of ignorant foreigners who flood our manufacturing districts are the people most responsible for this hue and cry against the colored citizen and it is growing ominous. With about 8,000,000 of colored people in our midst it is idle and worse than idle, it is criminal to give ear to any class or race denunciation of them. It can only lead to bloodshed, revolting crimes by way of retaliation, incendiarism and all the horrors of a civil war, without any of the restraints of organized warfare. The idea is not to be tolerated, for the destructions it would wreak on white and black alike would be too awful to contemplate. Moderate counsels must prevail. Pulpit and press and forum and bench must all preach humanity, justice, moderation, suppression of prejudice. If we are as a people to reprove Russia for her massacre of the Jews, we cannot consistently proceed to massacre our own colored citizens and drive them from their homes. DECATUR, Ind., July 7.—As the outcome of the negro outrage here Saturday evening Will Foreman, of this city, was arrested and fined $1 and costs, amounting to $9.80. This was the only arrest made, and the charge was assault and battery.

Leading citizens are planning to put a stop to any similar outbreak in the future, and an effort is being made to have the negro John Johnson, living at Wren, east of here, return and file affidavits against the members of the mob charging them with inciting a riot. The business men will do all in their power to cause the arrest of every member of the mob. Foreman was not one of the ring leaders, but was one of the persons who was beaten by the police.

Another Negro Run Down in Decatur.
the city of Decatur Friday evening by "being game" and running a colored man out of town.

Friday evening a colored man from Wren came to the city to do some trading. As soon as he entered the city he was "spotted" by some of the fellows who "hate the niggers" and a "gang" was soon organized to run him out.

The colored man went about his trading in a quiet manner, paid attention to nothing but his business and offended no one.

After he had finished his trading he went to a saloon. It happened to be the saloon in which the "mob" was organizing. The colored man however, suspicioning nothing wrong, bought his drink and also bought drinks for the crowd. When he started to leave he was grabbed by some of the "gang." He resisted and attempted to break away. A crowd had assembled on the outside and the attention of night policeman Mangold was attracted. He saw at once what the trouble was and went to the saloon. He finally managed to get to the door through the crowd and arrived there just as the negro was trying to pull himself loose from the persons holding him. The negro with members of the mob hanging to his arm succeeded in reaching the walk where Mangold was standing. The instant the person who was trying to hold the negro stepped out of the door in reach of the policeman that officer "landed" on the member of the gang with his club with such telling effect that the rioter was nearly floored.

At this the negro broke through the crowd and ran south on Second street followed by the mob. The use of Mangold's club had considerable effect and the mob became careful.

The frightened negro ran down street and into a clothing store to get his goods. He was again caught by the "mob," but again succeeded in breaking away, and with policemen Mangold and Cordua went to the Erie railroad and started home.

The public feeling is very bitter against the actions of the members of the "gang," and Mayor Coffee has taken the matter up.

An affidavit was filed by Policeman Mangold against Will Foreman, charging him with assault and battery. Foreman was taken before Mayor Coffee at three o'clock, and given a fine of one dollar and costs, amounting to 9:30. The docket was stayed.

Mayor Coffee gave Foreman and others who might have been implicated, a decidedly hot reprimand. In part he said:

"This man has the same right in Decatur as any other American citizen, under the law, and as I am sworn to enforce the law, and when the law is violated, by which a cisizen is deprived of his lawful rights or intruded upon in violation of law, independent of his nationality, color or creed, there shall be no discrimination in the enforcement of the law as far as justice is concerned in this court.

The law was made for all alike, and as we are all citizens of the same country and are all under the same law, and were created by the same God for the same immortal purpose, we should be allowed the undeniable rights of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. So the fact of this man being colored does not justify any person in unlawfully imposing upon him while attending to his own business. And if any colored man violates the law while in Decatur the same penalty will be inflicted on him as if he were white, and nothing more; for equality of rights among men is the fundamental principle of good law in all countries."—Journal.
