The jury in the case of Johnson Reed, colored, charged with assault upon Martha Hall, a little white girl, failed to agree upon a verdict. One report says that nine were for hanging and three for a life sentence, while another says all but one favored the death penalty. The crime was committed last October just across the river from Matewan, W. Va. The evidence showed it to have been one of the worst crimes in the history of the county. The little girl was criminally assaulted by the negro while hunting her mother's cow some distance from home. She was found and carried home, where she lingered between life and death for three weeks. The negro was arrested at Kenova. He was fully indentified and while in jail at Pikeville made a confession to the jail-
identified and while in jail at Pikeville made a confession to the jailer and others. He denied everything upon the witness stand. The death sentence will doubtless be inflicted at the next trial.

Attorney W. H. Flannery and W. H. Elliott broke the monotony of the court, as well as its rules, Saturday by engaging in a fight. They were not allowed to finish the combat, but were promptly fined $10 each for contempt of court. Hon. Roscoe Vanover was presiding at the time.

Earl, age 15 years, only son of John H. Hatcher, proprietor of the Williamson House, was drowned at the wharf on Wednesday night of last week by stepping from the steamer Grubbs, which had just landed. More than an hour passed before it was known who the unfortunate boy was, as no one recognized Earl as he went down into the water. Parents of all boys who were away from home at the time were frantic until their sons were found.

At this writing the body of Earl Hatcher has not been found. There has been considerable search made by the citizens here and $50 reward is offered for the recovery of the body.

Since the tragic fate of Earl, the people have partly awakened to the dangerous and careless habit of allowing their boys to rush pell-mell to the wharf every time a steamer arrives. Though Earl was sent on a mission to the boat, the parents of other boys realize, at last, that their own boys have been in danger of being drowned every time a boat arrives at our wharf. The parents of Earl have the very deepest heartfelt sympathy of the people here during these sad days of their bereavement.

Mrs. Caroline Williamson, who has been away sometime for medical treatment, returned Saturday, improved some, but not yet very strong.

Tom Williamson is constructing a large feed and livery stable on 2nd. street back of Williamson House.

There is no smallpox now in Pikeville. There were only three cases in all and they are well now.

The merchants are doing a lively business since the boats have brought so many new goods on the recent tide.

J. P. Roberts, age 35, living two miles above Williamson in Pike county, was killed by a freight train in the Williamson yards a few nights ago.

Almost a Lynching.
The Pikeville Independent says: "Last Sunday night came near being the last night on earth for Johnson Reed, the brutal assailant of Little Martha Hall. Late in the afternoon it became evident that something unusual was in the air. Mysterious movements on the part of several unknown men and the gathering of groups near the county jail and court house attracted attention. It was whispered about that the negro would be hung before morning. Nearly every man in town became aware of what was going on before 7 o'clock and a bigger wd had collected. Of course the officers so "got next" and took measures to save the prisoner.

About three dozen special guards were hurriedly deputized and several of the citizens set about urging the abandonment of the plan. After a good deal of quiet work the crowds melted away. Had there been an organization or a leader the negro would have been dead and buried by now. But the secret was known by too many and the leader did not develop. The negro will probably be taken to Lexington for safe keeping.

KILLED BY STREET CAR. Wealthy Bowling Green Broker Meets Sudden and Shocking Death. Bowling Green, Ky., March 1.—[Special.] — Walton Claypool, a wealthy broker and business man of this city, was run over this afternoon by an electric car and instantly killed. Mr. Claypool was riding horseback and his horse became frightened at the car. The animal reared and threw his rider in front of the car which passed over him. The motorman did not have time to apply the brakes. Claypool was disemboweled. He leaves a widow and three sons. WORLD'S FAIR FUND. Fayette County Men Hustling to Raise Necessary $6,000. Lexington, Ky., March 1.—[Special.]—The Fayette County Exhibit Association for the St. Louis World's Fair will make a canvass of Lexington on next Thursday in an effort to raise a subscription of $6,000 to go toward the exhibit to be made by this State. B. A. Jenkins, president of Kentucky University, is president of the Fayette County Association. LYNCHERS FRUSTRATED. Pike County Mob Wanted to Hang Negro For Assaulting Girl. Owingsville, Ky., March 1.—[Special.] News reached here to-day of an attempt made by a mob in Pike county to lynch Jackson Reed, the negro who assaulted little Martha Hall, a white girl. A large crowd gathered at the jail and the court house. Sixty guards were placed about the building and the attempt was frustrated. There is much feeling against the negro and he may yet be lynched. States Senator James B. McCreary and wife to John T. Hughes, of this county. The property is surrounded by the great Elmendorf estate of multi-millionaire J. B. Haggin, who wants the place, but thinks the price, $42,750, too high. Heaviest One-legged Man Dead.

Lexington, Ky., March 1.—[Special.]—Dennis Shea died here to-night of pneumonia. He was sixty years old, and probably the heaviest one-legged man in the world, weighing about 375 pounds. He was a watchman on the Southern, and fell two weeks ago breaking several ribs. He lost a leg fourteen years ago.

Mother Superior Sebastian, of the Sisters of Charity at Delhi Hospital, is one of several sisters of the deceased, all of whom are sisters of charity.

Olive Hill, Ky., March 1.—[Special.]—The body of an unknown man horribly mutilated was found on the railroad tracks at Meads station, a few miles east of here. One hand and several dollars in silver scattered along the tracks was all there was to identify it as being a human body.

Hickman, Ky., March 1.—[Special.]—Earl Steward, colored, who killed Dick Logan February 22, was arrested yesterday by Sheriff George Carpenter near Fulton, Ky., the scene of the crime. Steward, who is only sixteen years old, was placed in jail here.

johnson-reed-pikeville-1903-02.A12: June 23rd has been fixed as the date for hanging the negro ravisher, Johnson Reed, at Pikeville.
johnson-reed-pikeville-1903-02.A14:
OUR NEIGHBORS.

N. & W. section men received notice this week of an increase in their wages to $1.40, to take effect July 1st.

Mrs. Pat Hager and sons, of Pittsburg, are at Round Bottom, W. Va., where they will visit for quite awhile with relatives.

At Grayson Mrs. Marie Ferguson was acquitted of the charge of poisoning Mrs. Louisa Wilson, of Olive Hill. The jury was out four days.

In Circuit Court, at Grayson, George Henderson, aged 18, convicted of killing Frank Underwood, of Enterprise, by shooting him from ambush last fall, was sentenced to eleven years in the penitentiary.

Pikeville, Ky., June 21.—Johnson Reed, colored, who was convicted and sentenced to be hanged for assaulting a white girl, will have a new hearing before the court in September. He was to have been hanged on June 24.

While making up a bed at her home, near Salyersville, Mrs. Ellen Deskins was shot and fatally wounded by the accidental discharge of a revolver falling upon the floor from the bed. Mrs. Deskins died later from the effects of above accident.
johnson-reed-pikeville-1903-02.A16:
A gentlemen from Pikeville, Ky., was in Williamson yesterday and informed us that the stay of execution granted to Johnson Reed was given because the judge who tried the case received the report of the jury and discharged it on Sunday. The people in that section are very indignant and the gentlemen stated that unless precautionary measures are taken by the authorities, lynching will be resorted to.—West Virginian.

T. M. Ryan, Chief Clerk C. & O. office, this city, after a lingering illness, died Thursday morning at 11 o'clock. Typhoid fever caused his death. The remains were taken to Whitehouse Thursday evening and placed aboard a special train and taken to Richmond, Va., his home, for burial. Mrs. Ryan and daughter, mother and sister of the deceased, were constantly by his bedside during his illness.—Paintsville Herald.

TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES The correspondent of the Vienna D
The correspondent of the Vienna Die Zeit at Constantinople telegraphs that the porte declares that the news from Salonika gives grounds for the gravest apprehension.

Ladenburg, Thalmann & Co., of New York, announce that they have completed negotiations whereby new and important interests have become identified with the Seaboard Air Line Railroad Company.

Announcement was made this morning that the headquarters of the General Agent of the Seaboard Air Line of this district are to be removed from Washington to Philadelphia. General Agent W. E. Conklyn will be in charge.

President and Mrs. Roosevelt spent most of the day cruising about the sound on the Sylph. Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Riis were the President's guests on the little voyage. President Roosevelt has received word from Sir Thomas Lipton, accepting the invitation sent him to view the naval manoeuvres off Oyster Bay next Monday from the Mayflower.

Frederick MacMonnies, the distinguished American sculptor, has been awarded the contract to design a model for the statute of General McClellan which is to be added to the public art collection of Washington. The award was made by a commission consisting of Secretary of War Root, Senator Wetmore, of Rhode Island, and General Ruggles.

Kay Wood, colored, shot James Sanders, while in an argument over how much education a negro should have, this morning at Indianapolis, Ind. A score of white men attacked the negro who fled. The mob pursued him and Wood was finally shot by his pursuers. The excitement is high as the affair hap-
who had. The mob pursued him and Wood was finally shot by his pursuers. The excitement is high as the affair happened on down town streets. Both men will recover. Peter McCarthy, while drunk, had a row with his landlady, Mrs. Anna Haslem, in Cleveland, Ohio, this morning, about board. He seized a tumber, filled it with carbolic acid, and threw it over Mr. Haslem and two women boarders. Mrs. Haslem was blinded and will probably die. One of the other women will lose her arm and the third was frightfully burned. McCarthy is in custody.

YOUR SUMMER VACATION. If you take one you will want to keep in touch with home. The best way to do this is to have the Journal mailed to you. Leave your order before starting. We will change the address as often as you desire.
It is sincerely to be hoped that Mr. Stone, the new grand chief of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, will prove as conservative and able a man as was his predecessor, P. M. Arthur.

The shooting affray of yesterday, growing out of a trivial cause, was due, as a large majority of such affrays are, to the pistol habit. Every unauthorized carrier of a pistol who can be convicted should be made an example of.

The best way for a saloon keeper to show his good intent in the matter of obedience to the law is to tear out the partitions, if he have a wineroom down stairs, or to sublet the rooms if they be upstairs to some more reputable business.

Patrolman Dugan deserves credit for facing a mob yesterday and threatening to shoot if they laid hands on a fugitive negro whom they were pursuing with the usual cry of "lynch him." Better a dozen persons killed by an officer in the discharge of duty than one lynched.

It is understood that the Citizens' League is looking up the record of each candidate and will publish such information as it can obtain for the benefit of voters. If this work is done honestly and without bias a real service can be done to the average citizen too busy to fully inform himself of such details. He will want to know, for instance, how many gambiers, wine-room keepers and others of that element were indicted on the initiative of Mr. Holtzman while he was prosecutor, or how much he helped or retarded the efforts of the Denny administration to clean up the city.

The announcement of Secretary Root's intended retirement from the Cabinet will be received with regret by the country. Entering national politics at a critical time and assuming important duties without previous experience in that line he has developed rare executive ability and resourcefulness. No secretary of war in recent years has impressed himself more distinctly on the affairs of his department and of the country generally. Mr. Root will not retire for several months yet, so the President will have ample time to select his successor.

The Colorado miners who were run out of Idaho Springs by a mob of business men are making it very warm for leaders of the mob through legal proceedings. On Tuesday a much worse outrage was committed on officers of the United Mine Workers in Alabama, and it is to be hoped that the national organization will use the money and legal talent at its command to pursue the matter until the perpetrators of the deed are properly punished. When people undertake to seize the functions of the law and commit mob violence their prominence in social or business life does not make the deed one whit better, but rather worse, for they should have intelligence enough to uphold the majesty of the law, instead of trampling it under foot.

Within the last week or two several large defalcations have been reported of bank officers or managers of trust funds. In Boston the custodian of a preachers' aid fund embazled several hundred thousand dollars and is now a fugitive from justice. At Newbern, N. C., a bank cashier absconded leaving behind him a shortage of $125,000. At Circleville, O., a bank cashier is missing and the books show a shortage of $75,000. In each of these cases the defaulters had stood high in the estimation of all who knew them and their downfall was due to one and the same cause—speculating in stocks or on the grain market. That sort of thing is sufficiently dangerous when one speculates with his own money; but whoever begins it with other people's money invites ruin and disgrace.

The Journal sees no reason for regret or criticism on the part of anyone over the agitation that has resulted in the mayor's rigid order against the winerooms, except on the part of the keepers themselves. When the revelations came up in the form of arrests of young girls in these dives the judge of the Juvenile Court and the news-

papers of the city very promptly raised an outcry against this hideous form of vice. When the matter came to the Police Court the prosecutor and judge thereof did their full duty. The revelations came during the absence of the mayor, and he had not returned more than a few hours when his edict against the dens went forth. It is now the duty of the police force, from the superintendent down to the last patrolman, to see that the mayor's order is carried out to the letter, and the Journal has no doubt the police will do their full duty in the matter.

GREAT BRITAIN TO RESTRICT IMMIGRATION.

The report of a British royal commission in favor of a new immigration law excluding undesirable classes is a step towards a new departure in British legislation. Great Britain has furnished a large number of emigrants to other countries and to her own colonies and has wholesome laws regarding it, but she has received comparatively little immigration from other countries. There was a time when the immigration of Irish laborers to England and Scotland was greatly deprecated by leading men of those countries as a menace to home labor. Carlyle said the Irish laborers, barefooted and ragged, restricting themselves to potatoes and whisky, had carried their habit of living in cellars and of congregating several families together into one room, even with pigs as companions, over to England. Even so liberal a man as John Stuart Mill favored prohibiting such an immigration to protect English workmen. The Scotch census report of 1871 spoke strongly against what it termed "The Irish Invasion," which it said "can easily have more ruinous effects upon the Scotch population than even the inroads of the Saxons, Danes and Normans." It said the immigration of such a multitude of laborers of the lowest class, with scarcely any education whatever, could have only the most injurious influence and that "It is painful to think what the ultimate consequences of this Irish immigration will be for the character and habits of our people and for the future prospects of the country." This gloomy view expressed in a Scotch census report little more than thirty years ago was not realized and neither did Parliament adopt the surprising suggestion that emigration from one part of the British islands to another should be prohibited.

The legislation now proposed will be the first that Great Britain has adopted to restrict foreign immigration. It is based on the American idea of excluding undesirable classes and follows the American law pretty closely except that it does not include Anarchists. Political refugees and Anarchists have never been excluded from Great Britain, her dependence as to these being on police surveillance and enforcement of law. The right of one country to refuse to accept the criminals, paupers, etc., of another is admitted by all, the only question being as to how it shall be exercised. That England proposes to exercise it now for the first time shows that some
closed. That England proposes to exercise it now for the first time shows that some reason has arisen for it, though the report of the royal commission does not name any. The undesirable classes whom it is proposed to exclude are "prostitutes, lunatics, convicted criminals and any one who is in danger of becoming a public charge." Our law includes in addition to these classes assisted emigrants and contract laborers. Other provisions of the British bill relating to the deportation of undesirable emigrants, holding steamship lines responsible, etc., are modeled closely on our law. RACE DUEL IN A STREET Each Duellist Wounded and Policeman Holds Crowd at Bay.
[SPECIAL DESPATCH TO THE HERALD.]

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind., Wednesday.—Comments made upon recent race riots resulted this morning in a street duel between a white man and a negro, in which both were wounded. A riot followed, in which the negro was the central figure, and his escape with his life was due to a policeman, who held the mob at bay by drawing his revolver and promptly summoning assistance.

The trouble started at half-past six o'clock in a saloon. James Saunders, a night watchman, declared to a friend with whom he was drinking that what had happened had "served the niggers right." Kay Woods, a negro, rushed at Saunders. In the struggle both men went into the street, drew revolvers and exchanged five shots each, emptying the weapons. Saunders was hit in the hand and Woods in the arm.

Woods started to run and the gathering crowd shouted:—"Lynch the nigger!" Several men seized Woods, when Policeman Dugan came to his assistance with a drawn revolver, and held him until several bicycle policemen arrived. Woods and Saunders were both held by the police.
kay-wood-indianapolis-1903-08-12.A6:
LYNCHING IS PREVENTED BY OFFICER WITH A GUN
Indianapolis, Aug. 14. — Two hundred white men pursued a negro with cries of "Lynch him," "Lynch him," on one of the city's principal business streets. A pistol shot was fired by some one in the crowd, and the fleeing negro's right arm fell helplessly to his side, broken by the bullet. Workingmen crowded the streets and street cars on their way to work. John Saunders, white, and Kay Woods, colored, had an argument in a saloon at West and Washington streets, which ended in a pistol fight, in which Saunders was shot in the hand.

Woods started to run, and in an instant the crowds on the street started in pursuit, several shots being fired at the fleeing negro, who finally ran into the arms of a policeman just as his right arm was broken by a bullet. The officer had hard work to keep the crowd at bay with a drawn revolver till assistance arrived from the Central station. Woods was taken to the station, the crowd following with angry demonstrations nearly to the jail doors.

ANDERSON, S. C., WEDNESDAY, AUGUST 19, 1903.
GENERAL NEWS.
The government crop report indicates much improved condition of cotton.

New York is going to make a cheese that will weigh two tons and will likely exhibit it at the St. Louis exposition.

A madman at Winfield, Kan., fired into a crowd of 5,000 people, killing three people and seriously injuring many others.

The yellow fever epidemic in Mexico is being closely guarded by United States authorities, to prevent it from entering this country.

Sol Benjo and wife of Winston-Salem, N. C., have been arrested on the charge of murdering their own daughter more than a year ago.

Albert W. Deibel, teller of the City National bank of Canton, O., has been arrested on the charge of embezzling $22,000 of the bank's money.

The Mexican cotton boll weevil has crossed the Mississippi river and has appeared in the government experiment station near New Orleans.

The legislature of Georgia has enacted a law permitting counties to use their convicts under sentence of five years and less for working highways.

It is said if Tammany be successful in the city elections in New York that organization will declare for Grover Cleveland for the presidency.

The records show that the trade between this country and Russia, has been larger during the year just ended than it has for the past twenty years.

The West Indian storm was more destructive to life and property than at first supposed. Fifty persons were killed and the property loss is placed at $10,000,000.

By shutting down the cotton mills at Fall River, Mass., 7,500 hands are idle. Sixteen mills are affected. They are not expected to start up till the new crop goes into market.

The Bulgarian insurgents have begun their bloody work. They attacked and captured the Turkish village of Renatti, killing all of the inhabitants of the place except two.

Kay Wood, colored, shot James Sanders, white, in Indianapolis, Ind., on Wednesday in a discussion of how much education a negro ought to have. A mob pursued Wood and shot him.

Dr. Stiles, the discoverer of the parasite that is said to destroy the mosquito, is busily engaged in breeding them in large numbers with a view to turning them loose on the mosquitoes.

An attempt was made at Hillsboro, Ohio, to lynch Maynard Hudson, colored, for assaulting a 12-year-old white girl. The mob broke into the jail, but the negro had been spirited away.

A mob dynamited a negro's house in Oklahoma City, Okl., on Thursday. The whites in a certain section of the city have ordered the negroes to leave, and a race war is threatened.

It is said that experiments with X-rays have nearly cost Mr. Edison his eyesight. His assistant, Charles Dally, has lost one of his arms, and it is possible that the other will also have to be amputated.

A pretty young woman was arrested at Bristol, Tenn., on Monday charged with robbing guests at various hotels. She had several sums of money when arrested and some checks payable to other persons.

Pittsburg, Pa., claims to be the home of the champion chicken thief of the United States, in the person of Henry Vaunt, colored. Vaunt confesses to having stolen for 10,000 to 13,000 chickens in the past five years.

In Macon, Ga., last week the recorder sent a white woman and a negro woman to the Bibb county chasingang for a term of four months for getting drunk. They got drunk together and were handcuffed together when sent out to work.

— Willard S. Allen, of Boston, treasurer of the Preachers' Aid society of the New England Methodist conference, after fleeing to Canada wrote back on Wednesday a confession that he was a defaulter to the amount of more than $80,000 of the society's funds.

— Astonishment prevailed in Asheville, N. O., railroad circles when it became known Monday that O. D. Guire had been arrested on the charge of embezzlement. Guire held the position of yardmaster with the Southern Railway Company an a warrant which was served during the forenoon charges him with having embezzled $1,000 by reporting overtime on the wages of the large number of men employed

TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES
The factory of Janeway and Carpenter, wall paper manufacturers of New Brunswick, N. J., employed 300 hands, was forced to shut down today on account of the shortage of coal. The company has been unable to obtain soft coal in sufficient quantity to steadily run the plant.

Thomas J. Conrad, manager of the Macon Baggage Transfer company at Macon, Ga., was shot this morning at the Union Depot by a negro wagon driver named Arthur Shiver. The ball struck Conrad in the head killing him instantly. The trouble rose over a dispute about some baggage. The negro is still at large.

A man supposed to be Henry D. Williams of Pittston, Pa., was found dead in a room today at the Lion hotel, New York, asphyxiated by gas. His death is supposed to have been accidental. The dead man was about 35 years of age, five feet six inches tall, weight 140 pounds with light hair and mustasche. The left hand was gone.

Conrad Vincent, aged 21, a cloak salesman, is dying at the Sacred Heart Hospital, in Manchester, N. H. He was to have been married to a Miss Rivard at 8 o'clock last night. He was dressing and was told to hurry as the carriage was waiting. In his wish to obey he fell down stairs, dislocating his neck and receiving concussion of the brain.

J. Rogers, a Hammontown druggist and with interests in an oyster business in Port Norris, N. J., has disappeared, leaving behind, it is alleged, indorsed paper to the amount of $35,000. Warrants are out for his arrest.
macon-macon-1903-01-03-2.A4:
NEGRO KILLED CONRAD.
Shooting Occurred at the Union Depot at Macon. Macon Jan. 5-Thomas J. Conrad
Shooting Occurred at the Union Depot at Macon.

Macon, Jan. 5.—Thomas J. Conrad, baggage master at the Union Depot, was shot and killed this morning at 8:30 o'clock by a young negro employee named Oscar Shiver, as the result of a trafling dispute a few hours before in regard to the negro coming to work late Sunday morning.

The shot was fired while the office force was inside and no one was near except Jim Shiver, the brother of the negro who did the killing. The bullet which was 38-calibre, entered just above the right eye. Conrad fell to the ground and never spoke a word, dying twenty minutes after he had been taken up and carried into the office by Jim Geeslin and Car Inspector Dillon.

The murdered man was about 35 years old, was genial, accommodating and liked by everybody. Indignation was rife as soon as the deed became known. Jim Shiver was arrested and declared by the coroner's jury to be an accomplice.

Oscar Shiver made a dash for the swamp and has not since been seen. He is a stout black negro, wearing a tan overcoat and a brown hat turned up on one side. Sheriff Wescott and a strong posse are now on his trail, and it is thought that by morning he will be captured.

B. F. Merritt testified that on Saturday night he overheard Jim Shiver declare with reference to Conrad that he knew "when a white man got advantage" and that he would be "fixed for him." It is thought from this and the other evidence that the negro had planned the death of Conrad in cold blood. There are many who say that if caught Shiver will never be put in jail, but the authorities are taking every precaution against violence.

The dead man leaves a wife and three children.

BAGGAGE AGENT IS KILLED.
People Indignant Because Negro Shot Him Over Trifling Dispute
(By the Associated Press.)

Macon, Ga., Jan. 5.—Thos. J. Conrad, the baggage agent at the Union depot here, was shot and killed at nine o'clock this morning by a young negro employee named Oscar Shiver. The killing was the result of a trifling dispute with reference to the negro being late on Sunday morning.

Shiver made a dash for the swamps and has not been seen since the shooting.

Jim Shiver, the brother of the negro who did the shooting, has been arrested as an accomplice.

WASN'T THE MURDERER.

The negro, Oscar Showers or Shiv.
WASN'T THE MURDERER.

The negro, Oscar Showers or Shivers, who shot Baggagemaster Thomas J. Conrad at the Union depot at Macon Monday morning, was thought to have captured on board the southbound Southern due at board the southbound Southern due at Macon at 12:55 a.m., which was an hour late. A negro boarded the train in the yards at Macon and rode in the blind baggage to Bullards, when he went into the coach and two negro passengers tried to conceal him with their coats, but Conductor John A. Eldson located him and pulled him out, though he thought at the time that he was only a tramp trying to beat his way. He told Baggagemaster Marion Baughan, who is an ex-detective of Macon, of what had happened. The idea suggested itself at once that the man arrested might be the murderer. Baughan then went back and found that the negro answered the description. He had Conductor Eldson to wire the night dispatcher at Macon so that the dispatcher could instruct the sheriff at Eastman to meet the train and take charge of the negro. When the train reached Eastman, the sheriff was on hand and the negro turned over to him. When officers from Macon arrived it was found the man was not Shivers. Crowds gathered at Macon to take the negro from the officers and lynch him, but they had no prisoner on their return.

Cream of News.
Brief Summary of Most Important Events of Each Day.
---

night. Mayor Mims retired, and first work of new council was to arrange to investigate police board.

—Atlanta Water Power and Electric Company is enjoined from constructing railroad from Roswell to Bull Sluice.

—Thomas Conrad, assistant baggage master at the Macon, Ga., union passenger station, was killed Monday by Arthur Shivers, a negro helper.

—The People's bank of Barnesville, Ga., makes an assignment, closing a long period of litigation.

—At Oneonto, Ala., Miss Alldreage, daughter of the sheriff, frees two prisoners and elopes with one of them.

—Richmond, Va., has an epidemic of smallpox, while deaths are still reported from lockjaw caused by wounds from toy guns.

—The South Carolina railroad commission decides that the charges against the Southern railway as to diverting cotton from Charleston have not been proven.

—Congress reconvened Monday after the holiday recess. The coal situation was discussed in the senate. In the house Mr. Bartlett had a sharp spat with Speaker Henderson.

—Governor Taft, of the Philippines, will be named to succeed Justice Shiras on the supreme bench. General Luke Wright will succeed Taft as Governor.

—Former Premier Lagasta, of Spain, died at his home in Madrid Monday. All his associates in the liberal cabinet were at his bedside.

—Muscogee county, Ga., schools will in the future use Uunied States histories of southern authorship.

—Governor Terrell accepts invitation to visit Savannah, Ga., on February 22. An elaborate military program is to be arranged.

—The number of deaths from lock-jaw caused by toy pistols reaches twenty-seven, seven deaths being reported from Charleston, S. C., and many from Norfolk, Va.

—The race between Teller and Wolcott in Colorado is an interesting one. Teller, the democratic candidate, has four republican opponents.

—Members of the Order of Railway Trainmen and Conductors met at St. Louis Monday to receive answer to demand for increased pay.

—Complete details of the wreck near Birmingham on the Southern Saturday night show that one man was killed and twenty-eight injured.

—The baby elephant Topsy, who has killed three men, was electrocuted Coney Island, New York, Saturday.

—A party of fifty-four negroes leave Savannah for Liberia.

—The Blue Ridge, Ga., Mining Company is put into the hands of receivers.

—The annual report of State Treasurer Whitfield shows Florida to be in excellent financial condition.

—In a recent fire at Gadsden, Ala., one man is burned to death.

—Georgia Society of New York will give its second annual banquet on February 3.

—Preachers of Richmond are fighting the proposition to legalize Sunday racing.

—Henry Watterson, editor of the Courier-Journal Louisville, Ky., makes another attack on New York's "four hundred."

—At Scranton, Pa., four houses were destroyed by a cave-in, caused by the earth giving way over the workings of a mine.

Castro says his course is correct and everything depends on the conduct of the allies.

Mexicans claim the bubonic plague came to their country from China on a ship arriving December 15.

Hon. J. R. Lamar, of Augusta, is appointed associate justice of the Georgia state supreme court to succeed Justice W. A. Little, who has resigned.

With vistors of a $150 payout float
SHIVERS CAUGHT AGAIN?

With visions of a $150 reward floating before him, Detective Jenkins of Macon has gone to St. Augustine, Fla., to take to Macon a man supposed to be Oscar Shivers, the murderer of Conrad. monroe-monroe-1903-09.A1:
ARMED WITH GUNS

MONROE, LA., PLANTERS PREVENT NEGROES LEAVING FOR PINE BLUFF.

Thought the Negroes Were Coming Here to Take Work in Cotton Fields of Jefferson County.
NEEDED ON LOUISIANA FARMS.
A negro excursion to this city from Monroe, La., was scheduled for Sunday, but none of the negroes came from Monroe by reason of the fact that they were prevented from boarding the train by a large number of white citizens of that city armed with shot guns and other weapons. The fear expressed on the part of the whites was that if the negroes came to Pine Bluff or this section of the state they would stay here, and negro help is badly needed in Louisiana to gather the cotton crop, which is a trifle earlier than in Arkansas. When the time came for the excursion train to leave Monroe nearly 400 negroes were at the depot and many of them had purchased tickets for Pine Bluff. The excursion party was met by the white citizens and told they could not leave the place. The excursion train would be allowed to pull out but the negroes would be compelled to stay in Monroe, as they were needed there to work. The whites emphasized their statements with loaded guns, threatening to make it hot for any of the blacks who tried to board the train.

This action on the part of the citizens of Monroe pays a deserved tribute to Arkansas, for it seems that the objection made to the excursion was that the negroes would find better wages here and not go back to Louisiana. Arkansas is ready to employ all cotton pickers that are willing to work, but the promoters of the excursion say it was not their intention of inducing the negroes to leave their homes as all excursion tickets were sold as round trip tickets.

The movement to keep the negroes from leaving Monroe was an organized one, many of the overseers on the large plantations stationing themselves on the principal roads armed with shot guns. Here they met the negroes as they started to the train and turned them back. For three stations out this was done and not a black man boarded the excursion train within thirty miles of its starting point. The train came to Pine Bluff, however, carrying about 250 negroes. It left last night at 11 o'clock and so far as can be learned all the excursionists went back to their homes.
monroe-monroe-1903-09.A2:
PECULIAR STORY TOLD BY NEGROES.
Louisiana Planters Feared That Their Negro Laborers Were About to Be Kidnaped.
Pine Bluff, Sept. 29.—A peculiar story is told by negro excursionists just arrived in Pine Bluff from Louisiana. The excursionists came from below Monroe, and at Monroe they state a large number of negroes were prepared to join the party, having secured tickets to Pine Bluff. Farmers in the vicinity had a posse at the train with shotguns, which were brought into play to keep the negroes from Monroe at home. The farmers feared that the negroes might come here and be kept by planters in this vicinity who are short-handed. Labor in North Louisiana is very scarce.

moultrie-moultrie-1903-08-29.A1:
WHIPPED AN INSOLENT NEGRO.
"Strangers" at Moultrie Cause a Mild Sensation over Unruly Black.
Moultrie, Sept. 1.—Saturday night, while the Atlantic and Birmingham train from Fitzgerald was at the depot, a negro employe of the road became involved in a quarrel with Walter LeGrave, a young boy, who is a clerk at the depot. Without any warning the negro, who is a big strapping fellow, kicked LeGrave in the face, rendering him unconscious. The conductor of the train started to the boy's rescue in a determined manner, but was stopped by Marshal Cason. The negro later in the evening gave bond and was released. While walking down the street after his liberation he was approached by two white men, one on either side, who commanded him to "keep walking," which he did, the men accompanying him. In the course of their walk they went beyond the city limits, and what happened after is mere conjecture, except that the negro has not since been seen, as he is not able to walk. It is reported that a buggy trace in the hands of a strong man played an important part in the punishment. It is impossible to ascertain the names of the white men, as they are said to be strangers in the city.

FRIGHTEN A LITTLE NEGRO
Chased by Soldiers, He Falls and Breaks His Leg.
(Special to News and Observer.) New Born N. C. July 28 As the S

(Special to News and Observer.)
New Bern, N. C., July 28.—As the Second Regiment passed through New Bern from the camp this morning, many soldiers got after and frightened a young negro boy of tender age. Frightened by their uniforms and their demeanor. He fled, chased by soldiers. The boy fell on the railroad track, breaking his leg in two places. Dr. R. S. Primrose was called to dress his wounds.
newbern-newbern-1903-08.A2:
WHO CHASED NEGRO?
Trouble at New Bern Where a Leg Was Broken.
Captain Stronach Exonerates Raleigh Company and Says it Was Some of the Detail in the Bagage Car.
Thre was published yesterday morning a telegram from New Bern telling of the chasing of a negro boy by soldiers returning from the encampment and that the negro had fallen and broken his leg.

The Oak City Guards, under command of Capt. Van Dalen Stronach, were on the train and Capt. Stronach was interviewed yesterday about the matter. In speaking of it he gave the following:

"The military trains were collected at New Bern after leaving Morehead City as certain companies were to diverge there while others went on to Goldsboro. The men of each company were in different coaches, a guard being at each door. The only men not under guard were those in charge of the baggage in the various coaches who got out, and apparently with only fun in view began chasing a negro, who, if he was a boy in age was certainly grown in size. I was out on the ground and saw the occurrence. The negro, who was some forty or fifty feet ahead of the men, started to run across the track. His foot caught under the railroad iron and he fell, breaking his leg near the foot. The men scampered back to the baggage car."

"Col. Bragaw asked me about the affair and I told him that I did not know any of the men. I am absolutely certain that no member of my company was engaged in the matter, as Mr. W. N. H. Smith was in the baggage car and was not in the crowd that chased the negro. Those who know him know that he would not engage in such an affair.

"Col. Bragaw could not give the men engaged. He had every attention given the negro while he was in New Bern and arranged to have him cared for after we left. He regretted the affair and handled it as best he could."

Capt. Stronach says that the encampment was a delightful and the instruction given was of great value. The men enjoyed themselves very much and all in all he thinks the encampment did good.

The soldiers were not paid off at Morehead but a check will later be sent, made out to each individual for the six days' service as follows: Captain, $30; first lieutenant, $24.96; second lieutenant, $23.33; first sergeant, $4.40; second sergeant, $3.40; corporal, $3; private, $2.60. The payments were not made at Morehead owing to the great number of checks to be signed after rolls were made out, but this will be attended to at once.

An incident at the Hamlet hotel more than a week ago has been pretty well noticed by the press of the country at large. Booker Washington, the Tuskegee Institute negro of Alabama, who has considerable ability, went to the Hamlet hotel for breakfast. There were twenty-seven other negroes with him. They were on a special train which was late and had telegraphed ahead for breakfast at Hamlet. When they arrived at Hamlet the dining-room was in readiness for them and they walked in and ate at the tables used for white guests and in the same dining-room. It turned out that there were white passengers on the train, one of them being United States Senator Bacon, of Georgia, but all refused to go into a side room prepared for them while Booker Washington and his companions occupied the main dining-room. Since the incident, the statement has gone out from Baltimore that three hundred traveling men have declared that they will never again eat at that hotel. Some days ago three negroes asked lunch at a white lunch counter in Raleigh, and because they were refused the white folks' seats at white folks' counter, they refused to take lunch. Do they want social equality? If they do they are doomed to disappointment forever in the South. Booker Washington and President Roosevelt have set the negro race back twenty-five years as regards the privileges to be accorded them by the white race.

It is a common thing to hear persons speak of "professional jurors." They mean, of course, those who hang about a courthouse during every court waiting for a chance to be called into the jury box. Every man who loves justice and wishes to see the law obeyed, and criminals punished and who hopes to see legal differences settled on a high plane of thinking and acting, would be glad to see the professional juror laid on the shelf for good and always. To be sure, the fact that a man served on a jury last year does not of itself unfit him to serve on a jury again this year; but to serve on a jury for every court year in and year out causes one to regard almost all the court proceedings as a matter of course—a sort of hum-drum business—and he
eyery court year in and year out causes one to regard almost all the court proceedings as a matter of course—a sort of hum-drum business—and he becomes careless of his duty. "A new broom sweeps clean" applies as well to a juror as to anything else. And then some people say it makes them tired to see a man hanging around a court house looking lor a jury job. Then, too, it smacks of a leisure that judges in our courts have come to look upon with disfavor. Whenever a man now-a-days asks a judge in the court house to excuse him from jury service because he is too busy to spare the time, the judge generally replies that he wants busy men on the jury, and therefore that plea does not excuse him. Again we say that a professional juror is in general disfavor with the best citizens of his county, and his decisions can never have the effect that follows the decision of jurors who would rather be at home.

AN EFFORT TO LYNCH
An Affray in Which a White Man Who Shot a Negro Was Beaten.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

CHATHAM, VA., Aug. 10.—In a general mix-up at Pecaway, Pittsylvania county, Saturday night, Joe Echols shot five times at a negro, four shots wounding him, but not seriously.

The negro's friends then turned upon Echols and gave him a severe beating, but did not inflict any serious wounds.

Thomas N. Williams, independent candidate for county treasurer of Pittsylvania, was opening a speech when the row began, and his hearers very soon disappeared, terrorized.

Later an effort was made to lynch the negro, but cooler heads prevailed.

philip-johnson-campti-1903-01-12.A1:
NEGRO CHURCH LEADER SHOT. Was Ordered Out of Town and Came Back Killed on Sight.
NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 13.—Philip Johnson, another leader of the Church of God, organized by the negro prophet, Smith, has been killed by the law officers of Natchiloches parish. Smith organized his church in Houston, Tex., from which town he was driven. He came to Shreveport, La., and he and his followers were ordered away by the police.

They moved their church to Bossier parish, where trouble ensued, resulting in the murder of John Gray Foster, one of the largest planters in Louisiana, and the lynching of Prophet Smith and the leader of the church. Johnson moved to Campti. He was ordered away from there by a committee of citizens and left. He returned yesterday and was shot to death by the two deputy sheriffs who tried to arrest him.

philip-johnson-campti-1903-01-12.A3:
MUST PROTECT NEGROES. Southern Judge Says Failure to Do So Reflects on the White Race.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Jan. 28.—In a stirring charge to the Grand Jury of Natchitoches parish, La., the District Judge has called for the indictment or for misdemeanor impeachment of all justices of the peace and other officials who have failed to suppress mob violence within their jurisdictions and noting the lynching of a negro at Robeline, two shot to death at Campti and two others badly beaten at Clarence.

"The white people of this State," said the Judge, in his charge, "now exercise all of the powers of government. Our laws are made by white men and administered by white men. To say that the courts and the laws are inadequate to the punishment of the negro when he deserves punishment, and to his protection when he is entitled to protection, is to confess that our race is incapable of administering the government. We cannot turn these helpless people over to the tender mercies of irresponsible mobs without incurring the contempt of all enlightened people and the wrath of a righteous God."

Indictments are looked for in consequence of the charge.
philip-johnson-campti-1903-01-12.A4:

Our laws are made by white men and administered by white men. To say that the courts and the laws are inadequate to the punishment of the negro when he deserves punishment, and to his protection when he is entitled to protection, is to confess that our race is incapable of administering the government. We cannot turn these helpless people over to the tender mercies of irresponsible mobs without incurring the contempt of all enlightened people and the wrath of a righteous God."

It is entirely true that if "the white man's government" that prevails in the South can't do better than it does in regard to the negroes it doesn't do the white race much credit. That race ought to govern by law instead of lawlessness if it is what it claims to be.

Colored Pastor Says They Should Buy Guns.
Colored Pastor Says They Should Buy Guns.

Chicago, June 24.—At a meeting of the colored people held last night to protest against the lynching of the negro, David E. Wyatt, at Belleville, Ill., Rev. C. H. Thomas, one of the speakers, advised his hearers that they should, if the hanging and burning of colored men is not stopped by the regular authorities, sell their coats and buy guns with which to defend themselves.

Others expressed similar sentiments and before the meeting adjourned the negroes present were worked up to a high pitch of excitement. Mrs. Ida Parnell said the negroes must organize to fight their own battle, adding that they never could expect the white men to fight for them until they had shown themselves capable of fighting for themselves.

Governor Yates's Secretary Received Notice That There Would Be Lynching at Belleville.
LETTER HAS BEEN RECOVERED.
Negro Pastor Thomas Informed Colonel Oglesby Two Days Before Wyatt Was Hanged.
REPUBLIC SPECIAL.
Springfield, Ill., June 25.—Colonel John D. Oglesby, private secretary to the Governor, was in error when he rebuked the Reverend C. H. Thomas, pastor of the African Methodist Episcopal Church at Belleville. In a speech in Chicago Mr. Thomas said he wrote to Governor Yates preceding the Belleville lynching, warning the executive of the condition of affairs existing there.

Colonel Oglesby in his communication denied that a letter had been received at the executive office from Thomas, and demanded a retraction of the statements made concerning Governor Yates.

But Thomas's letter, written June 2 last, has turned up in the Attorney General's office, and bears the file mark of the executive office, together with the date of its arrival, June 3. The letter was found upon a desk in the Attorney General's office, but there was no other communication with it. The original, bearing the executive file mark, has been preserved.

Thomas's letter, written on June 2, preceded the lynching of Wyatt, which did not occur until the night of June 6, by four days. Thomas had received an anonymous communication warning him to leave Belleville, and this, together with the other warnings, induced his communication of warning to Governor Yates. The warning to Thomas to leave Belleville, a copy of which is contained in his letter to Yates, is as follows:

WARNING TO THOMAS.

"St. Louis, Mo.: Charles Thomas, Colored—You have now drawn the color line and are trying to force the niggers on the white race. You are well aware that a nigger was not born to equal the whites. So, being you want to force matters, I will tell you plain, and you may take gospel heed that if you do not leave Belleville in two weeks you will, with your bravados, meet your place in line with other good niggers. So you may take this timely warning and go where the niggers have more rights than Belleville.

"This is no joke, but a plain warning, so if you fail to go then take the result.

"A CITIZEN."

The original of this copy was mailed to me the twenty-second day of May, and the time for the trouble to begin is June 5.

REVEREND C. H. THOMAS.
Pastor of A. M. E. Church.

Since an investigation of the Belleville lynching has commenced it is learned that a party of negroes at Thebes, Alexander County, asked for protection as far back as March 26 last. On that date a party of white men shot into a railroad camp of negroes, killing one negro and injuring another. The shooting, it was said, was the result of an attempted assault upon a white girl by one of the negroes in the camp. The negroes were driven from the vicinity, and their property confiscated.

Three letters bearing upon this incident, it is claimed now, were sent to the Executive office, asking for assistance in serving warrants. The negroes said they could identify the men who did the shooting, but that they were unable to get the civil authorities to serve the warrants necessary to a legal prosecution. The negroes who were concerned in the Thebes affair state they received one reply from the Executive office to their three letters.

NEGRO WOUNDED BY POSSE. Sheriff Captures Robert Bishop After Desperate Fight.
Robert Bishop, the negro who shot Samuel Ellis and a woman known as "Black Ida" in a graders' camp at Oakville, St. Louis County, last Friday night, was captured yesterday by the Sheriff of Ste. Genevieve after a desperate fight.

During the encounter Bishop was shot four times by the Sheriff and his posse, who had shotguns loaded with buckshot, according to information which reached the Sheriff's office in Clayton.

After Bishop shot Ellis and the woman he fled to avoid lynching, as the other graders tried to hang him and pursued him for a mile with that purpose. He escaped in the forests along the Mississippi River and continued southwardly.

Constable John Schaper of Carondelet Township sent the negro's description to Seward Missouri office, from which this Bishop was recognized when he appeared in the vicinity of Ste. Genevieve. The Sheriff was notified and organized a posse to capture Bishop. They found him in a clump of bushes on the outskirts of the town and called upon him to surrender.

In answer Bishop drew a 41-calliber bulldog revolver from his pocket and opened fire. The posse returned it, and in the melee four shots were buried in the negro, seriously wounding him. He was taken to a hospital.

Constable Schaper departed for Ste. Genevieve yesterday evening to bring Bishop back.

STRIKERS BEAT A DRIVER.
MOB HOLDS UP ONE OF CURTIS & BLAISDELL'S NEW MEN.
Knocked From His Seat and Pounded and Kicked Till He Fired a Revolver in the Air-Then the Yelling Crowd Chases His Cart-Another Assault.
The striking drivers who quit the firm of Curtis & Blaisdell, coal dealers, were responsible for a man hunt in West street yesterday afternoon.

Robert J. Hamlin, a negro, who with several others was employed to fill the places of the men on strike, was held up and assaulted at Dey and Washington streets shortly after noon by a band of husky strikers.

Hamlin was returning to the branch yard at 102 Washington street when one of the crowd dashed into the roadway and stopped the horses. At the same moment two other men climbed up to the driver's seat and ordered Hamlin to get down. When he refused one of the men struck him on the chest, knocking him into the wagon.

The two strikers jumped in after him and each time he attempted to rise floored him with a kick or punch. One of the two grabbed a heavy iron shovel and whacked Hamlin over the shoulders and back.

Hamlin drew a revolver and fired two shots in the air. The two strikers couldn't get out of the wagon fast enough, and Hamlin started his team at a gallop down Dey street, while a yelling crowd trailed behind him.
At West street Hamlin turned north. There were fully a thousand people after him then.

At Barclay street Hamlin steered for the Hoboken ferryhouse. A line of cabs blocked his way and he jumped from his wagon and ran into the ferryhouse waiting room.

Patrolman Filan of the Church street station, ran over when he saw the mob. He thought a murder had been committed and arrested Hamlin.

When Hamlin had told his story he arrested James O'Brien of 79 Oliver street and Robert Nelligan of 102 Washington street, whom the negro pointed out as his assailants.

They were held by Magistrate Pool in the Tombs Court in 2,000 bail each for examination to-day. Hamlin, against whom a charge of carrying concealed weapons was made was, paroled in the custody of his counsel. His injuries were not serious.

Henry Thomas, a non-union negro driver for the same firm, was arrested yesterday for protecting himself from a crowd of the striking drivers. When he took his team from Curtis & Blaisdell's place at Eightieth street and the North river on Tuesday he was stoned by a gang of men and boys.

When he started out yesterday he took along a razor. Charles Oakley, one of the strikers, attempted to pull Thomas off his wagon yesterday afternoon and Thomas used his razor with such effect that Oakiey went to the hospital. A policeman took Thomas to the West Sixty-eighth street station.

G. B. Curtis, head of the firm, said yesterday that they were getting all the men they needed.

Magistrate Pool Prefers Ball for an Arrested Striker.
John Deveey, one of the striking drivers for Curtis & Blaisdell, coal dealers, was arrested in the Tombs police court yesterday afternoon on a charge of assaulting Robert J. Hamlin, the negro, who was attacked by several strikers on Wednesday afternoon.

When two men who were arrested after the attack were arraigned, Hamlin said that he recognized a man who was sitting among the spectators as one of his assailants. The man was Deveey. He was arraigned on a charge of assault and Lawyer Sullivan, who appeared for him, asked Magistrate Pool to parole the prisoner until to-day.

"The union will guarantee his appearance in court when he is wanted," said Mr. Sullivan.

"I can't take the guarantee of a union," said Magistrate Pool. He held Deveey in $500 bail for examination to-day.

The other two prisoners were held in $1,000 bail each.
robert-hamlin-new-york-1903-09-09.A7:
DIDN'T BELONG TO THE UNION. TEAMSTER TELLS COURT HE WAS ASSAULTED ON HIS WAGON. Two Union Men, He Says, Called Him "Scab" and Beat Him Over the Head With a Shovel, and He Fired a Shot to Scare Them Away-Verdict To-day.
A jury will be called upon to report to Recorder Goff in the Court of General Sessions this morning as to the guilt of Robert Nelligan and James O'Brien, members of the Teamsters' Union, accused of felonious assault upon a man who was impertinent enough to take a job which had been made vacant by orders of the union.

Evidence in the case was given yesterday by all the participants in the fray which led to the arrest of Nelligan and O'Brien. Robert Hamlin, a negro driver for Curtis & Blaisdell, coal dealers, testified that on Sept. 9 he was on his way with a coal wagon to the Washington street yard of the firm when the prisoners jumped out from the curb at Washington and Dey streets, yelling "Scab! Scab!" and climbed on his wagon. With Hamlin on the wagon was James Flood, a "trimmer," or shoveller. Flood jumped off.

Hamlin told the jury that one of the two prisoners caught up a shovel from the wagon and beat him on the head with it. They then tried to drag him from the wagon seat. Hamlin said that he pulled a revolver, with which he had provided himself by advice of his employers, and fired a shot in the air to scare his assailants. He then jumped from the wagon.

"Why," asked Assistant District Attorney O'Connor, "did you jump?"

"Because," he said, "bout five hundred men made a jump to kill me—an' o' co'se I run!"

He ran to the Barclay street ferry house, where Policeman Finlan arrested him.

Flood, the treasurer, corroborated Hamlin's testimony. Policeman Finlan told how he saw Hamlin chased by Nelligan, O'Brien and a crowd, yelling "Kill the nigger!" and how he arrested Hamlin, who said that he had fired at the two accused men in self-defence. He said that he took a revolver from Hamlin and that one cartridge in it was exploded.

For the defence Nelligan testified that he had seen Hamlin driving "one of our wagons" on Washington street; that he had yelled "scab" at Hamlin; that Hamlin had fired at him twice and that he and O'Brien had then tried to close with Hamlin, who ran.

Assistant District Attorney O'Connor cross-examined.

"How did you happen to see your washing ton street just at that time?" he asked.

"We were going to supper at my house," said Nelligan, whose home is at 102 Washington street.

"Had you been at a meeting of your union at Forty-second street that morning?" asked Mr. O'Connor.

"Yes," said Nelligan.

"Had you been appointed at that meeting to interfere with any effort of Curtis & Blaisdell to run wagons?"

Nelligan hesitated. Then he said that he guessed he hadn't.

"Had O'Brien?"

"Not," said Nelligan, "as I know of."

Mr. O'Connor, despite the objections of counsel for the union men, put several questions tending to show that Nelligan and O'Brien were on "picket duty." Nelligan simply admitted that he and O'Brien had gone to the Curtis & Blaisdell yards, "to see what was going on there."

This was Nelligan's version of the approach he and O'Brien made to Hamlin:

"We went up to the truck and asked him didn't he know he was a 'scab' and wasn't he ashamed to take jobs that belonged to other people and why didn't he get off the wagon and quit, like a man?"

O'Brien's testimony was like Nelligan's except that he was sure that Hamlin only fired once.

Mrs. Hughes, Nelligan's sister, swore that "Bob was a poor hard working boy and never harmed no man."
In the summing up, counsel for the de-

fendants told the jury that jails were not built as places of confinement for hard- working men, even if they were a bit rough at times. Recorder Goff will charge the jury this morning. IRON LEAGUE WILL CONFER.

But Without Promises to Help Parks's Union—Gompers Arranged It.

President Gompers and Vice-President Duncan of the American Federation of Labor, who came here last week to "settle the building trades troubles," returned to Washington yesterday afternoon, having arranged for this afternoon a conference between a sub-committee of the labor members of the Employers' Association arbitration board and the executive committee of the Iron League. The employers have made it clear, however, that while the conference has been agreed to, the Iron League will not recede from its position in regard to Sam Parks's old union, Local No. 2 of the Iron Workers' International Union.

The labor sub-committee of the conference consists of Philip Weinseimer of the Plumbers, James J. Daly of the Tile layers and James P. Archibald of the Paper Hangers. If any proposition is made on which action seems desirable it will be submitted to a full meeting of the Iron League to-morrow.

About 150 members of Local No. 2 applied at the headquarters of the New York Housesmiths' Union yesterday for permits to work, but only twenty-two permits were given. Each recipient signed the arbitration agreement and joined the new union. Among the applicants who didn't get permits were one or two former officers in Local No. 2. P. C. McGuire, secretary of the union, said that in about two weeks the foundations for six new buildings for which members of the Iron League have contracts will be ready, and this will enable 500 or 600 more iron workers to be employed.

Frank Buchanan of the International Association of Iron Workers returned to town yesterday, but had nothing to say. His hope now is to get the remaining members of Local No. 2 into the new union and to bring the latter under the jurisdiction of the International Association.

POLICE CALLED TO NEW UNION MEETING.

A dozen or more of the old Sam Parks type of unionists went around last night to the meeting of the new union in Teutonia Assembly Rooms, in Sixteenth street, determined to make trouble. Apparently, their plan was to start disputes all over the hall and fighting later. The officers of the new union sent to the East Twenty-second street police. Capt. Gallagher rushed out with his reserves and got ten more men from the East Thirty-fifth street station. The police scattered around the hall and all signs of violence ceased.

UNION SLUGGERS CONVICTED
For Thumping a Non-Union Driver—Extreme Penalty Five Years.
Robert Nelligan and James O'Brien, members of the Teamsters' Union, were convicted yesterday after a trial before Recorder Goff in the General Sessions of feloni us assault upon Robert Hamlin, a negro, driver for Curtis & Blaisdell, coal dealers.

Hamlin, who had taken a job after a strike called by his union on Curtis & Blaisdell for ordering their drivers to work part of Labor Day, was beaten over the head with a shovel on Sept. 9 at Washington and Dey streets while he was driving a wagon to the Washington street yard of the firm.

In summing up Assistant District Attorney O'Connor said that the State does not object to a reasonable amount of argument to get men to join trade unions. It does not contemplate, however, he said, that the argument shall be carried beyond reason. The accused men, he said, had gone too far and the cause of union labor could receive nothing but damage from such advocacy as they had used.

The jury agreed with him. Nelligan and O'Brien may get five years for their crime. They were remanded for sentence

Investigation of Crimes Under Alabama Peonage Laws Discloses That Blacks Were Often Beaten to Death—Laborers Bought and Sold at Convict Farms While Under Sentence of a Year for Such Petty Transactions as Borrowing a Dollar.

Having once signed the contract, the negro must live up to its very letter. The alternative is slavery.

When a negro is convicted of violating a contract in any degree he is promptly sentenced to imprisonment and fined.

Very rarely can he pay the fine, and so he is sent to a convict farm to work it out. Then his slavery begins, and that he ever regains his freedom is not the fault of his "owner." It is always easy to trump up accusations under which he is kept in bondage.

NEGROES WHIPPED TO DEATH.

It is almost impossible to exaggerate the horrors of the peonage system which have been brought to light since the Federal Grand Jury has been investigating the matter.

Murder of the "slaves" has been common. Negroes have been whipped to death, clubbed to death, and, more mercifully, shot to death. Scores and scores have been maimed for life.

Women and children have been torn by savage dogs and have suffered like the men. Case after case has been found by the Grand Jury in which affidavits and testimony under oath have left not a trace of doubt of the tortures inflicted upon their helpless victims by the brutal "slave drivers."

One negro, who appeared before the Grand Jury, exhibited his legs, which were scarred from the thighs to the heels. They had been torn and mangled by dogs sent in pursuit of the negro on one occasion when he endeavored to escape from his tortures.

sarah-nealy-1903-04-15.A5:
SLAVERY IN ALABAMA.
Government Starts an Investigation Into Awful Outrages. The investigation of the postage cases
The investigation of the peonage cases by the federal grand jury at Montgomery, Ala., has brought out evidence of more shocking crimes than existed in the slave days. Many negroes have shown scars from the lash and others showed where their bones had been broken with clubs.

One affidavit signed by six negroes told the following story of the murder of Sarah Nealy, a negro woman:

"I was at Mr. Turner's place. She came on Monday and stayed until Tuesday. She came down to Fletcher Turner's. We were in the new ground. She could not pile brush like he wanted her to and he took her down and placed her across a log. I held her feet and another negro held her by the head. Allen Turner whipped her with a buggy trace 100 lashes. Then he put a pair of hand-cuffs on her and tied a rope around her wrists, and made me draw her up so her feet would just touch the ground, and he let her hang two hours.

"Just about dinner we lowered her and she crawled over to some brushes. Mr. Turner told me to throw her a pone of bread. She said she couldn't eat. After dinner I was told to go and tell her she must go to work. She pulled the lid of her eye down and said she could not see. She then crawled behind the brush pile and laid down and never got up any more. Allen Turner beat her over the head with a pistol again and she died."

The principal offender against the peonage law, John W. Pace of Tallapoosa County, has practically confessed. He did not believe that he could be punished. Indeed, he told Mr. Reece and Mr. Sternfeldt that he had committed no crime. There are others among the indicted men who have turned government evidence. Their stories disclose the conspiracy to violate not only the laws of Alabama, but of the United States for the purpose of maintaining a system of slavery. They have trafficked in negroes to the extent of buying and selling them.

sarah-nealy-1903-04-15.A11:
PEONAGE IN ALABAMA.
Some of the Alarming Reports Upon Which the Grand Jury Has Found 99 Indictments.

The trial of the quarry owners, landlords, constables, magistrates and guards involved in depriving negro citizens of their liberty began this week at Montgomery, Ala. The grand jury unanimously found 99 indictments on sworn testimony by blacks, corroborated in many cases by white men. The New York Evening Post printed Monday night a letter several columns long from a correspondent in Montgomery, who relates several astonishing stories of the "new slavery." based largely on the evidence upon which indictments has been found. A negress in good health was beaten so much and subjected to such awful tortures from 8 o'clock until 2 that she died at 3. After being beaten she was hanged up by the wrists. When she was cut down she lay down behind a log. She was soon ordered back to work, and not being able to comply, she was struck and jumped upon until she soon died. The body was buried hastily and quietly early the next morning. Under the peonage system in Alabama, negroes, says the correspondent, would often have no trial at all; the usual method, however, was to have a mock trial, which would lead the negro to think he had been through a court and convicted; but the record would not be put upon the docket. Suppression of records was part of the agreement between the persons who profited by peonage. Therefore the county treasury received no part of the fine, or what was practically the purchase money exacted; that was divided between the constables and men who made a business of gathering stray or idle negroes and arresting them on fictitious charges. The magistrates were either relatives, creatures or employes of the landowners. In one instance the proposition came first in this form: A planter said to a justice of the peace: "Now, these are just ordinary cases, and we needn't put them on your docket."

The justice was complaisant, for he owed his position to the man who made the suggestion. Besides, in certain counties, the proprietors are a terror to the countryside. They have political power, and a disturbing recklessness about taking human life.

Up to the present time evidence of 99 instances of peonage, or conspiracy, or depriving of liberty, or brutality, or murder, has been obtained in two counties in this judicial district. The Montgomery Advertiser, deploring exaggeration, points out that these cases are against less than a score of persons, and concern only two plantations. There is no need for exaggeration for any purpose—here are 99 cases in which the grand jury found true bills; all the crimes took place on live farms within three years; and the investigations have only just begun! As one views Coosa and Tallapoosa through the testimony of black men who have suffered, of white men who have felt outraged to see these things going on, the confessions of magistrate and constable, and landowner (Mr Pace, who

pleaded guilty to the acts charged, speaks quite frankly in private), the conditions are awful.

Negroes wandering through are picked up by the constable, who charges them with carrying razors, or of running away from a contract, or of stealing a ride on a train, or of vagrancy, or of owing a debt, or of allowing a master's mule to bite another man's corn, and they are taken before a magistrate, who fines them $5, or six-months' labor; and then a planter who needs laborers comes and says he will pay the fine if the prisoners will work it out on his place. They have been convicted; it is jail or agree to work out the sentence, and they agree and sign a contract. Often the form of trying them is dispensed with. Constable and landowner take the arrested negroes out behind the saw-mill, talk with them, return, and say to the magistrate, "draw us up a contract." And the magistrate draws up the contract and approves it and the landowner pays the constable or whoever captured the negroes, $17, or $40, or $75, whatever bargain can be struck. Then, tied together, the peons are carted away to the plantation. Arriving there, they are untied, locked up over night, and put to work in the fields next day. There are guards to see that they do their labor without escape. On one or two plantations involved there is a stockade; on two there is always a guard patroling with a rifle. On all the plantations are frequent whippings—one negress was beaten to death last year.

Some 40 negroes and negresses have been found whose grievances as to whippings have not been outlawed by the statute of limitation (three years). The details are distressing, and do not vary much. There is testimony that one negro was killed with a spade by the son of the proprietor: that a negress who ran away was chased by dogs, "torn about the stomach." whipped when she got back, and kept three months more in servitude. Another negress is mentioned whose uncle says she was killed by the son of the proprietor, a young man, with close-set eyes, acting as overseer. One of three negroes who was "bought for $50" was whipped about every other day for four months, lying face down, one man on his head and one man sitting on his legs. Another was whipped with hickory sticks with empty cartidges on the end. Another was whipped twice; once his hands were tied under his knees, and the guard told him to "count the licks" he was giving him on the bare back—after counting to 15 the negro could not count any more. Another, working out a debt of $6.16 with seven months' labor, was whipped every day with plow lines, and cut on the nose once with a hoe. The guards on X's place had a strap, "the leather about 18 inches long, the handle about the same—the strap is about as broad as three fingers"; with this "Joe" Patterson, who worked a year for a dollar debt, was whipped. A boy of 18 was whipped two or three times a day. One tells of being "licked" with a stick as big as a broom handle; a negress shows scars on her back from a buggy trace; a 16-years-old girl was whipped once in her 12-months' service—they placed her over a bench, pulled up her clothes, and struck her "15 or 20 times with a strap that was doubled four times, and was fastened at the end with tacks."

"Great" is Alabama justice and law!
sarah-nealy-1903-04-15.A15:
TURNERS IN COURT
LAWYERS CONSUMED ALL OF TIME ARGUING DEMMURRERS.
Taking of Evidence in Peonage Cases May Begin Today—Defendants Contend There Was No System.
Fletcher Turner, a farmer of Tallapoosa County, and his son, Allen Turner, charged with peonage, appeared for trial in the United States Court yesterday, but the lawyers consumed all of the session in arguing demurrers.

The argument will be concluded this morning and one of the cases against Fletcher Turner may go to trial.

There were four cases each against the Turners, but it is understood the District Attorney will nolle prosse the cases which alleged that the Turners beat to death a negro girl, Sarah Healy, while she was held in servitude.

When the court convened at 12 o'clock yesterday the Turners sat near the bar with their lawyers, Col. T. L. Bulger, W. M. Lackey, J. G. Sorrell of Dadeville and W. W. Pearson of Montgomery.

District Attorney W. S. Reese said that the first case would be that in which the Government claimed the Turners had held Glenny Helms, a negro, in servitude. Mr. Reese also announced that the lawyers had agreed to argue the demurrers to the indictments filed by lawyers for the Turners. These demurrers contend that no system of peonage existed in Tallapoosa County and consequently the Turners are not guilty of peonage within the meaning of the law. Judge Jones overruled this contention on the part of lawyers for J. W. Pace, who pleaded guilty and appealed one of his cases.

After Judge Jones had discharged the jurors until 10 o'clock this morning, Mr. Pearson opened the argument sustaining the demurrers. He spoke about one hour and was answered by District Attorney Reese and Assistant District Attorney Julius Sternfeld.

About 2 o'clock Mr. Sternfeld concluded and the court recessed until 10 o'clock this morning, when Colonel Bulger will conclude the argument.

John W. Pace reached Montgomery yesterday. It is expected that he will be an important witness in the Turner cases. Many other citizens of Tallapoosa County are in town.

It developed yesterday that the government had already agreed to continue the three cases against Allen Turner, the young son of Fletcher Turner until the next term of the court.

Fletcher Turner yesterday bitterly denied the reported cruelty to Cornelia Hammock, a negress who was a County convict at his place. He said the woman was not beaten to death on his farm by his son Allen Turner as had been repeatedly stated by sensational newspapers. He says the woman died of disease.

The case growing out of the alleged holding of Cornelia Hammock in peonage by Turner was not pressed by District Attorney Reese after Turner had had his witnesses summoned. One of the most important witnesses in this case for Turner was Gus Oliver, a brother of the Hammock woman. Oliver had moved from Tallapoosa County and Turner spent considerable money locating him. He was found by officers in Birmingham and came to Montgomery yesterday at the expense of Turner and before Turner could advise the officers that his presence here was not necessary.

Oliver, who is an educated negro, said yesterday that he had known Mr. Turner all of his life and had always been treated well by him. His sister, he said, had been convicted of stealing a ring and he tried to get some one in Dadeville to confess judgment for her but failed. Mr. Turner, he said, offered to lend him money to pay her fine but he replied that he could not spend any more money on her. Mr. Turner, he said, did not want to take her to his place because she was too ill to work.

Turner had a contract with the City Council of Dadeville to take all of its hard labor prisoners.

Oliver said that the woman finally went to Turner's place and a few days afterwards he heard she was dead and buried. He said he heard conflicting reports about the death of his sister. Mr. Turner, he said, volunteered to have the body exhumed at his expense if Oliver wanted to remove it from the cemetery in the country to Dadeville, but Oliver had replied he did not care to do so.

Oliver came to Montgomery to testify concerning the treatment of his sister in behalf of Turner but the case having been not pressed his evidence was not necessary.

Turner declares that the woman died of disease and was buried in a respectable manner. He expressed regret that the court had failed to enquire into her death since the incident had been given so much publicity.
