seab-sharp-milltown-1903-05.A1:
WHITES AND NEGROES ROW.
Trouble Began in a Fight at Naylor. Valdosta News Notes. Valdosta, Ga. May 15. Reports from
Valdosta, Ga., May 15.—Reports from Milltown, in Berrien county, are to the effect that the white people and negroes have been having some trouble this week, which grew out of an assault made by a negro engineer, named Seab Sharp, upon the white conductor of the Gress Railroad, Charlie Clanton. Clanton ordered the negro back to his engine to make a coupling to some flatcars at Naylor. The negro did not obey the order, and a quarerl ensued. The engineer got off of his engine and gave the conductor a sound drubbing, being much the larger man.

When the train went back to Milltown, Clanton's friends started out to find Sharp. He dodged them and skipped out. Then the white citizens got up a petition, asking Mr. Gress not to employ any more negroes as engineers on his trains. A negro at Milltown heard of the petition and expressed himself pretty freely in regard to it. That night a committee waited on him and gave him a thrashing.

Miss Carrie Beamus of Atlanta and Prof. J. P. Haber of Alabama are in Valdosta to work up interest in a negro industrial college at this place. Miss Beamus was here several months ago and will remain until next week. The business men and citizens met with her last evening to hear her plans discussed, and they were pleased with them. Another meeting will be held Monday at noon to take up the matter again. Her idea is to get up a school that will teach the negroes to work with their hands and to try and make good, industrious people of them.

She has large moneyed connections at the North, and as soon as she selects the place for the school she will go North and make her financial arrangements. She wants from 100 to 150 acres of land within three miles of the city.

News from the Clyatteville district relates of the attempted assassination of Silas Smith, a well known negro man, as he was going from his kitchen to his dining room, the shot being fired at him by some one hid in the bushes just outside of his yard. No one knows who did the shooting, though the supposition is that a woman was in the case in some way. Silas was not dead at last accounts, though he was not expected to recover.

The heaviest rain of the season fell here last night, accompanied by a terrific thunderstorm. The rain drenched the streets and overflowed the water mains. The canal in the northern part of the city overflowed and the water stood from one to three feet deep in yards and gardens along its route. The car line on Patterson street was covered with water to a depth of two feet. The streets were badly washed.

shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A2: EXCITEMENT IN WINCHESTER.—Winchester was thrown into excitement at midnight Thursday night over a murderous attack made by two negroes upon Capt. James H. Haymaker, a City Councilman and a night watchman for Baker & Co., wholesale grocers, and when one of the negroes (Shack Johnson) was captured several hours later he narrowly escaped lynching at the hands of an infuriated mob. As he was being taken to the station a revolver was pressed against his breast by a member of the mob, who was prevented from killing the negro by an officer snatching the weapon from him. Johnson was severely handled. His scalp was laid open in numerous places by members of the mob who sought to kill him, and he was glad to reach the protection of an iron cell. About 10 o'clock Johnson and another negro supposed to be Harry Wilshire had a fight in an alley over some women. The two men continued cursing each other, and Captain Haymaker ordered them to desist. Johnson knocked the aged night watchman down, and while the latter was drawing his revolver Wilshire grasped him and took the weapon away from him. They then kicked the prostrate man into an unconscious condition and once returned to kill him with his own revolver. Charles Brown, another negro, went to Captain Haymaker's assistance, and the arrival of others scared the negroes off.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A3:
Drunken Negroes Attack Captain J. M. Haymaker.
THURMAN DIVORCE CASE
Judge Harrison Allows the Lady $40 a Month and Court and A.torneys' Fees-No Trouble Between Rhea and Thurman.
---

Rhea and Thurman

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

WINCHESTER, VA., August 28.—Captain James M. Haymaker, one of the most prominent citizens of Winchester, a Confederate veteran, fireman and Councilman, was murderously assaulted shortly after 11 o'clock last night by two drunken negro brutes, Shack Johnson and Henry Thompson, while he was discharging his duty as a special policeman and watchman at Baker and Company's wholesale merchandise house. He was knocked down and beaten in the face with his own revolver, and kicked and cuffed in a vicious manner. His life was saved by Charles Brown, a colored man, who scared the negroes off. Captain Haymaker's condition is quite serious.

The negro Thompson escaped on a freight train, but was arrested and will be brought back. The police prevented an infuriated crowd of armed men from making an attempt to lynch Johnson. He was hurriedly taken to jail and placed in a strong steel cage.

Arguments were begun in the Circuit Court this afternoon before Judge Thomas W. Harrison for attorney's fees and allowance by attorneys in the celebrated suit for divorce filed by Mrs. Thurman against her husband, General Charles Thurman, of Clarke county. A large crowd was attracted to the court-room in the City Hall to hear the speeches of Judge W. F. Rhea, of Bristol, and Lewis Bumgardner, of Staunton, for Mrs. Thurman, and Messrs. A. and Conrad Kownslar, of Berryville, for the defendant. So far no trouble has occurred between Judge Rhea and General Thurman, who have exchanged newspaper interviews. General Thurman is not here, but his wife is.

At 10 o'clock to-night Judge Harrison signed a decree allowing the complainant $40 per month for support, pending a proper presentation of the case to the court; $250 court expenses and $400 attorneys' fees, to be paid upon certified vouchers, all of which is to come from General Thurman.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A4:
WOULD-BE LYNCHERS.
Yesterday a new turn was given the Haymaker assault case in Winchester on which Shack Johnson, an negro tough, narrowly escaped lynching, when a number of well-known white men were arrested on complaint of Mollie Smith, colored, charged with breaking into her house Monday night and firing off revolvers. It was learned Monday night that Johnson's accomplice, Harry Johnson, was in hiding in Winchester. The police endeavored to locate him and searching parties of young men were formed. A report was spread that the negro was at the Smith woman's house, and an attack was made on the place. Revolvers were fired, the door was broken down and the place thoroughly scarched, but Johnson had escaped. The crowd fired their revolvers in the house, and if Johnson had been found he would undoubtedly have been lynched on the spot. Last night the members of the crowd who were arrested were discharged in the Winchester Police Court.

A mob of 50 masked men went to the jail at Shawneetown, Ill., yesterday morning and demanded that Jailer Galloway turn over to them John Griffin, colored, who was under arrest for an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Hobbs, a white woman, near her own home. Griffin had been frightened away by the woman's screams and had been arrested a short while afterward. When the mob demanded that Jailer Galloway turn the negro over to them Galloway armed himself, and after reasoning with the men from the jail door, he warned them that any effort to force the jail would be at their own peril. The mob, in spite of the jailer's words, made several ineffectual attempts to break down the jail doors, finally dispersing about daylight. Many of the colored people are taking sides with Griffin, though some of them have, in fear of a race riot, left the town. No trouble has followed the visit of the mob to the jail yesterday morning, but preparations are making to take the negro to Carmi for safekeeping.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A7:
NARROWLY ESCAPED LYNCHING
NEGROES MAKE A BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WATCHMAN.
One of the Men Arrested and is Saved by the Timely Arrival of the Police.
Capt. James M. Haymaker, city councilman, of Winchester, was the victim late Thursday night of a murderous assault by two negroes, in which one of his assailants escaped lynching only by the timely arrival of the police. Captain Havmaker is a night watchman for Baker & Co., wholesale grocers.

About 11 o'clock "Shack" Johnson and another negro, who is thought to be Harry Wiltshire, of Atlanta, Ga.. got into an altercation. Afterward the men were walking up the railroad track cursing loudly, when Captain Haymaker ordered them to desist. Johnson knocked the aged night watchman down, and kicked the prostrate man in the face until he was unconscious. People were attracted to the scene and scared the negroes off. Search for the negroes was then instituted and Johnson was found. He resisted arrest, and was beaten almost into insensibility by the infuriated crowd. Twice on the way to the station house the prisoner was stopped with the intention of lynching. and as he entered the police station a man pointed a revolver against his heart.

As he was about to pull the trigger the police snatched the weapon from him.

Johnson was finally landed in a cell. Late yesterday Wiltshire was arrested at Brunswick, Md., and sentenced to four months in the Maryland House of Correction for stealing a ride on a freight train. The Virginia authorities will endeavor to have him brought to Winchester for trial.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A9:
PURSUIT OF CRIMINAL
A Posse of Citizens Try to Capture Henry Thomas.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

WINCHESTER, VA., Sept. 5.—Led by Chief S. A. Seabright and Officers McIntosh and Taylor, a party of armed men to-day endeavored to capture Henry Thomas, the negro who assaulted Capt. James M. Haymaker last week.

Thomas was located in a corn field near the Shenandoah River, in Clarke county, but it is believed he saw the men approaching and escaped.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A11:
A PREACHER'S HEROISM
Captain Haymaker's Assailant Given a Penetentiary Term.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

WINCHESTER, VA., Sept. 21.—In the City Court this afternoon Shack Johnson, a negro, was found guilty of a brutal attack upon Councilman James M. Haymaker, and given nine years and six months in the penitentiary. Last August, Johnson and Harry Thomas knocked Captain Haymaker down, kicked him into insensibility and would have killed him but for timely interference. Thomas escaped.

While attempting to ride a horse across Opequon last Saturday, Miss Nannie Maynard, who was attending a church picnic, fell into the stream. Hearing her eries, Rev. Charles D. Bulla, pastor of the Southern Methodist Church, plunged into the icy water and rescued the girl from danger.
shack-johnson-winchester-1903-08-28.A12:
QUICK TRIAL.
Indicted, tried, found guilty and sentenced all within a few hours—such was the experience Tuesday of Shack Johnson, the negro who brutally assaulted City Councilman James M. Haymaker in Winchester. The negro was found guilty and was sentenced to nine and a half years in the penitentiary. His accomplice, Harry Thomas, who is at large, was also indicted.

sharman-stevens-roanoke-1903-06.A1:
SHERMAN STEVENS IN JAIL.
Negro Accused of the Murder of His Father.
Wedowee, June 22.—(Special.)—Saturday afternoon, Sherman Stevens, colored, was lodged in jail after having eluded the officers for nearly a year.

Last October, during a protracted meeting at the negro church just west of town, a disturbance was raised and Stevens shot and mortally wounded his father, Lee Stevens, who died a short while afterward. He is thought to be the negro who criminally assaulted a Mrs. Kelly, about fifteen miles northeast of Wedowee some two weeks ago.

Stevens was captured about eight miles south of Wedowee by A. L. Kent and Z. T. McMurray.

A reward of $100 was offered by the State for the arrest of Stevens for the murder of his father. If he is shown to have been guilty of the other crime mentioned, a reward will be paid by the citizens of the community in which it was committed.
sharman-stevens-roanoke-1903-06.A2:
LYNCHING PREVENTED.
Sherman Stevens Carried to Wedowee For Safekeeping.
Wedowee, July 2.—(Special.)—News was received here yesterday afternoon that Monday evening about 100 persons from Cleburne County were at the iron bridge five miles from Wedowee, and were to meet a crowd from near Graham, this County, and would then proceed to the jail here and secure the person of Sherman Stevens, who, it is thought, criminally assaulted Mrs. Kelly, near Graham, a few weeks ago.

Sheriff Kent and Deputy Fuller made arrangements immediately upon the receipt of the information, and carried Stevens to Opelika last night for safe-keeping. The crowd from Graham failed to show up and consequently there was no "party." The Sheriff and his deputy deserve credit for the protection of their prisoner
sharman-stevens-roanoke-1903-06.A3:
STEVENS WAS CONVICTED.
Notorious Parricide is Given the Death Sentence.
Death Sentence.

Roanoke, Aug. 22—(Special.)—One of the largest crowds ever seen in Wedowee was assembled there yesterday to witness the trial of Sharman Stevens, colored, on the charge of murdering his father in this County last November. The murderer escaped at the time of the killing, and was only captured two months ago. In the time that he was at large a criminal assault was made upon Mrs. Kelley, a respectable lady of Lamar beat, and circumstances pointed to Stevens as the guilty wretch. When he was captured a mob was organized to lynch him, but the officers brought him here and boarded the early train for Opelika, where the negro had been in jail since till brought back to the scene of his crime this week. He was tried upon the original charge of murder, but there were open threats that the negro would be lynched if the jury failed to affix the death penalty. The evidence was very strong, however, and the jury consumed only a few minutes in agreeing upon a verdict. When it was read many in the vast audience began to applaud, but were promptly and harshly approved by Judge Denson. The late for the execution has not yet been fixed.

Thomas F. Pate died at his home here yesterday at the age of 74 years. He had been living in this community about sixty years, and for a long while had been a member of the Board of Trustees of Roanoke College.
sharman-stevens-roanoke-1903-06.A4:
HANGING IN WEDOWEE:
Second Legal Execution in the History of the County.
Roanoke. Sept. 26.—(Special.)—Sharman Stevens, a negro, was hanged in Wedowee yesterday, having been convicted at the last term of the circuit court of killing his father at a negro camp meeting.

Sheriff Kent allowed all the features of the execution to be public except that the body of the criminal was concealed from view after it passed through the trap door. It is estimated that there were 3,000 people present from this and several adjoining counties.

This was the second legal hanging in the history of the county. The first was the case of Tom Barsh last spring, when the report was sent out all over the country that the condemned man had come to life after being cut down. In both these cases, however, the negros' necks were broken and death had done its work before the bodies were cut down.

taylor-gibbs-stanford-1903-11-25.A1:
SAVED FROM MOB VIOLENCE. County Attorney's Plea Prevents a Lynching in Kentucky.
FRANKFORT, Ky., Nov. 26.—Taylor Gibbs' a negro under arrest at Stanford for assault, was saved from mob violence by an angry gathering of incensed citizens of Garrard county last night by the plea of County Attorney James Hamilton and the promise that prompt trial would be had.

Gibbs was charged with attempting to stop the buggy of Mrs. Jack Hamilton and daughter as they drove from Stanford to their home. They reported the attempted assault to Joe Burnside, a farmer living on the road, who telephoned to Stanford, and posses were started in pursuit.

Gibbs was captured and confessed. He was landed in jail, and as the night drew on a mob gathered, and but for the prompt plea of Hamilton he would have been lynched. An indictment will be filed tomorrow, and the trial will be taken up immediately.

taylor-gibbs-stanford-1903-11-25.A6:
The Jail Closely Guarded.
The Jail Closely Guarded. Lancaster, Ky., Nov. 27.—The jail where the Negro Gibbs, who attempted to assault Mrs. and Miss Henderson, is still being closely guarded, and rumors have been afloat all day that a mob was forming in the upper end of the county.
taylor-gibbs-stanford-1903-11-25.A9:
Almost A Lynching.
Wednesday afternoon, of last week, as Mrs Jack Hendren and daughter were returning to their home in the county, they were met, just beyond Mrs Hansbury West's by Taylor Gibbs, a trifling Chute negro, who had driven a drummer to Kirksville. The brute turned his buggy directly across the turnpike, jumped out and went ahead to meet the ladies' buggy. He grabbed at the bridle and the ladies began to whip the horse, which was a spirited one and jerked loose from the negro. He then grabbed the buggy, but the ladies continued to whip the horse and succeeded in passing the negro's vehicle. They thought the brute was on the rear of their buggy, and continued to run the horse on home. A telephone message was sent to Lancaster, and in almost less time than it takes to tell it, a number of citizens were on the road to meet the negro. He was met near W S Ferguson's farm, placed in a buggy and driven back to Mr Hendren's, where he was promptly identified. All the while the negro protested his innocence, but as the posse was returning, they were met by a band of infuriated citizens who would have hanged the negro had not the officers claimed they were not certain he was the right man. By the time the party reached town, the Public Square was filled with people, and cries of "Hang him!" soon set the town in an uproar. The negro was hustled into jail, and County Attorney Jim Hamilton came out and addressed the crowd, assuring the people that the grand jury, which was in session, would immediately indict, the trial would be pushed and the negro promptly landed in the penitentiary. As the crowd was composed principally of substantial citizens, men of good judgment, they took the right view, left the jail and the excitement died down. The next day being Thanksgiving, no court was held, but promptly Friday morning the case was taken up and an indictment returned. The case was called for trial, and the jury quickly sent him to the penitentiary for seven years, which is the limit of the law under the circumstances. The people were indignant when the crime was reported, and determined to hang the scoundrel, and, had the jail been entered, the other negro, "Ugs," who broke into the depot, would have been strung up, too. While we do not advocate violence, yet, had those two brutes been left swinging in the Park to be viewed by other notorious Chute "citizens," it would have had a decidedly good effect. Gibbs is only about nineteen years of age, and is a son of "Black Suse." He is about on a par with the rest of the gang of toughs which Lancaster must get rid of.

thomas-gilyard-joplin-1903-04-14.A2:
KILL AND BURN.

Mob of Infuriated Citizens of Joplin, Mo.,

Hang a Negro for Killing a Po- lice Officer.

RAID BLACK QUARTER.

Drive Out All the Residents and Fire Houses.

Peace Officers and Firemen Are Swept Aside.
RAID BLACK QUARTER.
Mayor Issues a Call for 500 Men.
Joplin, Mo., April 16.—Despite the efforts of the police and against the pleas and personal resistance of law-abiding citizens, an infuriated mob of several hundred men battered down the wall of the city jail last evening at 6 o'clock and dragged out Thomas Gilyard, a 20-year-old negro, charged with murdering a policeman, and in broad daylight hanged him to a telephone pole two blocks from the jail in the heart of Joplin.

The mob then threatened to drive every negro from the city and charged through their section of the town, shooting and setting fire to houses, five of which were burned.

The negro was charged with having murdered Police Officer C. Leslie, who was shot dead in the Kansas City Southern railroad yards while endeavoring to arrest several negroes suspected of theft.

Officer Leslie had ordered several negroes who had taken refuge in a boxcar to surrender and when they failed to do so he fired several shots at the car. During the shooting a negro slipped from the car and coming up behind the officer, shot him through the head.

Bloodhounds were brought from Webb City and placed on the trail, but the negro eluded the posse and remained in the thicket through the night on Turkey creek, two miles north of the city. In the morning the man hunt was resumed. Several hundred armed men and boys took to the woods after him.

At 2 oclock in the afternoon the negro came from his hiding place and went into a slaughter house near Midway park, where he told a story of having fallen from a train and being badly injured. Instead he was suffering from the wound he received at the hands of the officer he killed. Lee Fullerton and N. R. Bullock, two employes of the place, suspected him as the guilty negro and prepared to capture him. Fullerton pulled a six-shooter and Bullock drew a long butcher knife and commanded him to surrender. The negro had a rifle and defied arrest, but was finally captured and taken to Joplin.

News of the capture spread rapidly, and soon the jail where the negro had been taken was surrounded by a howling mob. Cries of "lynch him" arose on all sides, and City Attorney Decker and other prominent citizens mounted the steps of the jail and made strong pleas for law and order, which temporarily stayed, but did not appease the mob.

At first it was thought the wrong man had been captured, and several other prominent citizens climbed upon boxes to warn the crowd. The mob would not listen and hissed them down.

Securing a battering ram, they proceeded to break down the east wall of the jail. Every effort was made to prevent the entrance of the mob, but without avail, and within 15 minutes the infuriated men had gained entrance to the jail and secured the trembling negro, who was carried out, begging piteously for his life. He claimed to be innocent, and said he did not shoot the officer, but admitted that he was present at the time. The mob beat him furiously, and the negro fought like a tiger. He was partially dragged and carried two blocks away to the corner of Second and Wall streets.

Here several fights took place, and guns were flashed. Officers and citizens were on one side and the men who wanted the negro's life on the other.

During this time the negro lay upon the ground, begging for mercy. Three ropes were thrown to the leaders of the gang, but each time they were cut. Finally Sam Mitchell, one of the leaders, climbed a telephone pole and strung a rope over it. A score of men attempted to pull the negro from the ground. As many more seized the negro and pulled to prevent his being hanged. For some moments it was a veritable tug-of-war, but reinforcements on the free end of the rope proved the stronger and the negro, despite his protestations of innocence, was finally swung into the air and strangled to death, while shouts of satisfaction went up from the mob.

Several men in the crowd carried guns, but only one shot was taken at the body. The negro was apparently dead when strung up, and made but three or four struggles.

The crowd quickly quieted and the body was cut down and taken to the undertaking rooms by the coroner. The rope that did the hanging was cut into fragments by the curious as souvenirs.

Some claim the mob hanged the wrong man, but the evidence is so strong that there is little doubt of his guilt.

The lynching of the negro only temporarily satisfied the mob, and later hundreds of men again assembled and rioted through the negro section of the city, burning houses, stoning negroes, and finally drove every negro from the confines of Joplin. The police were powerless.

The first act of the mob after hanging the negro was to demand the release from jail of a local character known as "Hickory Bill," who was under arrest on the charge of assaulting a negro. In the hope that this would appease the mob the prisoner was set free.

But the mob did not disperse. Instead, a rush was made through Main street, the principal street of Joplin, and every negro was frightened off the street and fled to the north part of the city, where the colored population resides. In this way the negroes were driven from all parts of the city to the negro section. Then the mob charged down on the section. Stones were thrown, shots fired, doors and windows of negro houses were broken in and

OPLIN, MO., April 15.—Despite the pleading of City Attorney P. H. Decker and the efforts of law-abiding citizens, who were overcome in a tug-of-war over the body of the victim, a mob tonight hanged a negro tramp to a telegraph pole, after forcibly taking him from jail on the suspicion that he might be the man that last night shot to death Policeman Leslie while the officer was trying to arrest some negroes in the Kansas City Southern railroad yards.

The lynching of the negro served only temporarily to satisfy the indignation of the mob, and later tonight hundreds of men again assembled and rioted through the negro district, burning houses, stoning negroes, and finally driving every negro from Joplin. The police were powerless.

The negro who was lynched was found today in a slaughter house east of Joplin by Lee Fullerton. He was armed with a rifle. Fullerton slipped into the structure unobserved and crept up behind the negro. Fullerton sprang at the man and threw him down. The captor held a knife at the captive's throat until the negro surrendered the rifle. Pointing the rifle at the prisoner, Fullerton marched him to jail, which was surrounded by hundreds of people.

Lynched Negro Buried.
Joplin, Mo., April 16. After the coroner's jury had held an inquest over the body of Thomas Gilyard, the young negro lynched last night, he was buried early today at the city's expense. The bullet in Gilyard's leg corresponded with that missing from Officer Leslie's revolver, which fact makes the identity of the dead man sure. There was no excitement today and all fear of further trouble in the negro district has been dispelled.

Lefftwa: A colored man killed a soldierman in this city. The colored man was supposed to be a tramp. A large crowd of white rifflers broke he jail and lynched the man. Then, o satisfy their bellish wrath, they organ to drive all the colored powerhouse homes. Nearly all the colored citizens are leaving for St. Louis and the erritories—Reporter.

The Supreme Court Criticised JOPLIN LYNCHING DENOUNCED
What a harvest there will be if national injustices are punished with the same surety as individual wrong-doings! Brought here against his will, compelled to give his labor unrequited, every spark of manly principle repressed with the diabolical cunning and cruelty of the slavery system, the Negro has waited until now to feel the most cruel blow of all. So long as the slavery system continued the addition of such a wrong as the Dred Scott decision was endurable because of the enormity of our other wrongs. But now when we are told we are men with constitutional rights, it is too much to tell us that courts cannot maintain us in them. When the Supreme Court refused to hear the plea of Alabama Negroes to help them in their fight for their franchise, knowing as the world knows that they are deprived of it not because of ignorance or crime, but because they are black, it reaffirmed the celebrated dicum, "A Negro has no rights which a white man is bound to respect." The revolutionary fathers who fought for representation in the British Parliament have waited all these years to have their course declared improper, their cause unjust. Taxation without representation is right, so says the august Supreme Court by an overwhelming vote. The lives and property of Negroes are at the mercy of the rabble all over the land without fear of punishment. What, then, is left for us? Shall we offer up our lives for a country that refuses to deal justly by us politically, that persecutes us commercially and is diffident concerning our lives? Too late the good people of the various communities come to aid us when attacked by mob violence after seizing in motion the machinery that accomplishes our distranchement and would also remove our school facilities. It is true the better element of the South pleads for us. But of what avail? The mine has been fired and the awful catastrophe must come. An educator of that state in speaking of it says: The hanging of the Negro tramp, in broad daylight, with a course of delighted, applauding spectators, women included, was no unlooked for termination of the sentiment to which the murder of Patrolman Lester was a sequence. It was a premeditated outrage—an atrocity without palliation or the shadow of excuse. Its culmination in a perfect pandemonium of riot, outrage and arson could have been prevented if city and county officials had but availed themselves of the means offered them and which they declined to accept. The chief of police sat smoking a cigar while the mob battered in the jail door, after the unfortunate wretch had been placed in the hands of those sworn to maintain order and uphold the law. thomas-gilyard-joplin-1903-04-14.A37:
Acquitted of Leading Mob.
Samuel Mitchell, charged with being implicated in the mob that hanged a negro, Thomas Gilyard, in Joplin last spring, was acquitted in the circuit court at Carthage. The jury was out only thirty minutes. Mitchell was tried for the crime last spring, convicted and sentenced to ten years in the penitentiary but got a rew trial. J. C. Seifried, one of the witnesses for the defense, was arrested for perjury shortly after he had testified in the case. He testified that he was with Mitchell at a paint house south of Joplin at the time of the lynching, and it was his evidence that caused Mitchell's acquittal. He was arrested on information filed by the prosecuting attorney and taken before Judge Perkins, who fixed his bond at $1,000.

LYNCHING PROBABLE.
Three Negroes in Jail in Kentucky May Be Strung Up.
Maysville, Ky., Feb. 2.—John Sanford, his son Charles and Tom Mann, negroes, were arrested at 9:30 tonight charged with assaulting and robbing Mr. and Mrs. Farrow, an aged couple at Mount Gilead, Fleming County.

They were lodged in jail where they were identified by Mrs. Farrow. Feeling against the negroes is intense and a lynching is probable.

The men, it is alleged, entered the home of Mr. and Mrs. Farrow and awakening the couple from their sleep demanded money. Mr. Farrow gave them $50, but the robbers insisted on having more, and bound both Farrow and his wife. After making some threats, the men shot Mr. Farrow, inflicting a serious wound, and then made their escape.

The company is a good one and one of the best popular price Company's on the road. ROBBERS LANDED. Men Who Perpetrated Mt. Gilead Shooting Now in Jail.
Thomas Manns, Charles Sanford and Charles Morris, all colored, are now languishing in Jail in this city to answer for the attack made Sunday night on Mr. and Mrs. John B. Farrow of Mt. Gilead, as detailed in yesterday's paper.

The trio was arrested last night, the two former about 10 o'clock and the latter at 1:30 this morning.

After being Jailed Sanford made a statement of the shooting.

They secured their buggy Sunday from the stable of Mr. Joseph H. Brown, and going to Mt. Gilead got in their vicious work as before noted.

Sanford claims that Manns fired the first shot at Mr. Farrow, and that on leaving the house some one fired a second shot.

The men returned to Maysville immediately after the shooting and were here until arrested.

Taking into consideration the meager clues on which they had to work, the Maysville police did very creditable work in getting the parties in so short a time.

The reward for their capture had been increased to $500.
tom-manns-maysville-1903-02-03.A5:
TAKEN TO COVINGTON.
Lynching Prevented by Prompt Action of Maysville Officers.

Maysville, Ky., Feb. 3.—[Special.]—Charley Saunders, Tom Manns and Ed Morrison, all colored, charged with assaulting John Bruer Farrow, were hurried off to the Covington jail this afternoon to avoid a mob that was coming to-night from Mt. Carmel, Mt. Gilead and Orangeburg. Several hundred excited men followed the prisoners from the jail to the depot, and officers kept the crowd back with pistols. Men from Farrow's neighborhood have been quietly watching the jail, and there was no concealment that a mob was coming. The transfer to Covington was unexpected, else the movement would have been thwarted. The demonstrations toward the prisoners at the depot made them tremble. Charles G. Calvert, a prominent farmer of Orangeburg, was so frantic in his efforts to stop their removal that he was arrested.

Charley Saunders made full confession before the grand jury to-day, putting most of the blame on his two companions. Indictments were returned against all three prisoners for burglary and for shooting with intent to kill.

Farrow's physicians have hope of his ultimate recovery.
tom-manns-maysville-1903-02-03.A6:
TAKEN TO COVINGTON. Mann, Morris and Sanders Removed From Jail Here.
Thomas Mann and Charlie Sanders, two of the Negroes arrested for making an attack on Mr. and Mrs. John B. Farrow at their home near Mt. Gilead Sunday night, were taken before the Grand Jury yesterday afternoon.

Ed. Morris, the third man, was not taken out. Morris claims that the principal part of the work was done by the other two, and that he was simply their tool.

After examination Mann and Sanders were remanded to Jail.

Later, at 4:20 p. m., to avoid any further trouble, the three men were taken to the Covington Jail for safe keeping.

STATE TROOPS. Will Be Sent to Maysville to Protect Three Negroes on Trial. Frankfort, Ky., June 13. — State troops will go to Maysville Monday to protect, during trial, the three colored men accused of shooting John B. Farrow, an aged farmer, whom they had robbed. About 100 men will go, under command of Maj. Nelson Edwards, of Newport. The three men have been in the Covington jail for safe-keeping since they were arrested, last January. An armed mob gathered at the Maysville station last week to lynch the men, when it was tipped off they were to be brought back for trial. Seeing the danger, the authorities wired to Covington to hold the men there. TOBACCO PLANTS SOLD. Wm. Clarke Sons Co. Deeded to the Imperial Tobacco Co.
Henderson, Ky., June 13.—The William Clarke Sons Co. Friday deeded to the Imperial Tobacco Co. their plant in this city with its machinery and appurtenances, which is valued at $30,390. The deed also conveys the Clarke tobacco plant in Paducah. The consideration named is $5 and other valuable considerations. The Imperial Tobacco Co. was incorporated in the state February 26 of the present year by George A. Willis, Bristol, Eng.; Charles S. Clarke, Liverpool, Eng., and others.

JUDGE D. B. REDWINE.

He is a Candidate For the Circuit Judgeship.

Richmond, Ky., June 15.—The democratic committee of the 23d judicial district has been called to meet June 23 to fix a date for holding a convention to nominate candidates for circuit judge and commonwealth coroner.

There are three candidates to judge, D. B. Redwine, of Jackson; Robert Riddell, of Irwin, and D. D. Sublett, of Salyersville. The former is the present judge, and is presiding in the murder cases of Jett and White at Jackson.

One of the Mullins Dead.

Livingston, Ky., June 15.—In a drunken brawl at Sinks Station Sunday John Suttles shot and killed Obe Mullins. Two of the Mullinses were sentenced to the penitentiary at the May term of court for the murder of young James Scott, in the same neighborhood last fall. The two older brothers of Obe, Ed and Bee Mullins, served a term each in the penitentiary for murder and robbery.

A Defective Omission.

McCarty, of Kenton, indicted for operating a slot machine, but the indictment failed to allege that money was bet, won or lost on the slot machine, which was a defective omission, according to the ruling of the circuit judge and the court of appeals.

A Farmer's Sudden Death.

Carrollton, Ky., June 12.—Richard Davis, a prominent farmer of Upper White's Run, this county, died suddenly. He had gone into a doctor's office for medicine, and complained of feeling faint. He had scarcely reached the couch in the room before life was extinct.

Damage Suit Compromised.

Elizabethtown, Ky., June 12.—The suit of B. P. Perry, aministrator of Herman Callahan, who was killed in the coal chutes at Lebanon Junction in May, against the L. & N. railroad for $30,000 damages, has been compromised for $3,500.

Girl Died Suddenly.
Lancaster, Ky., June 12.—Miss Kate Stone, aged 46 years, while preparing to go out for a call at 2 o'clock Thursday afternoon, was stricken with cerebral hemorrhage and died at 7 o'clock.

Lexington, Ky., June 12.—Thomas Norris, aged 94, died in this city Thursday. He established the first news bureau in Lexington while the civil war was in progress, and for a number of years he was a newspaper agent in this city.

Big Fire at Mayslick.
Mayslick, Ky., June 12.—Fire Thursday destroyed the Ryan & Worthington livery stables, the Owsley saloon and several cottages. The Bank of Mayslick and Presbyterian church were damaged.

Mills of Justice Grind! THREE CAPITAL PRIZES! Sanders, Manns and Morris Get Five Years Each. Will Be Tried Today For Burglary May Some Day Be Tried For Murder.
Immediately on reassembling of Court yesterday morning the Commonwealth rested, and the Attorneys for defense put Sanders on the stand, who, in chief and on cross-examination, told substantially the story printed yesterday, emphasizing the statement that Manns was the leading spirit in the airfair and dragged him into it.

Officer Robert Thompson was called. He arrested Sanders and Manns, taking a pistol off the latter. Officer Pollitt arrested Morris. The pistol was muddy, Manns saying he had dropped it.

On motion of his counsel, Sanders withdrew his plea of "Not Guilty" and plead "Guilty."

The Court thereupon instructed the Jury, and without argument by counsel the Jury retired, returning in thirty-five minutes with a verdict fixing the penalty at five years in the Penitentiary—the limit provided by law.

An attempt at applause was promptly suppressed by the Court.
The witnesses in the cases against Manns and Morris were called, and both Commonwealth and defense announced ready as to Manns.

The former Jury was accepted by both sides and defendant Tom Manns entered a plea of Not Guilty.

THE TESTIMONY.

Charles Sanders, colored—Live in Maysville; know Tom Manns and Ed. Morris; Manns and I have been together frequently; Manns and Morris were with me at Farrow's house Sunday night, February 1st;—and then witness practically repeated the statements made on his own trial.

R. Clayton Farrow, Dr. J. J. Cook, 'Squire Sam T. Farrow, Joseph H. Brown, Henry Willis, George N. Crawford, Nick Gollenstein, R. P. Thompson and Millard F. Williams were examined, the result of their testimony being same as on trial of Sanders.

Thomas M. Russell was called to prove the ownership of the bicycle lamp which the fellows had, and Simon Nelson to prove that he had sold Manns the hat that was found at Farrow's.

The Attorney for defense moved to exclude the testimony of Sanders; and the Court overruled the motion.

Then the Attorney asked for peremptory instructions for the defense; and the Court overruled the ask.

Whereupon the Court took its pen in hand and instructed the Jury that if it believed Tom Manns guilty of "shooting and wounding J. B. Farrow with intent to kill," it would find a verdict giving him not less than one nor more than five years in the Pen.

Counsel on both sides submitted the case, and the Jury, at the expiration of ten-and-a-half minutes, returned a verdict for five years residence at Frankfort.

Ed. Morris, the remaining criminal, was brought in, both sides accepted the panel and announced ready, the Jury was sworn, the Clerk read the indictment, Morris entered a plea of Guilty, and the Jury gave him five years in the Pen.

All three will be tried today on the charge of burglary, the penalty for which is from two to ten years; and it is possible they may plead guilty.

If Mr. Farrow should die within a year, these men can be released from their present sentences and tried for his murder.

The citizens of Maysville and Mason county are to be congratulated on the outcome of these trials. Disorder gave way to peace and security; the mob spirit has been suppressed, and Law reigns supreme. To the accomplishment of these ends, the family of the victim have lent a strong influence, 'Squire Sam T. Farrow and his brother R. C. Farrow counseling obedience to the law and proving themselves most exemplary citizens under the most trying circumstances.

TROOPS TAKE NEGROESTOPRISON
MAYSVILLE, Ky., June 19.—The three negroes who were sentenced to five years for assaulting the Farrow family, were tried to-day for burglary as the Farrows were robbed at the time of the assault.

Morris and Mann were found guilty and sentenced to ten years each on the charge of burglary. The burglarly charge against Sanders was continued. This makes an accumulative sentence against Mann and Morris of fifteen eyars each and against Sanders of five years. The charge of murder against Mann and Morris may be tried if Farrow shall die within one year and one day from the shooting. He is now in Lexington asylum. The prisoners left here this afternoon on a special train for Frankfort, accompanied by the troops.

QUAKES ACCOMPANIED STORM.

Houses Rocked and People Were Frightened Into Panic.

LONDON, June 19.—The storm off Carnarvon, Wales, to-day, was accompanied by two strong earth shocks. The inhabitants were alarmed by the rocking of their houses but no damage was reported. The earth shocks were so severe at Bangor, North Whales, that the patients were carried out of the hospital into the grounds and the congregation, badly frightened, evacuated the Cathedral.

COLORED SHOOTER ARRESTED.

[Special Telegram to the Register.]
CLARKSBURG, W. Va., June 19.—Dury Banks, colored, was arrested here this afternoon by Chief Howe as he was boarding a train to go to Fairmont and taken to jail. He will be sent to Tyreconnel to stand trial for feloniously shooting a man at that place. Banks is the fellow who was shot by Roy Green, colored, here a few weeks ago.

TRUST CO. OF THE REPUBLIC
REDUCES DIRECTORY BOARD.

NEW YORK, June 19.—A meeting of the stockholders and reorganization committee of the Trust Co. of the Republic was held here to-day. The proposition to reduce the number of directors from twenty-five to thirteen was unanimously adopted.

SEWICKLY GOLF
MATCH POSTPONED.

PITTSBURG; Pa., June 19.—The finals between the sixteen eladers in the preliminary golf club contest of the Allegheny Country Club's open tournament at Sewickley Heights, was postponed on account of rain. The matches will be resumed Saturday.
tom-manns-maysville-1903-02-03.A18:
TROOPS GUARD AT TRIAL.
Negro Murderer, Makes Confession at Maysville, Ky., and Receives a Light Sentence.

Maysville, Ky., June 19.—The trial of the three negroes for murderously assaulting the Farrow family continued Thursday with the troops holding the large crowd at bay. Sanders one of the negros, took the stand in his own defense. He testified that Mann was the leader, and on the day of the assault called for the witness in a buggy. En route to the Farrow farm Morris was picked up at a cemetery, where he was in waiting. When they reached the Farrow home, he (Sanders) held the horse While Mann and Morris entered the house. He heard the noise and then the shooting, after which all returned to Maysville in the rig. After this confession the attorneys of Sanders withrew the plea of not guilty, and Sanders pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to five years in the penitentiary.

TEXAS MOB ACTS

SEVERAL HUNDRED MEN FORCE THE JAIL WITH A POLE.

Take Out a Negro Prisoner and Hang Him to a Tree.

Marshall, Tex., Oct. 1.—Tonight a mob of several hundred men forced their way through the brick wall of the city jail with the aid of a telephone pole and with sledge hammers and crowbars, took out Walter Davis, a negro, and marched him to the west side of town, where he was hanged.

The lynching was the result of the killing of Constable Hayes this morning while he was taking a negro to jail. Hayes was shot from ambush, being literally riddled with bullets. Shortly after the killing of the constable, Davis and two other negroes were arrested and lodged in jail at Marshall. A mob formed during the afternoon and attacked the jail. The Marshall musketeers were ordered and arrived at the jail after the mo bhad secured the negro.

BIDS ARE OPENED.

Two Companies Make Identical Offers on Battleships.

Washington, Oct. 1.—Bids were opened at the navy department today for 16,639 tons or armor for the battleships Vermont, Minnesota, Kansas, Mississippi and Idaho. The bids of the Carnegie Steel company and the Bethlehem Steel company were identical, namely $6,944,000, delivery to begin in nine months. The only other bidder was the Midvale Steel company, whose bid was $6,606,932, delivery to begin within twenty months.

DECLARE A LOCKOUT.

Assert That the Union Violated an Agreement.

Chicago, Oct. 1.—The Chicago Typothetae has decided to declare a lockout of press feeders in 460 book and job printing offices Monday morning.

Twenty-five hundred men will be locked out, the employers declaring that the union violated an agreement in presenting demands for wage increase without extending a notice six months in advance that a change was desired.

CONSTABLE SHOT WITH MANY BULLETS
As a Result Mob Batters Down Jail Doors and Hangs Negro to a Tree.
(By Associated Press.)

MARSHALL, TEX., October 1.—A mob of several hundred men to-night battered its way into the jail, took out Walter Davis, a negro, and marched him to the west side of town, where he was hanged to a tree.

The lynching was the result of the killing of Constable Hayes to-day while he was taking a negro to jail. The officer was shot from ambush, being literally riddled with bullets. Shortly after the killing, Walter Davis and two other negroes were arrested and lodged in jail at Marshall.

A mob formed during the afternoon and attacked the jail. The local militia was ordered out, and arrived at the jail after the mob had secured the negro. While part of the mob was talking to the militia officers, others slipped the negro out and spirited him away. Everything is now quiet.

GENERAL NEWS.
— Mrs. Jefferson Davis is rapidly recovering from her illness.

— A tornado at St. Charles, Minn., killed seven persons and destroyed many buildings.

— Tornado visits Wisconsin and many buildings at Plainfield destroyed. Several lives lost.

— Raleigh, N. C., has decided to establish one dispensary in lieu of barrooms. The new law goes into effect on January 1, 1904.

— Hon. Wilson S. Bissel, former postmaster general under Cleveland, died at his home in Buffalo, N. Y., on Tuesday, 6th inst.

— Negroes at Luxora, Ark., on Friday night took a negro from the county jail and lynched him. The negro was charged with assaulting two little girls.

— A crazy man named Elliott, from Minneapolis, called at the White House to see the president and when refused admittance became violent and tried to shoot the guards at the door.

— Two attempts have been made within the past week in Montana to wreck the trains of the Northern Pacific railroad by putting dynamite on the track.

— The New York supreme court has decided that a notary public comes within the provisions of the State law forbidding officers from accepting free passes from railroads.

— Porto Rico sent to the United States within a year $7,466,579 worth of sugar and Hawaii $25,310,684 worth. These two amounts equal one-fifth of the sugar we consumed.

— Walter Davis, colored, was taken from jail at Marshall, Texas, on Thursday night by a mob and was hanged. He was lynched for killing Marshal Hayes, whom he shot from ambush.

— Two worthless sons of J. A. Scott, a confectioner, of Richmond, Va., have been arrested on suspicion of having murdered their father, who was shot and killed in his store on Saturday night.

— The Turks and Bulgarians have been fighting, with heavy losses on both sides. Russia and Austria have served notice to Turkey that they will insist on those reforms which were accepted by the sultan.

— At Starke, Fla., a negro named William Tison was presented with two boys and two girls by his wife Sunday morning about 8 o'clock. The babies had regular features every way, but only lived about six hours.

— The announcement is made, that by the will of Dr. Washington West, of St. Louis, Mo., who died in August, one half of his estate, the whole of which is valued at $250,000, is left to the Southern Presbyterian Church.

— Negroes of Pine Bluff, Ark., invite former President Grover Cleveland to visit the Normal school at that place, in the event of a trip South by him. Mr. Cleveland says he is not contemplating a trip South just now.

— Fifteen new indictments have been returned at Washington as the final result of the postal scandal investigation. James N. Tyner, late assistant attorney general of the post-office department, is one of those indicted.

— Gen. Bradley T. Johnson, a gallant Confederate general who served under Stonewall Jackson, died at the home of his son, Bradley S. Johnson, in Virginia, on Monday morning, 5th inst., of Brights disease, in the 75th year of his age.

— Statistics for September show that 47,852 aliens arrived at Ellis Island, New York, during the month, being an excess over the corresponding month last year of 5,543. October opened with the arrival of 3,013 for the first two days.

— At the opening of the New York public schools it was found that there were no accommodations for 65,000 pupils, which will be put on half time. The reason is that the school buildings ordered by the Board are incomplete in consequence of strikes.

— Louisiana will make a wonderful exhibit of cotton at the World's Fair at St. Louis. A field of the growing staple will show visitors from the North the beauty of a cotton plantation. A miniature cotton gin will be in operation and a small press will form the lint into miniature bales. A cotton oil press will illustrate how the cotton seed oil is made.

— The handsome monument erected at Orchard Knob to the joint memory of the Federal and Confederate troops of Maryland, who fought and fell on the historic battlefields about Missionary Ridge, was dedicated with impressive ceremonies in the presence of a large delegation of prominent men from Maryland and distinguished visitors from Georgia, North Carolina, Alabama and Tennessee, including several governors accompanied by their staffs.

Advertiser Bureau. Salme April 9

This afternoon about 2 o'clock there was excitement and plenty of it along the river front. The occasion was the sight of a negro struggling in the water near the south bank of the river while five or six young white men were standing on the bank threatening to cut his throat at the same time brandishing a razor before his eyes.

The negro who fortunately caught on some limbs of a tree tells one story while another is gleaned from parties who were in that vicinity, but who declare they were not eye witnesses to the affair. The negro's name is Will Baker. He is a strapping six-footer and says that he was coming up the river in his boat when he noticed six white men on the bank shooting craps. He was watching the game when one of the men asked him if he didn't have some money. He pulled $3 out of his pocket and he claims the young white men set upon him and after taking his money away from him struck him with a stick and threw him into the river. One of the young men had a razor and kept threatening to cut his throat.

The story that is most credited is that the negro came along and asked to be allowed to get in the game. This was at first refused, but finally he was allowed to come in and having a streak of luck won all the money from the white men. They then demanded that he give it up and upon his refusal he was set upon and the money taken away from him. Then fearing that such an act might get them in trouble they threw him in the river and would possibly have killed him had they not been frightened away.

Where the affair occurred has of late been made a rendezvous for crap shooters. Today several of the employes of the Estelle cotton mills took a day off and went across the river for a sort of picnic. Four young men were arrested at the ball park, but the negro who suffered violence says they were not in the crowd. The names of the other six are known to the authorities and they will perhaps be rounded up.
